entries.title: Corporate sends MT101 for EUR 120,000, bank cannot read the extra data
entries.text: Corporate sends MT101 for EUR 120,000, bank cannot read the extra data Foundations A corporate sends an MT101 for EUR 120,000. It wants to attach rich remittance data for its supplier. The MT101 has no room for it. The supplier is paid, but cannot match the payment. Here is how that happens: → MT101 sent, customer to bank, ISO 15022 flat files and tags → Corporate needs richer data for the supplier → MT101 cannot carry it → pain.001, ISO 20022 XML, holds far more information The assumption was: "MT101 and pain.001 are the same instruction in different wrapping." Both messages carry credit transfer instructions to the bank, but they are built on different standards. Why? The MT101 leg rests on ISO 15022, a SWIFT MT message built on flat files and tags, while pain.001 is built on ISO 20022, with XML files and message elements. ISO 20022 is far richer, so pain.001 holds far more information than MT101 can, and the supplier matching fails on the thinner message. Same instruction,

entries.title: MT101 sent for EUR 90,000, team waits for money that has not moved
entries.text: MT101 sent for EUR 90,000, team waits for money that has not moved Foundations A corporate sends an MT101 for EUR 90,000. The beneficiary bank waits for the money. Nothing arrives. The team is waiting on an instruction, not a payment. Here is how that happens: → MT101 goes out before execution, customer to bank → Ordering bank receives the instruction → Ordering account debited → MT103 follows, bank to bank, moving the money The assumption was: "MT101 moves the money." MT101 belongs to the customer-to-bank space and MT103 to the interbank space. Why? An MT101 goes out before execution, carrying the payment instruction to the ordering bank. The MT103 follows as the next step, leaving the ordering bank for the beneficiary or correspondent banks after the ordering account has been debited. Waiting for funds on an MT101 is waiting on the wrong message. MT101 instructs. MT103 moves the money. Why does the beneficiary wait for money an MT101 can never bring? BA Takeaway Read MT101 as an

entries.title: EUR 600 mandate unused for three years, no one told the creditor
entries.text: EUR 600 mandate unused for three years, no one told the creditor Foundations A creditor holds a mandate for EUR 600 a month. No collection runs under it for three years. On the fourth year the creditor sends a collection. It is rejected. The mandate expired silently. Here is how that happens: → Mandate signed for EUR 600 monthly collections → 36 months pass with no orders related to it → Mandate expires after 36 months with no orders → No message tells any party it expired The assumption was: "A mandate lasts until someone cancels it." A SEPA mandate expires after 36 months with no orders related to it. Why? Expiry triggers no SWIFT message to any party. The mandate simply lapses quietly after three years without use, so a creditor that does not track inactivity discovers the expiry only when the next collection is rejected. Silent expiry, loud rejection. Why does a mandate nobody cancelled stop working? BA Takeaway Track mandate inactivity like a deadline, and warn long before the 36

entries.title: EUR 15,000 on-us transfer built on a different standard, breaks reconciliation
entries.text: EUR 15,000 on-us transfer built on a different standard, breaks reconciliation Foundations A bank moves EUR 15,000 between two accounts it holds itself. A team builds it on a different message standard from interbank payments. Reconciliation breaks, because the two standards do not line up. The payment never left the bank. Here is how that happens: → On-us transfer, both accounts in the same bank → Team uses a separate standard for intrabank traffic → Interbank traffic uses the standard ISO 20022 set → Reconciliation fails across the two standards The assumption was: "Inside the bank, any standard will do." Intrabank book transfers run on the same standard messages as interbank ones. Why? For a SEPA credit transfer that means the standard ISO 20022 set. Running different standards for interbank and intrabank traffic would create many problems over the long term, so an on-us transfer travels on the same message standards as any other payment. Same bank, same standard. Why does a

entries.title: EUR 8,000 foreign cheque, the bank cannot tell what type it is
entries.text: EUR 8,000 foreign cheque, the bank cannot tell what type it is Foundations A customer deposits a cheque for EUR 8,000 from another country. The deposit slip says "foreign cheque". The bank cannot process it. Foreign is not a complete type. Here is how that happens: → Cheque arrives from another country, EUR 8,000 → Recorded as a foreign cheque, no type named → Clearing team asks: bank cheque or order cheque? → No answer on the slip, processing stalls The assumption was: "Foreign is a type of cheque." Foreign on its own is not a complete cheque type. Why? A cheque from another country still carries a type in that country, so it may be a foreign bank cheque, or equally a foreign order cheque. The word foreign only says where the cheque comes from, and the type must be named as well, or clearing cannot decide how to handle it. Origin is not type. Why does a cheque with a clear origin stall in clearing? BA Takeaway Record origin and type as two separate fields, and never let one stand in

entries.title: USD 2,000,000 trade, no rule says which instrument comes first
entries.text: USD 2,000,000 trade, no rule says which instrument comes first Foundations A buyer and seller agree a USD 2,000,000 trade. The buyer asks which instrument starts it, letter of credit or bank guarantee. There is no rule that answers that. The team waits for a rule that does not exist. Here is how that happens: → Trade agreed for USD 2,000,000 → Buyer asks for the first instrument → Team searches the rulebook for a fixed order → No rule fixes which instrument a trade starts with The assumption was: "The rules pick the first instrument." No rule fixes which instrument a trade starts with, whether a letter of credit or a bank guarantee. Why? The choice depends on many factors, above all how much security both parties want. Greater appetite for security on both sides calls for more sophisticated payment techniques, so the answer is a judgement about the parties, not a lookup in a rulebook. Security appetite picks the instrument, not a rule. Why does the team wait for a rule that cannot

entries.title: Approved in one click, EUR 75,000 never reached the supplier
entries.text: Approved in one click, EUR 75,000 never reached the supplier Core A maker raised a corporate payment of EUR 75,000 in one click. Workflow approved it. The supplier never received it. Here is what happened: → Maker initiates the payment → Preprocessor checks entitlement, account, limits, fees and payee → Workflow approves the payment → Bank screening holds it → Account never debited, network never clears it, ledger never closes it The requirement said: "Once workflow approves, the payment is sent." So the screen showed approved, and everyone assumed the money was on its way. Why? Fifteen steps and nine decisions stand between maker and ledger. Every Yes moves the payment forward, and every No stops or re-routes it. A No at bank screening stops the payment after approval, and an approved payment that never clears is still an unpaid payment. Approval is not settlement. BA Takeaway Approval, screening, debit, clearing and ledger posting are separate stages, so keep them separate: →

entries.title: EUR 300,000 corporate payment, stuck between channel and core banking
entries.text: EUR 300,000 corporate payment, stuck between channel and core banking Core A corporate sends EUR 300,000 through its channel. The payment never reaches core banking. Nobody can say where it stopped. There are seven hand-offs, and no one owns the gaps between them. Here is how that happens: → Corporate channel starts the payment → API gateway, entry point into the bank systems → Validation, payment checked before it moves on → Payment hub, central processing → Compliance screening, a failed screen stops the payment here → Routing and clearing, then core banking debit and credit posting The assumption was: "A payment flows in one smooth line from channel to ledger." A corporate payment starts in a channel, passes an API gateway, validation and the payment hub, then compliance screening, routing and clearing, and finally the core banking debit and credit posting. Why? Each hand-off is a place where the payment can be checked, enriched or stopped. That chain of hand-offs is what makes the

entries.title: VND 500,000,000 domestic payment, nothing reaches the rail until the preprocessor clears it
entries.text: VND 500,000,000 domestic payment, nothing reaches the rail until the preprocessor clears it Core A corporate in Vietnam sends VND 500,000,000 to a supplier. The payment sits, unmoving, for hours. The rail is fine. The beneficiary bank is fine. The payment never cleared the preprocessor. Here is how that happens: → Corporate initiates the payment → Preprocessor, the central control point → Payment hub, central processing after the preprocessor → NAPAS, the domestic rail in Vietnam → Beneficiary bank credits the beneficiary The assumption was: "The rail carries the payment, so check the rail first." In a domestic payment in Vietnam, the payment preprocessor is the central control point. Why? The flow runs from the corporate, through the preprocessor, to the payment hub, then NAPAS, then the beneficiary bank. Nothing reaches the rail until the preprocessor has cleared it, so a payment stuck before the rail looks like a rail failure from the outside. The gate is before the rail. Why does

entries.title: VND 200,000,000 sent in Vietnam, supplier says it never arrived
entries.text: VND 200,000,000 sent in Vietnam, supplier says it never arrived Core A corporate sends VND 200,000,000 to a supplier in Vietnam. The channel says sent. The supplier says nothing arrived. The payment is somewhere in the middle, and reconciliation is the only proof of where. Here is how that happens: → Channel, where the payment is sent from → Core banking, payment enters the bank core → Payment hub, central processing and control → Validation and routing, checked, then routed → NAPAS, the domestic rail that carries it → Receiving bank, then reconciliation The assumption was: "Sent means arrived." A domestic payment in Vietnam moves from the channel to core banking, then the payment hub, validation and routing, NAPAS, the receiving bank and reconciliation. Why? Each stage has a job, and reconciliation at the end proves the money arrived where it should. A payment that is only tracked to the rail has no proof at the far end, so the supplier's word and the channel's word disagree with

entries.title: VND 800,000,000 payment, a duplicate slips past six checks
entries.text: VND 800,000,000 payment, a duplicate slips past six checks Core A corporate sends VND 800,000,000 in Vietnam. The same payment is sent twice by mistake. Six checks pass. The duplicate check is the one that matters. It catches it, minutes before the money moves twice. Here is how that happens: → Account validation, account exists and is valid → Format check, message format is correct → Authorisation check, payment is properly authorised → Limits, AML and sanctions, all checked → Duplicate check, payment is not a repeat → Routing and enrichment, then it moves on The assumption was: "Any one check is enough. They all check the same thing." Before a domestic payment moves on, the preprocessor runs the full gate: account, format, authorisation, limits, AML and sanctions, duplicates, routing and enrichment. Why? Those checks are the reason a payment can be trusted to reach the right account. Each check catches a different failure, and the duplicate check is the only one that sees a payment

entries.title: EUR 400,000 cross-border payment, rejected three times, preprocessor was missing
entries.text: EUR 400,000 cross-border payment, rejected three times, preprocessor was missing Core A bank sends EUR 400,000 across borders. It is rejected three times. Each rejection names a different fault. There was no control tower watching the payment before it left. Here is how that happens: → Payment prepared, no preprocessor in the flow → Sent with thin data, no enrichment → Compliance check fails downstream → Wrong route, rejected again, then rejected a third time The assumption was: "Each system checks its own part, so no one needs to watch the whole payment." In cross-border payments the preprocessor is the control tower: it validates, enriches, checks compliance, routes and processes the payment, so fewer payments are rejected and more go straight through. Why? A strong preprocessor is what makes straight-through processing possible. Without it, each fault is found by a different system downstream, and the payment is rejected again and again for faults one gate would have caught

entries.title: EUR 250,000 payment fails, every layer says the fault is in another layer
entries.text: EUR 250,000 payment fails, every layer says the fault is in another layer Core A EUR 250,000 payment fails. The technical team blames the data. The data team blames the business rules. The business team blames compliance. Every layer is pointing at another layer. Here is how that happens: → Technical layer, format and transport → Payment data layer, fields and values → Business layer, rules and limits → Compliance layer, screening and sanctions → Routing layer, path and destination The assumption was: "Validation is one check. Find it and fix it." Preprocessor validation works in layers: technical, payment data, business, compliance and routing. Why? Each layer catches a different kind of error, and the full lifecycle runs from initiation through to settlement and reconciliation. A failure with no layer named is a failure nobody owns, so each team blames the next layer down. Name the layer, own the fault. Why does every team blame another layer for the same failed payment? entries.title: EUR 600,000 payment enters GPP, vanishes before the rail
entries.text: EUR 600,000 payment enters GPP, vanishes before the rail Core A EUR 600,000 payment enters the payment hub. It is parsed, validated, mapped and screened. Then it vanishes. The rail never sees it, and core banking never posts it. Here is how that happens: → Channel, where the payment starts → API gateway and message queue, entry and queuing → GPP parse and validate, parsed, validated and duplicate-checked → Map to ISO 20022, payment mapped to the rich data standard → Compliance screening, screened before routing → Route to SWIFT or domestic rail, then acknowledge, post and reconcile The assumption was: "Once it is inside GPP, the payment is safe." From a Tech BA view, a payment flows from the channel through the API gateway and message queue into GPP, where it is parsed, validated, checked for duplicates, mapped to ISO 20022, screened for compliance, routed to a SWIFT or domestic rail, acknowledged, and finally posted to core banking with reconciliation. Why? Exceptions are handled at

entries.title: EUR 600,000 GPP payment, the mapping that nobody tested
entries.text: EUR 600,000 GPP payment, the mapping that nobody tested Core A EUR 600,000 payment goes through GPP. The ISO 20022 mapping was never tested with this message type. The payment fails at mapping, is routed wrong, and posts twice. Three failures, one untested stage. Here is how that happens: → ISO 20022 mapping, mapping can fail or delay the payment → Routing, wrong route delays or fails the payment → Duplicate handling, duplicates must be caught before posting → Core banking integration, integration gaps stall the payment → Testing and reconciliation, each stage needs its own proof The assumption was: "Test the flow end to end and every stage is covered." The GPP end-to-end flow has real implementation challenges: ISO 20022 mapping, routing, duplicates, core banking integration, testing and reconciliation. Why? Each of these is a place where a payment can fail or be delayed, and each needs its own design and test coverage. An end-to-end test that passes on the happy path proves nothing

entries.title: EUR 180,000 corporate payment, the issue has no stage to belong to
entries.text: EUR 180,000 corporate payment, the issue has no stage to belong to Core A EUR 180,000 corporate payment fails. The support team cannot say where. They have no list of stages to place it against. The issue floats, unowned, for two days. Here is how that happens: → Initiation, payment origination starts the journey → Validation, payment checked before it moves on → Compliance, checked before routing → Routing, payment routed to the right rail → Clearing, payment cleared through the network → Settlement, funds move to complete the payment → Posting and reporting, final posting closes the journey The assumption was: "Knowing the flow in general is enough to find a failure." In corporate banking, GPP runs a nine-step journey from payment origination to settlement and reporting. Why? The steps cover initiation, validation, compliance, routing, clearing, and the final posting and reporting. Knowing the nine steps lets a BA place any issue at the right stage, and without the list, an issue

entries.title: EUR 500,000 on four rails, four views, one customer asking where it is
entries.text: EUR 500,000 on four rails, four views, one customer asking where it is Core A bank runs EUR 500,000 a day across four rails. Domestic, cross-border, real-time and high-value each have their own view. A customer asks where a payment is. Four teams give four answers. Here is how that happens: → Domestic payment, one platform view → Cross-border payment, another view → Real-time payment, a third view → High-value payment, a fourth view → Same customer, same question, four different answers The assumption was: "Each rail needs its own platform and its own controls." GPP orchestrates multiple payment types and rails from one platform: domestic, cross-border, real-time and high-value payments, with routing, compliance and reconciliation. Why? One platform means one set of controls and one view of the payment, whatever the rail. Separate platforms give each rail its own truth, and the customer hears all four at once. One platform, one view, whatever the rail. Why do four teams give four

entries.title: EUR 750,000 cross-border payment, the weakest hand-off breaks it
entries.text: EUR 750,000 cross-border payment, the weakest hand-off breaks it Core A EUR 750,000 cross-border payment crosses seven hand-offs. Six are strong. One is weak. The payment fails at the weak one. The integration was judged by its best hand-off. Here is how that happens: → Initiation, payment starts in the channel → Validation and enrichment, checked and enriched → Compliance, checked before routing → Routing and orchestration, routed across rails from one platform → ISO 20022 and SWIFT, mapped and sent → Exceptions, handled when a stage fails → Settlement and reconciliation, settled, then reconciled The assumption was: "Most hand-offs strong means the integration is strong." GPP integration in cross-border payments covers initiation, validation and enrichment, compliance, routing and orchestration, ISO 20022 and SWIFT, exceptions, and settlement with reconciliation. Why? Each stage is a hand-off, and the integration is only as strong as the weakest hand-off. A chain judged by its

entries.title: EUR 900,000 payment works, the lending product beside it breaks
entries.text: EUR 900,000 payment works, the lending product beside it breaks Core A BA fixes a EUR 900,000 payment flow. The payment works. A lending product that shares the same platform breaks the same week. The BA never looked beyond payments. Here is how that happens: → Payment flow fixed, tested, working → Wider platform untouched, never reviewed → Lending product shares platform services → Change in payments breaks lending, no one saw the link The assumption was: "Payments is the whole platform." The banking technology platform is a banking ecosystem, broader than a payment processor alone. Why? Its products cover more of the bank than payments, so a BA working with the platform must understand the wider platform, not only the payment flow. A change that is safe inside payments can break a product that shares its services, and the BA who never looked wider never sees the link. Payments is one part of the platform. Why does a safe payments change break lending? BA Takeaway Map the wider

entries.title: EUR 1,200,000 a day, channels connected, hub never reached
entries.text: EUR 1,200,000 a day, channels connected, hub never reached Core A bank connects its channels and systems to the payment hub. EUR 1,200,000 a day should flow end to end. It does not. The plumbing was connected, but the nine-step journey was never tested through it. Here is how that happens: → Channels and systems connected to the hub → Payment enters the channel → Hub receives it, journey should run end to end → One hand-off in the middle was never wired, journey stalls The assumption was: "Connecting the systems is the same as connecting the journey." Integration connects the bank's channels and systems to the payment hub so that a payment can flow end to end. Why? The integration is the plumbing that makes the nine-step journey possible, but plumbing alone is not a journey. A connection that was never tested end to end leaves a hand-off unwired, and the payment stalls in the middle of a flow everyone believed was connected. Connected systems, disconnected journey. entries.title: EUR 50,000 paid twice, the retry had no idempotency key
entries.text: EUR 50,000 paid twice, the retry had no idempotency key Core A customer retries a EUR 50,000 payment after a timeout. The retry succeeds. So does the first attempt, a second later. EUR 100,000 leaves the account for a EUR 50,000 payment. Here is how that happens: → First call times out, outcome unknown → Customer retries the same payment → API has no idempotency protection → Both calls post, EUR 50,000 paid twice The assumption was: "A retry is safe. The system will know it is the same payment." A reliable payment API rests on stateless validation, synchronous fraud and risk checks, idempotency, metadata-driven configuration, orchestration, compliance and reconciliation. Why? Idempotency matters because a retried call must never create a duplicate payment. Without it, a timeout plus a retry is a duplicate by design, and the second posting is not a system error, it is the missing control. A retry without idempotency is a second payment. Why does a careful retry double the payment? BA

entries.title: EUR 200,000 API change, the endpoint looked simple, the blast radius was not
entries.text: EUR 200,000 API change, the endpoint looked simple, the blast radius was not Core A team changes an API endpoint for a EUR 200,000 payment flow. The endpoint looks simple, one field added. Three downstream systems break. Nobody mapped the consumers. Here is how that happens: → Endpoint changed, one field added → Data, consumers and dependencies never mapped → Downstream systems read the changed payload → Three break, each in a different way The assumption was: "The endpoint is the API." Analysing an API means looking beyond the endpoint. Why? A BA must understand the data, the consumers, the dependencies and the impact of a change, because an API that looks simple at the endpoint can have deep downstream effects. The endpoint is only the surface, and the blast radius lives underneath it. The endpoint is only the surface. Why does one added field break three systems? BA Takeaway Map data, consumers, dependencies and impact before any API change ships. Keep these controls separate: →

entries.title: EUR 350,000 requirement written without API knowledge, misses the payload gap
entries.text: EUR 350,000 requirement written without API knowledge, misses the payload gap Core A BA writes a requirement for a EUR 350,000 payment flow. The requirement looks complete. Development finds a payload gap on day one. The BA could not see it, because the API was never understood. Here is how that happens: → Requirement written from the business view only → Endpoints, payloads and data gaps never examined → Impact, security and backward compatibility never assessed → Development stalls on a gap the requirement never named The assumption was: "Business requirements do not need API knowledge." A BA who understands APIs can work with endpoints, payloads, data gaps, impact analysis, security and backward compatibility. Why? Without that knowledge, the BA cannot write a complete requirement or assess the impact of a change. The gap is not a development surprise, it is a requirement that was written blind to the API it describes. A requirement without API knowledge is incomplete by

entries.title: EUR 4,000 collection due Friday, creditor bank closed, collection never sent
entries.text: EUR 4,000 collection due Friday, creditor bank closed, collection never sent Core A creditor plans a EUR 4,000 collection for Friday. The debtor bank is open. The scheme is open. The creditor bank is closed for a holiday. The collection is never sent. Here is how that happens: → Due date arrives, Friday → Debtor PSP open, ready to debit → Creditor PSP closed on the due date → Collection cannot be submitted into the scheme that day The assumption was: "If the debtor bank is open, the collection can run." If the creditor PSP is closed on the due date, the collection cannot be submitted into the scheme on that date, even if the debtor PSP is open. Why? The creditor-side processing constraint moves the collection to the next business day. The creditor must plan for its own closure days, not just the debtor's, because its own calendar is a hard gate on submission. Your own holiday stops your own collection. Why does a collection fail when the debtor bank is open and ready? BA Takeaway Plan

entries.title: EUR 4,000 collection due Friday, debtor bank closed, debit lands Monday
entries.text: EUR 4,000 collection due Friday, debtor bank closed, debit lands Monday Core A creditor sends a EUR 4,000 collection for Friday. The creditor bank is open. The scheme is open. The debtor bank is closed for a holiday. The debit lands on Monday, and the creditor had promised the money for Friday. Here is how that happens: → Due date arrives, Friday → Creditor PSP open, collection submitted → Debtor PSP closed on the due date → Debtor account cannot be debited that day, debit moves to Monday The assumption was: "Submitted on Friday means debited on Friday." If the debtor PSP is closed on the due date, the debtor account cannot be debited on that date, so the debit moves to the next business day the debtor PSP is open. Why? The collection is not lost, but the timing shifts, and the creditor must know which date the debit will actually happen. This is why the debtor PSP calendar matters as much as the creditor's: it fixes the real debit date. Submitted is not debited. Why does a Friday

entries.title: EUR 12,000 in collections due, both banks open, clearing closed
entries.text: EUR 12,000 in collections due, both banks open, clearing closed Core EUR 12,000 in collections is due today. Both banks are open and working. Nothing settles. The clearing mechanism between them is closed. Here is how that happens: → Due date arrives, collections ready → Creditor PSP open, debtor PSP open → Clearing and settlement mechanism closed on the due date → Collections cannot be submitted and settled that day The assumption was: "If both banks are open, the payment can settle." The clearing and settlement mechanism is the infrastructure that moves collections between the creditor PSP and the debtor PSP. Why? If it is closed on the due date, the collections cannot be submitted and settled that day, even when both banks are open and working. Both banks being open is not enough: the infrastructure between them must also be open, so the mechanism's calendar belongs in every collection plan. Two open banks, one closed road between them. entries.title: EUR 950 debited with permission, customer wants it back in week seven
entries.text: EUR 950 debited with permission, customer wants it back in week seven Core A debtor authorised a direct debit of EUR 950. Seven weeks after the debit, the debtor asks for the money back. The creditor calls it an exception. It is not an exception. It is a scheme right. Here is how that happens: → Debtor authorises the collection of EUR 950 → Debit happens, collection completes → Week seven, debtor asks for a refund → Creditor treats the request as a dispute The assumption was: "An authorised debit cannot be refunded." When a debtor authorised a SEPA Direct Debit collection, they can ask for a refund within eight weeks of the debit date. Why? The eight-week rule is the stated scheme position, but the exact application can vary by jurisdiction, so it must be checked against the current rulebook. A refund inside this window is a normal scheme right, not an exception, and treating it as a dispute delays a right the debtor already holds. Authorised does not mean unrefundable. Why does a

entries.title: EUR 1,100 taken without authorisation, claim arrives in month twelve
entries.text: EUR 1,100 taken without authorisation, claim arrives in month twelve Core A debtor finds a direct debit of EUR 1,100 on the statement. The debtor never authorised it. Twelve months have passed. The creditor says it is too late. It is not. Here is how that happens: → Direct debit of EUR 1,100 taken, no authorisation behind it → Debtor discovers it months later → Claim filed in month twelve → Creditor handles it as an authorised refund, and refuses it The assumption was: "All refunds work the same way, with the same window." When a debtor says a direct debit was never authorised, they can claim a refund for up to 13 months after the debit. Why? The 13-month period is the stated scheme position, and the precise legal and scheme conditions must be checked against the current rulebook. An unauthorised claim is a different process from an authorised refund, with a longer window and different evidence, so the two must never be handled as one case type. Unauthorised is a different case, not a

entries.title: EUR 2,000 comes back, the ledger books it as the wrong event
entries.text: EUR 2,000 comes back, the ledger books it as the wrong event Core EUR 2,000 comes back after a direct debit. The ledger books it as a refund. It was a return, started by the debtor bank because the account could not be debited. The timeline, the message and the accounting are all wrong now. Here is how that happens: → Collection of EUR 2,000 presented → Debtor PSP cannot debit the account, sends it back → Team books it as a refund, debtor asked for money back → Real event was a return, different initiator, different rules The assumption was: "Money back is money back. One event covers them all." A return, a refund and a reversal are three different money-back events with different initiators, reasons, messages and accounting treatment. Why? A return is started by the debtor PSP, usually because the account cannot be debited. A refund is started by the debtor asking for money back. A reversal is started by the creditor PSP to undo a collection. Treating them as the same thing causes

entries.title: EUR 1,500 return and EUR 1,500 refund land the same day, team nets them
entries.text: EUR 1,500 return and EUR 1,500 refund land the same day, team nets them Core Two EUR 1,500 amounts land on the same day. One is a return, one is a refund. The team nets them and closes both cases. Both cases are still open, and both are now wrong. Here is how that happens: → Collection presented for EUR 1,500 → Debtor bank sends it back, insufficient funds, pacs.004 → Debtor asks for an authorised collection to be repaid, refund → Both arrive the same day and look similar The assumption was: "Same day, same amount, same event." A SEPA Direct Debit return and a refund can arrive on the same day and look similar, but they are different business events. Why? A return happens when the debtor bank sends the collection back, for example because the account has insufficient funds, and it travels as a pacs.004, while a refund happens when the debtor asks for an authorised collection to be repaid. Each has its own trigger, timeline and accounting treatment, so the system must handle them as

entries.title: EUR 3,200 collection returned, reason code unread for four days
entries.text: EUR 3,200 collection returned, reason code unread for four days Core A collection of EUR 3,200 is returned. The pacs.004 carries a reason code. Nobody on the returns team can read it consistently. The creditor finds out four days late, with no clear explanation. Here is how that happens: → Collection returned, pacs.004 arrives → Reason code inside pacs.004 explains why → Returns team interprets the code differently each time → Creditor learns days late, with no clear explanation The assumption was: "The return message is enough. The code will explain itself." When a direct debit collection is returned, the pacs.004 carries a reason code that explains why, and the scheme sets a timeline for when the return must happen. Why? The creditor needs to learn about the return quickly and understand whether the collection can be presented again. If the returns team cannot interpret the reason codes consistently, creditors find out days late with no clear explanation, so code interpretation is

entries.title: EUR 10,000 to a non-euro account, euro leg done in seconds, rest waits hours
entries.text: EUR 10,000 to a non-euro account, euro leg done in seconds, rest waits hours Core A customer sends EUR 10,000 from Europe to a non-euro account. The euro leg finishes in seconds. The customer expects the whole payment done. Nothing happens for hours while the other leg is processed. Here is how that happens: → Euro leg inside SEPA, completes in seconds → Non-euro leg outside SEPA, different rules, different timeline → Customer sees the euro leg finish, expects the whole payment done → Hours pass, nothing happens, other leg still processing The assumption was: "One payment, one speed, one status." In an instant cross-border payment from Europe, the euro leg inside SEPA can complete in seconds, but the non-euro leg outside SEPA follows different rules and a different timeline. Why? The two legs must be explained separately, with their own coverage and responsibilities, because a single status cannot describe two different journeys. A customer who only sees the fast leg believes the

entries.title: EUR 25,000 instant payment, three steps fast, one step slow, promise broken
entries.text: EUR 25,000 instant payment, three steps fast, one step slow, promise broken Core A bank promises EUR 25,000 instant payments. The channel is fast. The engine is fast. Clearing is fast. Settlement is slow. The customer promise breaks, even though three steps are instant. Here is how that happens: → Customer channel, fast → Payment engine, fast → Clearing, fast → Settlement, slow, the bottleneck → Customer waits, promise broken The assumption was: "The rail is instant, so the payment is instant." For an instant payment to feel instant end to end, every step must be fast: the customer channel, the payment engine, clearing and settlement. Why? If any one step is slow, the customer promise breaks even when the other steps are instant. The work is to find which step is the bottleneck and optimise it, rather than assuming the rail alone makes the payment instant. One slow step breaks an instant promise. Why does an instant rail still deliver a slow payment? BA Takeaway Find the bottleneck

entries.title: EUR 5,000 sent abroad, beneficiary receives EUR 4,850, rate never shown
entries.text: EUR 5,000 sent abroad, beneficiary receives EUR 4,850, rate never shown Core A customer sends EUR 5,000 abroad. The beneficiary receives EUR 4,850. The customer was never shown the rate, the fees, or how long the rate held. The price was agreed after the fact, which is no agreement at all. Here is how that happens: → Customer pays in a different currency, EUR 5,000 → Rate and fees not shown clearly before confirmation → Rate changes before the payment completes → Beneficiary credited a different amount, customer cannot reconcile it The assumption was: "The rate at the time is the rate the customer agreed to." When a customer pays in a different currency, they need to see the exchange rate, the fees, how long the rate is valid, and the exact amount the beneficiary will receive. Why? If the rate changes or the fees are not shown clearly, the beneficiary is credited a different amount and the customer cannot reconcile the payment. Transparency means showing the total cost and the applied

entries.title: EUR 30,000 to a supplier, paid in full, cannot be matched to any invoice
entries.text: EUR 30,000 to a supplier, paid in full, cannot be matched to any invoice Core A company pays a supplier EUR 30,000. The money arrives in full. The supplier cannot match it to any invoice. The payment carries no structured remittance data, so the cash sits unallocated. Here is how that happens: → Payment sent for EUR 30,000, payer, beneficiary and purpose attached → Remittance data unstructured or incomplete → Supplier cannot match the payment to the invoice → Screening cannot run properly on the thin data The assumption was: "Data quality is a formatting preference." Every cross-border payment carries payer, beneficiary, purpose and remittance data that the supplier needs to allocate the cash and that compliance screening depends on. Why? If the data is unstructured or incomplete, the supplier cannot match the payment to the invoice and the screening cannot run properly. Structured data is what makes a payment reconcilable and compliant at the same time, so data quality is a payment

entries.title: EUR 80,000 instant payment, FX quote expires while screening runs
entries.text: EUR 80,000 instant payment, FX quote expires while screening runs Core A bank sends EUR 80,000 instantly to a non-euro account. The FX quote is locked at 09:00. Screening runs long. At 09:04 the quote has expired, and the payment cannot settle at the promised rate. Here is how that happens: → Bank relies on an FX provider, no liquidity in every currency → Provider sources quotes, locks rates, executes conversion → Screening runs while the quote clock ticks → Quote expires, or the provider has no currency when needed The assumption was: "The FX provider will be there when the payment needs it." A bank that does not hold liquidity in every currency relies on an FX provider to source quotes, lock rates, execute the conversion and supply the settlement currency. Why? The arrangement works on quiet days, but a quote can expire while screening runs, or the provider may not have the currency when it is needed. The FX provider is a dependency in the payment chain, and its failure modes must

entries.title: USD 100,000 instant dollars promised, no dollars to settle with on Monday morning
entries.text: USD 100,000 instant dollars promised, no dollars to settle with on Monday morning Core A bank promises instant dollar payments. On Monday morning a customer sends USD 100,000. The rate is competitive. The system is ready. There are not enough dollars to settle with. Here is how that happens: → Bank offers instant dollar payments at a good rate → Customer sends USD 100,000 on Monday morning → Settlement currency not held in enough volume → Payment fails, not on price, on liquidity The assumption was: "A good rate means the payment can settle." Having a competitive exchange rate is not the same as having the settlement currency available at the moment it is needed. Why? A bank can offer instant dollar payments and still fail on some mornings because it does not hold enough dollars to settle. The constraint is liquidity, not conversion, and it must be managed by treasury, not just by the payment engine. Rate is not liquidity. Why does a payment with a great rate fail on a Monday morning?

entries.title: EUR 60,000 payment, app says pending, engine says processed, ledger says nothing
entries.text: EUR 60,000 payment, app says pending, engine says processed, ledger says nothing Core A customer sends EUR 60,000 abroad. The app says pending. The engine says processed. The ledger has no posting. Three systems, three truths, one customer on the phone. Here is how that happens: → Payment passes through several payment service providers → App says pending → Engine says processed → Ledger has no posting The assumption was: "Each system can use its own meaning of a status." When a cross-border payment passes through several payment service providers, each one can show a different status: the app says pending, the engine says processed, and the ledger has no posting. Why? The customer and the contact centre cannot tell whether the money has left, arrived, or is lost. The fix is consistent status meanings, a status enquiry path and clear customer communication at every step, because a payment whose state cannot be stated cannot be managed. Three statuses, no truth. Why can no one tell the

entries.title: EUR 45,000 across two instant systems, timeout, customer taps send again
entries.text: EUR 45,000 across two instant systems, timeout, customer taps send again Core A customer sends EUR 45,000 across two fast payment systems. The screen times out. The customer taps send again. Now the bank has two instructions and one debit, and nobody knows if the money moved. Here is how that happens: → Payment crosses two fast payment systems joined by an orchestration layer → Timeout occurs, outcome uncertain → Money may have moved, or it may not have → Customer taps send again, two instructions, one debit The assumption was: "A timeout means it failed, so sending again is safe." In a corridor where a payment crosses two fast payment systems joined by an orchestration layer, a timeout leaves the outcome uncertain: the money may have moved, or it may not have. Why? If the customer taps send again, the bank can end up with two instructions and one debit. The safe handling is to establish the true state, never retry blindly, and use an inter-PSP investigation to resolve the

entries.title: EUR 70,000 to a supplier, screen says pending, supplier says unpaid
entries.text: EUR 70,000 to a supplier, screen says pending, supplier says unpaid Core A company sends EUR 70,000 to a supplier. The screen says pending. The supplier says it has not been paid. The clerk cannot say where the money is, because the status hides every step in the middle. Here is how that happens: → Payment travels through a bank, a correspondent and the supplier bank → Customer screen shows only one status, usually Pending → Supplier says it has not been paid → Clerk cannot say where the money is The assumption was: "One status is enough for the customer." A payment that travels through a bank, a correspondent and the supplier bank shows only one status on the customer screen, usually Pending, while the supplier says it has not been paid. Why? The clerk cannot say where the money is because the status does not reflect the intermediary steps. Customer-facing statuses must stay accurate while the underlying processing is still pending, so the customer is not left guessing. Pending hides

entries.title: 90 percent of a remittance file lands in repair
entries.text: 90 percent of a remittance file lands in repair Core A corporate customer sends a daily remittance file with thousands of supplier payments, worth EUR 2.4 million. Around 90 percent of the payments land in the manual repair queue. The file is on time. The money is not. Here is how it happens: → File arrives with thousands of supplier payments → Account numbers fail the modulus check → Remittance information arrives incomplete or inconsistent → Payments drop into manual repair → The repair queue becomes the bottleneck The requirement said: "The repair team will handle the exceptions." Why? The data is bad at the source. The queue is a symptom of bad input, not of slow repair. Adding repair staff only feeds a bigger queue. The queue is a symptom, not the problem. BA Takeaway Fix the data at the source. Repair capacity is the last control, not the first. Keep these controls separate: → Source data quality → Validation at capture → Repair capacity The real requirement is not "How fast can

entries.title: The reject reason the customer must never see
entries.text: The reject reason the customer must never see Core A EUR 50,000 payment is rejected. Inside the bank, the reason is precise: the account is closed. The customer is told the same words. In that country, sharing it breaks the privacy rules. Here is how it happens: → Payment is rejected → Internal reason recorded: account closed → Privacy rules differ by country → The reason is shown to the customer without a country check → Sensitive information is exposed The requirement said: "Show the customer the reject reason." Why? The internal diagnostic reason can be precise and sensitive, and privacy rules differ by country. A reason that is safe to show in one country can be a breach in another. Precise inside, careful outside. BA Takeaway The bank must configure what reason is shown, at what scope and through which channel, so the customer gets a useful explanation without exposing sensitive information. Keep these controls separate: → Internal diagnostic reason → Country privacy rule →

entries.title: The EUR 150,000 payment that could not go instant
entries.text: The EUR 150,000 payment that could not go instant Core A customer sends a EUR 150,000 instant payment. The customer limit allows it. The scheme maximum does not. The payment cannot go as an instant payment at all. Here is how it happens: → Customer submits a EUR 150,000 instant payment → Customer limit check passes → Scheme maximum check fails → The payment cannot go instant, whatever the customer limit says → It must be rerouted to a standard transfer The requirement said: "Apply the customer limit." Why? The scheme maximum and the customer limit are two different numbers, and an older internal guide still carries the old scheme figure after the regulation changed it. The product configuration and the routing rules were never updated together. The scheme maximum is the hard gate, not the customer limit. BA Takeaway A payment above the scheme maximum cannot go as an instant payment at all. Update the configuration and the routing rules together, and check the guide against the current

entries.title: The vendor feature that worked everywhere except where it mattered
entries.text: The vendor feature that worked everywhere except where it mattered Core A vendor demos a capability the bank needs. It works beautifully on screen. It only works globally. The bank needs it per country. The feature is useless. Here is how it happens: → Vendor demos the capability → The bank signs up → Configuration only works at global level → The country rule cannot be set → The capability cannot be used where it matters The requirement said: "The vendor says the capability exists." Why? A capability that only works globally, when the bank needs it per country, by entity, by product or by payment type, is not fit for purpose. A demoed feature and a usable feature are not the same thing. A demoed feature is not a usable feature. BA Takeaway Verify the configuration granularity before accepting that a requirement is met. Ask at which level it can be configured, and prove it with a test, not a demo. Keep these controls separate: → The capability itself → The level it can be configured

entries.title: One payment, two amounts: USD 100,000 in, USD 99,400 out
entries.text: One payment, two amounts: USD 100,000 in, USD 99,400 out Core A customer instructs a cross-border payment of USD 100,000. The beneficiary receives USD 99,400. Nobody stole the difference. A rule took it. Here is how it happens: → pain.001 instructs USD 100,000 → Payment engine validates and converts to pacs.008 → Clearing applies fees and an FX conversion at a shifted value date → Clearing settles USD 99,400 The assumption was: "The instructed amount is the settled amount." Why? The payment engine and the clearing layer apply different rules. The engine validates the instruction, while clearing settles a different amount after fees, charges or an FX conversion at a shifted value date. The amount gap always has a rule behind it. BA Takeaway Start the investigation by comparing the instructed amount in the pacs.008 against what clearing actually settled, then find which rule changed it. Keep these controls separate: → Instructed amount in pacs.008 → Amount clearing actually settled →

entries.title: The payment settled, but Treasury funded from a stale screen
entries.text: The payment settled, but Treasury funded from a stale screen Core A payment settles correctly. Treasury funds from the screen. The screen is stale. The real funding need moved from USD 2 million to USD 5 million before cut-off, and nothing alerted Treasury. Here is how it happens: → Payment settles correctly → Nostro ledger feed fails → Treasury screen still shows USD 2 million → Real funding requirement moves to USD 5 million → Nothing alerts Treasury before cut-off The assumption was: "Treasury will see the funding need on screen." Why? The payment settled, but the Nostro ledger feed failed silently. Treasury kept making funding decisions from outdated data, which is a critical operational risk even though no payment failed. A settled payment can still leave the bank blind. BA Takeaway A feed failure is a funding risk, not just a data issue. Treasury needs a live feed and an alert when the feed stops, not just a screen. Keep these controls separate: → Payment settlement → Nostro

entries.title: One extra hour at the branch, and the RTGS payment bounced
entries.text: One extra hour at the branch, and the RTGS payment bounced Core A branch cut-off for RTGS is extended by one hour. It sounds small. It is not. A Rs. 50 lakh payment accepted inside the new hour is rejected downstream, because the clearing window never moved. Here is how it happens: → Branch cut-off extended by one hour → Payment accepted inside the new hour → Settlement windows stay fixed → Core banking hours, batch jobs, standing instructions and reconciliation still read the old clock → Payment accepted past the clearing window is rejected downstream The assumption was: "Moving the cut-off is a parameter change." Why? A cut-off is a contract between the bank, the clearing system and every downstream batch. Moving it means re-validating everything that depends on it. A cut-off is a contract, not a clock setting. BA Takeaway Treat a cut-off change as a full regression exercise, not a parameter tweak. Every dependent system must be re-validated before the new time goes live. Keep these

entries.title: camt.055 sent after settlement: EUR 75,000 already gone
entries.text: camt.055 sent after settlement: EUR 75,000 already gone Core A customer asks to cancel a EUR 75,000 payment. The team sends camt.055 to stop it. The payment already settled and the beneficiary is already credited. Here is how it happens: → Payment settles and beneficiary is credited → camt.055 sent to stop the payment → camt.055 is rejected → camt.029 arrives carrying RJCR → Recovery switches to the return route The assumption was: "Send camt.055 to stop it." Why? Cancellation and return are governed by lifecycle position, not by urgency. camt.055 can stop a payment only while it remains before settlement. Once settlement and credit have completed, the only route back is a camt.056 requesting the funds, or a pacs.004 carrying them back. camt.055 stops a payment. It cannot undo one. BA Takeaway Establish the lifecycle stage before choosing the message. The disciplined move is to locate the payment first, then pick cancellation or return. Keep these controls separate: → Lifecycle stage

entries.title: pacs.009 cover rejected, but the EUR 40,000 payment had not failed
entries.text: pacs.009 cover rejected, but the EUR 40,000 payment had not failed Core A pacs.009 cover is rejected with FF01, invalid account number. The team assumes the payment failed and re-credits the customer EUR 40,000. The funds were still held by the bank. The customer is now paid twice. Here is how it happens: → pacs.009 COV rejected, FF01 → Team reads the rejection as a failed payment → Customer is re-credited EUR 40,000 → Funds are still held by the bank → Customer is paid twice, or funds go to the wrong account The assumption was: "A rejected cover means the payment failed." Why? A rejected cover does not by itself prove the underlying payment failed. The credit advice may simply carry a wrong account mapping while the funds remain held. The reason code governs the next move. A rejection code is a clue, not a verdict. BA Takeaway Investigate the reason code before re-crediting. The rejection alone must never trigger the refund. Keep these controls separate: → Reason code → Funds

entries.title: The customer asked for Citi, the payment went through Chase
entries.text: The customer asked for Citi, the payment went through Chase Core A customer sends a USD 250,000 payment and names Citi New York as intermediary. The payment routes through Chase New York. Nobody changed the instruction. A standing rule overruled it. Here is how it happens: → Customer instruction names Citi New York → Standing Settlement Instruction names Chase New York → Engine applies the SSI → Payment routes through Chase New York → A reference data update does not displace the rule The assumption was: "The instruction decides the route." Why? Routing precedence puts the Standing Settlement Instruction ahead of a conflicting customer instruction, because an SSI is a settlement instruction agreed in advance between banks, naming the preferred correspondent for a currency and counterparty. Routing follows the governing rule, not the message alone. BA Takeaway A different intermediary requires the SSI to be updated first, or an explicit override in the payment message. Routing follows

entries.title: Treasury saw EUR 18 million and thought EUR 2 million was lost
entries.text: Treasury saw EUR 18 million and thought EUR 2 million was lost Core Treasury expects EUR 20 million. The advice shows EUR 18 million. The missing EUR 2 million is not lost. It is still in transit. Here is how it happens: → pacs.009 ADV arrives → Treasury reads EUR 18 million → The missing EUR 2 million is treated as lost → pacs.008, the payment itself, has not arrived yet The assumption was: "The advice is the payment." Why? A pacs.009 ADV is an advice that funds are on the way, giving treasury visibility before arrival for liquidity planning and forecasting. It is not a pacs.008 payment instruction, and it may carry only part of the amount. An advice is not a payment. BA Takeaway Read the advice and the payment apart. Treasury must know what has arrived, what is advised, and what is still in transit. Keep these controls separate: → Advice amount in pacs.009 ADV → Payment amount in pacs.008 → Funds still in transit The real requirement is not "How much does the advice show?" It is

entries.title: EUR 5 million valid on Monday, failed on Friday
entries.text: EUR 5 million valid on Monday, failed on Friday Core A EUR 5 million payment is accepted on Monday for Friday execution, against a EUR 6 million balance. By Friday it fails. Nothing was wrong on Monday. Everything moved in between. Here is how it happens: → EUR 5 million accepted Monday for Friday execution → Payment is warehoused → Balance, account details, sanctions status and cut-off times move before Friday → Friday arrives, and the payment is not re-validated → Execution fails The assumption was: "Accepted means it will execute." Why? Warehousing turns a future-dated payment into a commitment to execute, not merely a stored instruction. Validity on Monday proves nothing about Friday. Warehousing is a commitment to re-check, not a guarantee. BA Takeaway Re-validate on balance, account status, sanctions and cut-offs at execution, then execute or reject. Warehousing is risk management across the interval. Keep these controls separate: → Acceptance checks on Monday → Execution checks

entries.title: camt.056 sent, EUR 60,000 stuck in silence
entries.text: camt.056 sent, EUR 60,000 stuck in silence Core A bank asks for EUR 60,000 back with a camt.056. Nobody answers. The payment sits in a waiting state, neither completed nor rejected, and the funds just hang. Here is how it happens: → camt.056 sent to request the return → No answer arrives → Payment sits waiting, neither completed nor rejected → No status check is planned → No escalation route exists The assumption was: "The beneficiary will answer." Why? An unanswered camt.056 leaves the payment stuck while the return of funds hangs. The exit is a camt.029 status check, followed by waiting for a response or escalating when the beneficiary does not reply within the agreed time. Every waiting state needs a way out. BA Takeaway Design every waiting state in advance with an entry, an exit, a time limit, a status check and an escalation route. Keep these controls separate: → Waiting state and its time limit → Status check with camt.029 → Escalation route The real requirement is not "How

entries.title: 3,000 payments arrived at once, and the SLA broke on sequencing
entries.text: 3,000 payments arrived at once, and the SLA broke on sequencing Core Thousands of payments arrive together. Every control runs in sequence. The SLA breaks. The checks were all correct. The order was wrong. Here is how it happens: → Thousands of payments arrive together → Every control runs one after another → Compliance takes 3 seconds, fraud takes 4 seconds, run in sequence they take 7 → The SLA is missed → Payments queue behind checks that could have run together The assumption was: "Run every control in order." Why? Control design is a business decision about ordering, not a technical default. If the account is closed and rejection is the defined outcome, the payment can go to rejection once the account check is done. Compliance and fraud can run in parallel, so checks of 3 and 4 seconds finish in 4 seconds together instead of 7 in sequence. Control order is a business decision, not a technical default. BA Takeaway Spell out the intended outcome for a control that fails, times out

entries.title: The team asked for pacs.009 and got the wrong one
entries.text: The team asked for pacs.009 and got the wrong one Core A EUR 100,000 cover payment needs to move. The requirement says one word: pacs.009. The team builds Core. The payment needs Cover. The funding leg never moves. Here is how it happens: → Requirement says pacs.009 is needed → No use case is named → Team builds Core, a bank-to-bank transfer → The business needed COV, the cover leg → The cover cannot settle, and the customer payment stalls The assumption was: "pacs.009 is the requirement." Why? COV and ADV are not separate messages in the ISO 20022 catalogue. They share one underlying pacs.009 message, applied to a different business use case. CBPR+ sets out Core, Cover and Advise for cross-border payments, while the EPC SEPA schemes do not use pacs.009 at all. A message name is not a use case. BA Takeaway A requirement that says only that pacs.009 is needed stays incomplete until it also names the use case, the scheme, the usage guideline and the business context. Keep these controls

entries.title: The German Direct Debit flow met the Dutch customer, and failed
entries.text: The German Direct Debit flow met the Dutch customer, and failed Core A Direct Debit process defined for Germany works well there. The bank reuses it for the Netherlands. A customer moves to a new Dutch bank, the debit for the closed account is rejected, and a EUR 5,000 monthly payment bounces. It should have been redirected. Here is how it happens: → German Direct Debit process is reused for the Netherlands → Customer moves to a new Dutch bank → Debit arrives for the closed account → Local Overstapservice rule requires redirecting, not rejecting → Debit is rejected, and the payment fails The assumption was: "Reuse the process that worked in Germany." Why? The Netherlands has its own local specification, the Overstapservice, a bank-switching service that lets Direct Debits continue after a customer moves to a new Dutch bank. Reuse looks efficient, yet efficiency is not the test. Reuse is a delivery choice, not a business decision. BA Takeaway Before agreeing to reuse, check whether the

entries.title: One statement line, 400 entries, and one missing
entries.text: One statement line, 400 entries, and one missing Core A settlement batch holds 400 entries under one statement line worth EUR 850,000. One entry is missing. The whole group fails, and nobody can tell the customer why. Here is how it happens: → Settlement happens in a batch → One statement line stands for 400 ledger entries → Entries share one batch reference → One entry is missing → The whole group fails reconciliation → A temporary GL entry is raised while investigating The assumption was: "Match each entry to the statement." Why? Reconciliation must collect the entries by batch reference and reconcile that group as one against the statement line, rather than matching a single entry. If one entry is missing, the whole group fails. Reconcile the batch, not the entry. BA Takeaway The engine must preserve the batch reference linkage across the items. Grasp the reason the batch exists, not merely how it matches. Keep these controls separate: → Batch reference linkage → Group

entries.title: Treasury needed one answer before cut-off, and camt.053 could not give it
entries.text: Treasury needed one answer before cut-off, and camt.053 could not give it Core Treasury waits on a EUR 30 million Nostro credit before releasing an outgoing payment. The cut-off is an hour away. The team reads camt.053. It answers tomorrow, not today. Here is how it happens: → Treasury waits for a Nostro credit → Outgoing payment is held until the credit arrives → camt.053 shows movements and balance at close of business → The decision must be made during the day → camt.052 intraday report or camt.054 notification can answer it The assumption was: "Read the statement." Why? The camt.053 statement holds the account movements and the balance at close of business, so it cannot answer a question that must be decided during the day. Choose the message by the decision it must support, not by its definition alone. BA Takeaway Start from the business decision, then pick the message that can answer it in time. Keep these controls separate: → Decision that must be made → Timing the decision

entries.title: A flawless pain.001, a USD 200,000 payment in the wrong engine
entries.text: A flawless pain.001, a USD 200,000 payment in the wrong engine Core A customer sends a flawless pain.001 for USD 200,000. It lands in an instant payment engine that handles EUR only. The payment is held, delayed and then rejected, and the instruction was perfect. Here is how it happens: → Valid pain.001 arrives → Routing rules are set by the payment business and applied by the acquisition layer → pain.001 provides the clues: instrument, currency and amount → The rules are incomplete, and the route is wrong → USD payment lands in a EUR-only instant engine → Payment is held, delayed or rejected The assumption was: "A valid message finds its own route." Why? The engine never invents or overrides the route. If the rules are incomplete or incorrectly applied, a valid payment can land in the wrong engine despite a correct customer instruction. The message provides the clues, the rules decide the route. BA Takeaway Routing rules are a business responsibility. Test the rules against every

entries.title: The API said 200 OK, and the EUR 80,000 payment was still rejected
entries.text: The API said 200 OK, and the EUR 80,000 payment was still rejected Core An API call returns HTTP 200. The EUR 80,000 payment is still rejected. The call succeeded. The business decision failed. Here is how it happens: → API call succeeds, HTTP 200 → Account is open, so the first check passes → Account currency is EUR, and the product does not support FX → Fraud score comes back 95 → Engine rejects the payment The assumption was: "HTTP 200 means the payment will succeed." Why? Technical success and business outcome are different things. Checking whether an account is open or closed is not enough if the engine also needs the account currency. A fraud score works the same way: the fraud system controls its scoring model, while the engine must convert the score into an action, above 90 reject, 50 to 90 process with a customer alert, and below 50 process normally. API success is not a business decision. BA Takeaway Start with the business decision the process needs to make, not the API to

entries.title: The optional field that stopped a EUR 120,000 cover payment
entries.text: The optional field that stopped a EUR 120,000 cover payment Core In a four-bank cover payment, Bank A sends pacs.008 to Bank B and a pacs.009 cover to intermediary Bank C. Bank C cannot link the cover to the customer payment. The EUR 120,000 cover sits unreconciled, because one optional field was left out. Here is how it happens: → Bank A sends pacs.008 to Bank B → Bank A sends pacs.009 cover to Bank C → Bank C must link the cover using the same UETR and remittance reference → The pacs.009 RltdRmtInf field is left out, because it is optional → Bank C cannot reconcile the cover The assumption was: "Optional means we can leave it out." Why? The pacs.009 RltdRmtInf field carries the link, and although it is optional in the message, the intermediary cannot reconcile the cover without it. Optional in the message, mandatory for the flow. BA Takeaway Optional or mandatory is a property of the message, not of the process. Handle the message flow and the field status as two separate things.

entries.title: USD 10,000 to India: one message, or two?
entries.text: USD 10,000 to India: one message, or two? Core A US bank sends USD 10,000 to HDFC Bank in India, for an INR account. One pacs.008 with settlement will not work. There is no direct relationship, and the settlement currency does not match. The payment needs two legs, and the team sent one. Here is how it happens: → USD 10,000 instructed from a US bank to India → No nostro account exists in the beneficiary bank country → Settlement currency differs from the payer account currency → pacs.008 goes without settlement → A separate pacs.009 cover must move the funds through an intermediary The assumption was: "Send one pacs.008 with settlement." Why? Serial and cover are infrastructure choices, not customer choices. Serial suits cases where correspondent or nostro accounts exist and the settlement currency matches the payer account currency. Cover suits cases with no direct relationship or a different settlement currency. Serial or cover is a settlement decision, not a wording choice. BA

entries.title: The team heard MT was dead, and stopped planning for it
entries.text: The team heard MT was dead, and stopped planning for it Core The CBPR+ November 2026 deadline is announced as the end of MT for cross-border payments. The team stops planning for MT altogether. Then a EUR 500,000 payment type that still runs on MT after the deadline breaks, because nobody planned for it. Here is how it happens: → November 2026 deadline is announced → Team reads it as the end of all MT → Many MT messages do migrate to MX by then → Some were already retired, and others keep running after the deadline for specialised or domestic use → A payment type still on MT is left without a plan The assumption was: "MT ends in November 2026." Why? SWIFT is driving the migration because MT cannot carry the rich data, structured addresses and granularity that compliance and monitoring need. But the end date is not the same for every message, and that nuance matters in migration planning. MT is retiring, not retired. BA Takeaway Know the nuance rather than repeating the slogan. Plan

entries.title: The optional address field that cost EUR 12,000 in deductions
entries.text: The optional address field that cost EUR 12,000 in deductions Core A pain.001 is sent without the sending business agent address and postcode. The field is optional, so nobody captures it. The beneficiary bank falls back to default values, and the EUR 120,000 payment arrives EUR 12,000 short after deductions and a compliance flag. Here is how it happens: → pain.001 sent without the agent address → Field is marked optional in the message → Beneficiary or intermediary bank falls back to default values → Compliance issues, errors or deductions follow → Payment goes through, but short The assumption was: "Optional means not needed." Why? A field M, O or C status describes the message, while whether the information must be captured is decided by the business rules of the process. If the field is left out, the receiving bank may fall back to defaults. A field status describes the message, not the process. BA Takeaway Always ask whether the field is needed for the process, rather than

entries.title: The EUR 90,000 payment that waited for a check it did not need
entries.text: The EUR 90,000 payment that waited for a check it did not need Core A EUR 90,000 payment enters the engine. Validation checks run one after another, as they should. Then sanction screening, fraud screening, limit checks and risk checks also run one after another, for no reason at all. The payment is late. Here is how it happens: → Payment enters the engine → Validation checks run in sequence and stop on first failure → Screening checks also run in sequence → Each screening check waits for the previous one → The payment is delayed, and the SLA is at risk The assumption was: "Run all controls in order." Why? Control ordering follows dependency. Validation checks such as account number and currency, name matching, account status and closure depend on each other, so they run one after another. Sanction screening, fraud screening, limit checks, risk assessment and regulatory checks have no dependency, so they can run at the same time. Sequential for validation, parallel for screening. BA

entries.title: The MT103 that lost its address in translation
entries.text: The MT103 that lost its address in translation Core An MT103 arrives for a EUR 60,000 payment. The address is free text, four lines of 35 characters. In MX it must be structured: name, town, country. The mapping drops the town, and Compliance holds the payment. Here is how it happens: → MT103 arrives with a free-text address → Translator converts field by field to MX → Town and country are not carried across → MX arrives with an incomplete structured address → Compliance holds the EUR 60,000 payment The assumption was: "Conversion is a format change." Why? MT messages are FIN messages written as structured text with character limits, while MX messages are ISO 20022 XML with properly structured data. The translator must also look at the MT structure, correspondent and account information and the business rules to derive the right MX settlement method. MT to MX is a business mapping exercise, not a format change. BA Takeaway Get the mapping right early, because that is what keeps

entries.title: The EUR 45,000 payment that failed in the place nobody planned for
entries.text: The EUR 45,000 payment that failed in the place nobody planned for Core A EUR 45,000 payment is processed with the wrong details, and the verification of payee check fails. The team has no alternative ready, and no communication plan. The customer finds out from the beneficiary, not from the bank. Here is how it happens: → Solution goes live → Requirements change, and the change was captured wrongly → Processing is delayed, and a system slows down → Payment is processed with wrong details → No alternative is ready, and no one tells the customer The assumption was: "The solution will work." Why? A payment solution can fail in three places: functionally, when requirements change or were captured wrongly; technically, when processing is delayed, a system is down or performance drops; and in business terms, when a payment is processed with wrong details or a check like verification of payee fails. Design for failure, or failure designs the day. BA Takeaway Plan for each kind of failure,

entries.title: Schedule it for next week: the five rules hidden in one sentence
entries.text: Schedule it for next week: the five rules hidden in one sentence Core A customer asks to schedule a EUR 25,000 payment for next week. It sounds simple. It hides five rules. The system accepts a past date, cannot reschedule it, and nobody knows what happens when the date passes unprocessed. Here is how it happens: → Customer asks to schedule a payment → Requirement is written down as one sentence → No rule stops a past date → No rule covers rescheduling with a new effective date → No rule cancels it when it is not processed on the requested date → In a request to pay such as pain.013, the execution date shows even when the data is empty The assumption was: "Document what the customer asked." Why? A high-level need has to be decoded into business rules: a payment can be set for a future date, recreated or rescheduled with a new effective date, never scheduled for a date in the past, scheduled for several payment types, and cancelled when it is not processed on the requested date. A

entries.title: The Rs. 4,500 card payment that cleared but never settled
entries.text: The Rs. 4,500 card payment that cleared but never settled Core A customer pays Rs. 4,500 by card. Authorisation is approved. Clearing completes. Settlement breaks, and the ledger does not agree. The customer thinks the payment worked. The money is unaccounted for. Here is how it happens: → Authorisation: issuer approves the payment at the point of sale → Clearing: network exchanges records between acquirer and issuer → Settlement: funds should move between the banks → Reconciliation: clearing records, settlement positions and ledger postings do not agree The assumption was: "Authorisation means the money moved." Why? A card transaction moves through four stages across four parties, and a failure at any stage has a different owner and a different fix. The issuer, the acquirer, the network and the merchant each play a distinct role at each stage. Know the stage, and you know who must act. BA Takeaway Check each stage in order. Authorisation, clearing, settlement and reconciliation are

entries.title: Same terminal, same Rs. 10,000, two different kinds of money
entries.text: Same terminal, same Rs. 10,000, two different kinds of money Core Two customers each pay Rs. 10,000 at the same terminal. One pays by debit card, one by credit card. The terminal experience looks identical. The money movement is entirely different. Here is how it happens: → Debit card: payment draws directly on the customer balance → Funds leave the account at authorisation → Credit card: payment draws on a credit line → Issuer funds the payment, and the customer repays later → Settlement timing, interest treatment and issuer risk all differ The assumption was: "A card payment is a card payment." Why? A debit card moves money the customer already holds, while a credit card moves money the issuer lends. The terminal hides the difference, and the ledger does not. The terminal looks identical. The money movement is not. BA Takeaway Always ask which funding source a payment uses, because it decides settlement timing, interest and risk. Keep these controls separate: → Funding source →

entries.title: Balance was enough, and the Rs. 25,000 payment was still declined
entries.text: Balance was enough, and the Rs. 25,000 payment was still declined Core A customer tries to pay Rs. 25,000 by card. The balance is sufficient. The payment is declined. The customer is sure the bank made a mistake. The bank followed its own rules. Here is how it happens: → Card is presented → Card status check passes → Funds check passes → A fraud rule is breached → Decline returned with a response code The assumption was: "Sufficient funds means approval." Why? The issuer checks card status, available funds or credit, transaction limits and fraud rules together. A payment can be declined even when the balance is sufficient, if a fraud rule or a limit is breached. Sufficient funds alone never guarantee approval. BA Takeaway Design the decline to say which check failed, so the customer and the support team are not left guessing. Keep these controls separate: → Card status → Funds or credit → Limits and fraud rules The real requirement is not "Does the customer have the money?" It is

entries.title: The settlement that looked fine, and the Rs. 18 lakh that did not reconcile
entries.text: The settlement that looked fine, and the Rs. 18 lakh that did not reconcile Core Card payments clear for the day, and customers see their payments succeed. Behind the scenes, the ledger is Rs. 18 lakh out from the settlement position. Nobody notices, because nobody compared the three records. Here is how it happens: → Clearing completes → Settlement position is the net amount each bank owes or is owed → Ledger postings are made → Clearing records, settlement positions and ledger postings do not agree → The break is not investigated The assumption was: "The customer payment succeeded, so settlement is fine." Why? After clearing, the settlement position must match the ledger postings exactly. Reconciliation compares all three records, and any break between them is investigated rather than written off. A settlement that does not reconcile is a control failure. BA Takeaway A settlement that does not reconcile means money is unaccounted for, even if the customer-facing payment appeared to

entries.title: The Rs. 12,000 chargeback that changed hands three times
entries.text: The Rs. 12,000 chargeback that changed hands three times Core A cardholder disputes a Rs. 12,000 transaction. The issuer raises it. The merchant fights it with representment evidence. The loss moves between issuer, acquirer and merchant, and the reason code decides who holds it at each stage. Here is how it happens: → Cardholder disputes the transaction → Issuer raises the chargeback with the scheme → Acquirer and merchant respond with representment evidence → Scheme applies its timelines and reason codes → Financial impact moves between issuer, acquirer and merchant The assumption was: "The reason code is just a label." Why? The reason code decides what evidence is needed and who bears the loss at each stage. The wrong code means the wrong evidence, and the wrong party pays. The reason code is the case, not a label on it. BA Takeaway Start every chargeback from the reason code, and build the evidence around what that code demands. Keep these controls separate: → Reason code →

entries.title: The Rs. 40 lakh payment sent on the wrong rail
entries.text: The Rs. 40 lakh payment sent on the wrong rail Core A customer needs Rs. 40 lakh to reach a supplier today. The payment goes by NEFT, in a batch, because that is the usual rail. It arrives in the next cycle. The supplier is not paid today, and the customer is furious.
