Here is how it happens: → Payment is urgent and high value → NEFT is chosen by habit → NEFT settles in batches, and the payment waits → RTGS would have settled it individually in central bank money → IMPS would have settled it instantly, around the clock The assumption was: "Use the usual rail." Why? NEFT, RTGS and IMPS are three domestic rails with different operating models. Compare them on speed, availability, settlement model and customer use case, and use the current scheme rules rather than an old summary. The rail is chosen by the payment's need, not by habit. BA Takeaway Route by need: batch and can wait, individual and final, or instant and around the clock. Check the current scheme rules before choosing. Keep

entries.title: The Rs. 30 lakh loan that stalled between approval and money
entries.text: The Rs. 30 lakh loan that stalled between approval and money Core A customer is approved for a Rs. 30 lakh loan. The money does not arrive. Nobody can say where it stopped, because the failure sits at a later stage than the approval. Here is how it happens: → Application collects the request and supporting information → Decision assesses credit and affordability → Agreement records the terms → Disbursement should release the funds → Servicing collects repayments and manages changes → Closure confirms the balance is settled → A weak link at one stage shows up downstream The assumption was: "Approval means the money is on its way." Why? Each stage has its own data, controls and hand-offs, so a failure at one stage does not always show up until a later stage. A loan is a chain, and a weak link anywhere shows up downstream. BA Takeaway Trace the chain stage by stage. Do not assume the approval was the problem. Keep these controls separate: → Decision and agreement → Disbursement →

entries.title: Approved for Rs. 15 lakh, and the money never arrived
entries.text: Approved for Rs. 15 lakh, and the money never arrived Core A loan is approved for Rs. 15 lakh. The customer waits. The money never arrives. The team checks the approval first, and finds nothing wrong. The break is somewhere else. Here is how it happens: → Approval is given → Account validation runs → Disbursement instruction is sent → Ledger posting is recorded → Customer communication goes out → One of these stages breaks, and the customer simply sees that the money has not arrived The assumption was: "The approval was the problem." Why? A valid approval with a wrong account, a failed instruction or a missing ledger posting all look the same to the customer, who simply sees that the money has not arrived. Check each stage in order rather than assuming the approval was the problem. BA Takeaway Trace the path from approval through account validation, the disbursement instruction, the ledger posting and the customer communication, because the break can sit at any of these points. Keep

entries.title: Tomorrow, the customer was told, and the money came in two days
entries.text: Tomorrow, the customer was told, and the money came in two days Core A customer sends Rs. 2 lakh and is told the money will arrive tomorrow. It arrives in two days. The complaint was avoidable. The timing quoted was never the scheme's timing. Here is how it happens: → Payment is made → Customer is told it arrives tomorrow → Scheme settles in two days for this product → Customer waits, then complains The assumption was: "T+1 is the timing." Why? A settlement cycle is the period after which funds move between banks, and T+1 or T+2 are only examples of how long that can take. The actual timing depends on the scheme and the product. Tell the customer the real timing for that product. BA Takeaway Customer communication must state the real timing for that product, because telling a customer the money will arrive tomorrow when the scheme settles in two days creates a complaint that was avoidable. Keep these controls separate: → Scheme rule → Product rule → Customer message The real

entries.title: The EUR 20,000 payment that could be taken but never refunded
entries.text: The EUR 20,000 payment that could be taken but never refunded Core A customer pays EUR 20,000 through a new checkout. The payment goes through. Then the customer asks for a refund. There is no refund API. There is no reversal API. The money is stuck. Here is how it happens: → Checkout API initiates the payment → Authentication API proves who is paying → Status API reports where the payment stands → Refund API does not exist → Reversal API does not exist → A payment that can be taken cannot be refunded or checked The assumption was: "Build the payment API first." Why? A payment product exposes several APIs across the lifecycle, not just one for taking payment. Map each touchpoint to the lifecycle stage it serves, or the product ends up with a payment that can be taken but cannot be refunded or checked. Coverage of the whole lifecycle is what makes a payment product complete. BA Takeaway Cover initiate, authenticate, check status, refund and reverse before launch. A missing lifecycle

entries.title: Refund or reversal: the Rs. 8,000 that was posted twice
entries.text: Refund or reversal: the Rs. 8,000 that was posted twice Core A Rs. 8,000 payment should never have completed. The team issues a refund. A new credit posts to the customer, while the original posting still stands. The customer is credited twice. Here is how it happens: → Payment should not have completed → Team calls it a refund → Refund posts as a new credit to the customer → Original posting is never unwound → Customer is credited twice The assumption was: "Refund and reversal are the same thing." Why? A refund returns money for a completed payment and posts as a new credit, while a reversal cancels a payment that should not have completed and unwinds the original posting. Validate the rail and provider semantics before building either one, because the same word can mean different things on different rails. Build the ledger effect first, and the name will follow. BA Takeaway Decide the ledger effect before the name. A refund creates a credit, a reversal unwinds the posting. Keep

entries.title: The Rs. 50,000 payment failed, and three parties pointed at each other
entries.text: The Rs. 50,000 payment failed, and three parties pointed at each other Core A Rs. 50,000 card payment fails. The gateway says it is the bank. The bank says it is the merchant. The merchant says it is the gateway. The customer waits while three parties argue about ownership. Here is how it happens: → Gateway orchestrates the instruction → Bank authorises and processes the payment → Merchant is notified of the outcome → Payment fails → Nobody owns the fix, and nobody tells the customer The assumption was: "Someone will handle the failure." Why? The gateway, the bank and the merchant each own a distinct part. When a payment fails, knowing which party owns which step decides who must fix it and who must tell the customer. Unclear ownership turns every failure into a dispute between parties. BA Takeaway Make the boundary between gateway, bank and merchant explicit in the design, for the happy path and for every failure. Keep these controls separate: → Gateway ownership → Bank ownership →

entries.title: The customers failing five times a day that nobody noticed
entries.text: The customers failing five times a day that nobody noticed Core Customers are failing payments five times a day, every day. Nobody notices, because the rule to find them was never defined. By the time the complaints arrive, the customers have already left. Here is how it happens: → No time window is defined → No failure condition is defined → No threshold is set for what counts as repeated → Test transactions and duplicates are counted as real failures → The wrong customers are targeted, and the real ones are missed The assumption was: "Count the failures." Why? Finding customers with repeated failed transactions means translating the business rule into a time-windowed aggregation: define the window, the failure condition and the threshold, then aggregate and validate the data quality before acting. A count that includes test transactions, duplicates or a wrong window will target the wrong customers. A precise rule plus clean data is the whole method. BA Takeaway Define the window,

entries.title: The EUR 100,000 transaction with no audit trail
entries.text: The EUR 100,000 transaction with no audit trail Core A EUR 100,000 transaction is screened and cleared. Months later, an auditor asks for the evidence. There is none. The control ran, but nothing proves it ran. Here is how it happens: → Customer risk controls run → Transaction risk controls run → A case is escalated → The audit trail is incomplete → The control is treated as if it did not happen The assumption was: "We ran the control." Why? Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing controls cover both the customer and the transaction, and an analyst must understand them well enough to write requirements that keep the audit trail complete. A control that cannot be evidenced is treated as if it did not happen. Evidence is the control. BA Takeaway Write requirements that keep the screening outcomes, the case escalation path and the audit trail complete from the start. Keep these controls separate: → Customer risk controls → Transaction risk controls → Case escalation and

entries.title: The EUR 75,000 payment rule nobody could test
entries.text: The EUR 75,000 payment rule nobody could test Core A business asks for a rule on EUR 75,000 payments. The requirement is written down as one vague sentence. It is built, and the problem is found in testing, when fixing it costs ten times more. Here is how it happens: → Requirement arrives vague and ambiguous → It is written down without discovery questions → No concrete examples pin down the behaviour → No one observes how the work is really done → No playback confirms the understanding → Testing finds the misunderstanding The assumption was: "Write down what the business said." Why? Ambiguity is normal at the start of a requirement. Discovery questions find what is actually meant, concrete examples pin down the behaviour, process observation shows how the work is really done, and playback confirms the understanding with stakeholders. Ambiguity handled early is cheap; ambiguity found in testing is expensive. BA Takeaway The output must be a requirement that is testable: an observable

entries.title: The requirement that passed review and failed every test
entries.text: The requirement that passed review and failed every test Core A requirement for a EUR 60,000 payment flow passes review. It fails every test, because no test can prove it. The team argues about whether it was delivered, and there is no way to resolve the dispute. Here is how it happens: → Observable outcome is stated → Boundary conditions are missing → Negative cases are missing → Acceptance criteria are missing → No one can verify the requirement → Delivery is disputed The assumption was: "The requirement is written, so it is testable." Why? A requirement is testable when it defines an observable outcome, the boundary conditions, the negative cases and the acceptance criteria. Without these four, a requirement cannot be verified. Without these four, a requirement cannot be verified. BA Takeaway Check every requirement for all four parts before it leaves analysis. A missing part is a dispute waiting to happen. Keep these controls separate: → Observable outcome → Boundary conditions →

entries.title: Two stakeholders, one EUR 200,000 decision, no record of why
entries.text: Two stakeholders, one EUR 200,000 decision, no record of why Core Two stakeholders disagree over a EUR 200,000 payment flow decision. A compromise is reached in the meeting. Next month the same stakeholders meet, and the same argument reopens, because nobody wrote down the decision. Here is how it happens: → Competing requirements clash → Value, risk, urgency, customer impact and dependencies are debated → A decision is made → The decision, who made it and why, is not documented → The compromise is reopened at the next meeting The assumption was: "We agreed in the meeting." Why? The comparison must be evidence based, so each stakeholder can see why one requirement was chosen over another. An undocumented compromise will be reopened the next time the same stakeholders meet. Document the decision, who made it and why. BA Takeaway Facilitate a documented decision on evidence, and record who made it and why. Keep these controls separate: → Evidence based comparison → The decision → The

entries.title: The business asked in plain words, and the system was built in system words
entries.text: The business asked in plain words, and the system was built in system words Core A non-technical stakeholder describes a EUR 40,000 payment need in business language. The team builds it in system language. Playback is skipped, the misunderstanding is found after the build, and the rework costs a sprint. Here is how it happens: → Interviews hear the need in business language → Workshops build shared understanding → Observation shows how the work is actually done → Examples pin down the detail → Structured playback is skipped → The build reflects the misunderstanding The assumption was: "We heard the requirement." Why? Non-technical stakeholders describe what they need in business language, not in system language. Playback matters most, because it catches misunderstandings while they are still cheap to fix. Confirm before you write, not after you build. BA Takeaway Run structured playback before the requirement is written down, and let the stakeholder recognise their own need in it.

entries.title: The missing rule found in UAT, and the EUR 60,000 fix that followed
entries.text: The missing rule found in UAT, and the EUR 60,000 fix that followed Core A missing rule is found in UAT. The fix costs EUR 60,000, because the gap was lost in discovery and a whole stage must be reworked. The team fixes the symptom. The same gap recurs next release. Here is how it happens: → A piece of the need is missed → The gap is found late, in UAT → The fix is applied to the symptom → The origin is never traced → The same gap recurs The assumption was: "Fix the symptom." Why? Tracing the gap to its origin matters because it decides whether the fix is a small correction or a rework of a whole stage, and it prevents the same gap from recurring. The gap could have been lost in discovery, analysis, design, implementation or testing. Fix the origin, not just the symptom. BA Takeaway Trace the gap back to where it was lost, and agree corrective action with the owner of that stage. Keep these controls separate: → Discovery and analysis → Design and implementation → Testing The real

entries.title: The process diagram that misled everyone who used it
entries.text: The process diagram that misled everyone who used it Core A process diagram for a EUR 100,000 payment flow is drawn from assumptions. It looks right. It is wrong. The team follows it, and every hand-off goes to the wrong place. Here is how it happens: → Diagram is drawn → Actors, triggers, decisions, hand-offs and data stores are assumed → Nothing is checked against reality → Diagram is never validated with the people who do the work → Everyone who relies on it is misled The assumption was: "The diagram looks right." Why? A process diagram must show the actors, the triggers, the decisions, the hand-offs and the data stores, and each of these must be checked against reality rather than assumed. A diagram is only as good as its validation. BA Takeaway Validate the diagram with the people who do the work. Choose the diagram that fits the problem, then prove it matches reality. Keep these controls separate: → Actors and triggers → Decisions and hand-offs → Data stores and validation The

entries.title: The requirements signed off in a day, and rebuilt over six weeks
entries.text: The requirements signed off in a day, and rebuilt over six weeks Core Requirements for a EUR 80,000 payment change are signed off in a day. Validation is skipped to save time. The rebuild takes six weeks, because the misunderstandings were found in development and testing instead. Here is how it happens: → Walkthroughs are skipped → Consistency checks are skipped → Testability checks are skipped → Sign-off is given → Misunderstandings surface in development and testing → Fixes cost far more than validation would have The assumption was: "Sign-off means the requirements are ready." Why? A walkthrough catches misunderstandings, a consistency check catches contradictions, a testability check catches requirements that cannot be verified, and sign-off records agreement. Skipping validation does not save time; it moves the cost into development and testing. Skipping validation does not save time; it moves the cost. BA Takeaway Run walkthroughs, consistency checks, testability checks and

entries.title: The change nobody could trace, and the release it broke
entries.text: The change nobody could trace, and the release it broke Core A change is made to a EUR 120,000 payment flow. Nobody can trace it forward to its impact. The release breaks, and nobody can trace the defect back to its origin. Here is how it happens: → Business objective is set → Requirement is written → Story and design follow → Tests are run → A defect appears → No chain links the defect back to its origin The assumption was: "We know what changed." Why? A traceability matrix connects business objectives to requirements, stories, design, tests, defects and release evidence, with each row showing the chain from the objective through the requirement to the test that proves it. Any change can then be traced forward to its impact and any defect traced back to its origin. Without traceability, a team cannot prove what was built is what was asked for. BA Takeaway Keep the chain intact from objective to release evidence, or a change cannot be assessed safely. Keep these controls separate: →

entries.title: The scope that shrank one change at a time
entries.text: The scope that shrank one change at a time Core Requirements for a EUR 150,000 payment project change every week. Each change is small. The delivery date slips, and nobody can say why. The scope eroded one uncosted change at a time. Here is how it happens: → Change is requested → No change intake records what is asked and why → No impact analysis states the cost in scope, effort and risk → No prioritisation ranks it against other work → No decision governance records who approved it → Weekly changes silently erode the scope and the delivery date The assumption was: "It is only a small change." Why? Change intake, impact analysis, prioritisation and decision governance are the discipline that keeps weekly change visible. Without them, the erosion is silent. Without this discipline, weekly changes silently erode the scope and the delivery date. BA Takeaway Record every change, cost it, rank it and record who approved it, or the date will move without anyone deciding it should. Keep

entries.title: Two weeks wanted, six estimated, and the EUR 150,000 decision in between
entries.text: Two weeks wanted, six estimated, and the EUR 150,000 decision in between Core The business wants a EUR 150,000 payment feature in two weeks. Development estimates six. The meeting argues over the number, and nobody decides what to deliver. Here is how it happens: → Business wants two weeks, development estimates six → The minimum outcome that would still be valuable is never clarified → Scope is never sliced to the smallest useful increment → Dependencies that drive the estimate are never identified → Trade-offs are argued, not evidenced The assumption was: "Argue the estimate." Why? Clarify the minimum outcome, slice the scope, identify the dependencies, and present evidence based trade-offs. The decision is then about what to deliver and what to defer, not about whose estimate is right. The decision is about what to deliver and what to defer. BA Takeaway Turn an estimate argument into a scope decision, with evidence in front of the people who must choose. Keep these controls

entries.title: Build us the solution, said the board, and nobody asked what problem it solved
entries.text: Build us the solution, said the board, and nobody asked what problem it solved Core Senior management asks for a solution for a EUR 200,000 payment problem. No requirements are given. The team builds the solution anyway. It does not solve the real problem, because nobody asked what the problem was. Here is how it happens: → Solution is requested without requirements → No one asks what outcome is needed → No one asks what constraints apply → No one asks what options exist → No one asks what criteria will decide between them → The wrong solution is built on time The assumption was: "Build the solution they asked for." Why? Reframing the request around outcomes, constraints, options and decision criteria turns a request for a specific solution into a decision that can be made on evidence, and avoids building something that does not solve the real problem. Reframe the ask before you build the answer. BA Takeaway Ask what outcome is needed, what constraints apply, what options exist and

entries.title: Complete, said the business. Incomplete, said the developers.
entries.text: Complete, said the business. Incomplete, said the developers. Core The business believes the requirements for a EUR 90,000 payment change are complete. The developers disagree. Both sides read the same words and understand different things, and the rebuild starts before anyone notices. Here is how it happens: → Requirements are declared complete → Developers read them differently → Concrete examples are never used to show how each side reads them → No walkthrough surfaces the differences → Traceability never shows what is covered and what is not → Shared definitions are never agreed The assumption was: "The requirements are complete." Why? The gap is usually in interpretation rather than in content. Close the interpretation gap before development, because it is far cheaper to agree on meaning now than to rebuild later. Close the interpretation gap before development. BA Takeaway Use concrete examples, walkthroughs, traceability and shared definitions to prove both sides read the

entries.title: The new payment screen nobody used
entries.text: The new payment screen nobody used Core A new digital payment screen is launched. Nobody uses it. The team calls the users stubborn. The resistance has a cause nobody bothered to find. Here is how it happens: → Digital change is launched → Impacts on each user group are never mapped → Stakeholder concerns are never identified → Training needs are never defined → No champions support the change → Feedback is never collected, and adoption is never measured The assumption was: "Users are just stubborn." Why? User resistance to a digital change usually has a cause that can be identified. Resistance that is understood can be addressed; resistance that is dismissed as stubbornness will grow and will damage the change. Diagnose resistance before you try to overcome it. BA Takeaway Map the impacts, identify the concerns, define the training, find champions, collect feedback and measure adoption. Keep these controls separate: → Impacts and concerns → Training needs → Champions, feedback and

entries.title: The BA who could not prove the EUR 300,000 saving
entries.text: The BA who could not prove the EUR 300,000 saving Core A process change claims a EUR 300,000 saving. Stakeholders ask for the proof. There is none. Nothing was measured before, and nothing was measured after. Here is how it happens: → Process change is delivered → Cost is never measured before and after → Cycle time is never measured → Error rates are never measured → Customer experience is never measured → Benefits realisation is never done The assumption was: "The improvement is obvious." Why? An analyst demonstrates contribution by connecting process changes to measurable outcomes: link the change to cost, cycle time, error rates, customer experience and benefits realisation, and measure before and after so the improvement can be shown rather than claimed. Measured value is the analyst's evidence, not a claim. BA Takeaway Measure before and after, and finish with benefits realisation, because it proves the change delivered the value that justified it. Keep these controls separate:

entries.title: The mid-sprint change that broke the sprint goal
entries.text: The mid-sprint change that broke the sprint goal Core A change is requested mid-sprint on a EUR 100,000 payment feature. It is accepted on the spot, without assessment. The sprint goal breaks, and the team is held accountable for a target it never agreed to. Here is how it happens: → Change is requested mid-sprint → Scope is never assessed → Impact on the sprint goal is never assessed → Effort is never assessed → Dependencies are never assessed → Change is accepted, and the goal silently breaks The assumption was: "Just fit it in." Why? A change requested mid-sprint must be assessed before it is agreed: scope, impact on the sprint goal, effort required and dependencies introduced. Only then decide whether to accept it, defer it or swap it for something else. Accepting a change without assessment silently breaks the sprint goal. BA Takeaway Assess first, decide second. Accept, defer or swap only with the evidence in front of the team. Keep these controls separate: → Scope of the change

entries.title: The change that arrived when 70 percent of the sprint was done
entries.text: The change that arrived when 70 percent of the sprint was done Core A change is requested when 70 percent of the sprint is done. The team absorbs it quietly to be helpful. The sprint goal is compromised, and nobody decided that it should be. Here is how it happens: → Change arrives late in the sprint → Reason for the change is never established → Effort is never assessed → Dependencies are never assessed → Options are never laid out for the product owner → Team absorbs the change and the goal slips The assumption was: "The team can absorb it." Why? A late change needs a careful assessment: establish the reason, the effort, the dependencies and the options the product owner has, and do not silently compromise the sprint goal to absorb it. The product owner decides, with the evidence in front of them, whether the change is worth the disruption or whether it waits for the next sprint. A late change is a decision, not an instruction. BA Takeaway Present the options with the evidence, and

entries.title: Two senior stakeholders, opposite outcomes, one undocumented call
entries.text: Two senior stakeholders, opposite outcomes, one undocumented call Core Two senior stakeholders want opposite outcomes on a EUR 250,000 payment decision. A call is made in the room. It is never documented, and the debate reopens at the next meeting. Here is how it happens: → Two senior stakeholders want opposite outcomes → Value, risk, cost and customer impact are debated → Evidence drives the ranking → A decision is made → Who made it and why is never recorded → The debate reopens The assumption was: "The senior person decides." Why? Facilitate an evidence based prioritisation and document the accountable decision. A documented decision ends the debate; an undocumented one will be reopened every time the stakeholders meet. A documented decision ends the debate. BA Takeaway Lay out the value, the risk, the cost and the customer impact of each requirement, let the evidence drive the ranking, and record who made the decision and why. Keep these controls separate: → Evidence for each

entries.title: The process change that arrived the day before UAT
entries.text: The process change that arrived the day before UAT Core A process change arrives the day before user acceptance testing on a EUR 180,000 payment release. It is approved without assessment. The testing already done is invalidated, and the release date is at risk. Here is how it happens: → Process change is requested just before UAT → Requirement impact is never assessed → Test scope is never assessed → Release risk is never assessed → Decision rights are never confirmed → Change is approved, and completed testing is silently voided The assumption was: "It is a small process tweak." Why? A change approved without this assessment can invalidate the testing that has already been done and put the release date at risk. Never let a late change silently void completed testing. BA Takeaway Assess requirement impact, test scope, release risk and decision rights before approving any change this close to UAT. Keep these controls separate: → Requirement impact → Test scope → Release risk →

entries.title: Built exactly to sign-off, and the user still said no
entries.text: Built exactly to sign-off, and the user still said no Core A feature is built exactly to signed-off requirements. The user rejects it. The team argues about whether it is a defect, and the argument lasts longer than the fix would have. Here is how it happens: → Feature is built to signed-off requirements → User rejects it → No one classifies the cause → Defect, ambiguity, missed need and scope change are all treated the same → The wrong owner works on the wrong fix The assumption was: "It matches the sign-off, so it must be right." Why? A defect means the build does not match the requirement, an ambiguity means the requirement was read differently, a missed need means the requirement was incomplete, and a scope change means the need has moved. Each cause has a different owner and a different fix. Each cause has a different owner and a different fix. BA Takeaway Classify the rejection first: defect, ambiguity, missed need or scope change. The classification decides the owner and the

entries.title: The UAT that tested the system and missed the business
entries.text: The UAT that tested the system and missed the business Core User acceptance testing is planned for a EUR 110,000 payment release. The test cases cover the system mechanics. The business journeys are never tested, and acceptance fails on the first real journey. Here is how it happens: → Test cases are built from system mechanics → Business journeys are never mapped → Acceptance criteria are never defined per journey → Roles that must perform each journey are never identified → Exception paths are never covered → Tests pass, and the business says no The assumption was: "Test the system." Why? UAT coverage is derived from the business journeys, the acceptance criteria, the roles involved and the exception paths. Test cases built from this coverage test the business outcome rather than the system mechanics, which is what acceptance testing is for. Test the business outcome, not the system mechanics. BA Takeaway Map each business journey, define the criteria that prove it works, name the

entries.title: The defect debate that ran on opinion, not evidence
entries.text: The defect debate that ran on opinion, not evidence Core A system integration testing defect is raised on a EUR 70,000 payment flow. The discussion runs on opinion for an hour. Nobody has checked whether the defect can even be reproduced. Here is how it happens: → Defect is raised in SIT → Reproducibility is never assessed → Traceability to the requirement is never checked → Business impact is never assessed → Fix validation and regression are never planned → The debate runs on opinion The assumption was: "The defect is obvious." Why? Reproducibility decides whether the defect is real, traceability shows which requirement it breaks, business impact decides its priority, fix validation confirms the fix works, and regression confirms nothing else broke. Evidence, not opinion, decides a defect. BA Takeaway Assess reproducibility, traceability, business impact, fix validation and regression for every defect, in that order. Keep these controls separate: → Reproducibility → Traceability and

entries.title: Hypercare ended on a date, and the EUR 40,000 exceptions were still open
entries.text: Hypercare ended on a date, and the EUR 40,000 exceptions were still open Core A payment release goes live, and hypercare runs for two weeks. On day fourteen, hypercare ends, because the calendar says so. EUR 40,000 of exceptions are still unresolved, and nobody is watching them. Here is how it happens: → Deployment goes live → Critical journeys are monitored → Exception rates are monitored → Unresolved transactions are monitored → Stakeholder updates go out → Hypercare ends after a fixed number of days, while the measures are still unstable The assumption was: "Hypercare runs for two weeks." Why? Critical journeys show whether customers can complete their payments, exception rates show whether the system is handling failures, and unresolved transactions show what still needs attention. Hypercare ends when these measures are stable, not when a fixed number of days has passed. Hypercare ends when the measures are stable, not when the calendar runs out. BA Takeaway End hypercare on

entries.title: The behaviour changed in production, and nobody knew which layer broke it
entries.text: The behaviour changed in production, and nobody knew which layer broke it Core A EUR 50,000 payment behaves differently in production than intended. The team fixes the code. The fault was in the requirement, so the fix changes nothing, and the same miss recurs. Here is how it happens: → Intended behaviour diverges from production behaviour → Requirement layer is never checked → Development layer is blamed by default → Testing layer is never checked → Environment layer is never checked → Fix lands at the wrong layer The assumption was: "Fix the code." Why? Check the requirement first, then the development, then the testing, then the environment, and find the layer where the divergence was introduced. Locating the layer matters because it decides whether the fix is a requirement correction, a code change, a test improvement or an environment fix. Fix at the layer that introduced the fault. BA Takeaway Use a layered failure model to locate where it went wrong, and fix at that layer. Keep

entries.title: The dashboard that said healthy while customers failed
entries.text: The dashboard that said healthy while customers failed Core A digital banking dashboard shows adoption climbing. The dashboard says healthy. Customers are failing to complete their payments, and the KPI set never measures it. Here is how it happens: → Adoption is measured, and it climbs → Task completion is never measured → Failure is never measured → Service performance is never measured → Risk is never measured → Customer outcome is never measured → The dashboard reports health while customers fail The assumption was: "Adoption is the KPI." Why? Key performance indicators should cover adoption, task completion, failure, service, risk and customer outcome measures. Adoption shows whether customers use the feature, task completion shows whether they can finish what they start, failure shows where they are blocked, service shows whether the system performs, risk shows whether controls are holding, and customer outcome shows whether the feature delivered value. A KPI set that covers

entries.title: The payment page customers kept abandoning
entries.text: The payment page customers kept abandoning Core A merchant watches customers abandon the payment page every day. The team treats it as one problem with one cause. It is five problems wearing one label, and each needs a different fix. Here is how it happens: → Customers reach the payment page → The funnel shows where they drop off → Validation errors block them → Latency makes them wait → Payment options do not match what they want → The experience they report is poor → Each cause points to a different fix The assumption was: "Abandonment is one problem." Why? Customers abandon a payment page for reasons that can be found in the evidence: the funnel, the validation errors, the latency, the payment options and the user experience. The analysis must separate them rather than treating abandonment as a single problem with a single cause. Abandonment is several problems wearing one label. BA Takeaway Separate the five causes before choosing a fix, or the fix will treat the wrong problem.

entries.title: The loan approval that took two days, and nobody knew where the time went
entries.text: The loan approval that took two days, and nobody knew where the time went Core Loan approval time rises from hours to days. Everyone has an opinion about where the delay is. Nobody has measured it. Here is how it happens: → Approval time rises from hours to days → The process is never mapped → Queues where applications wait are never found → Manual checks that add delay are never found → Dependencies on other teams are never found → Rework where applications are sent back is never found → Opinions fill the gap where measurement should be The assumption was: "Ask people where the delay is." Why? Map the process to find the bottleneck: look for queues, manual checks, dependencies and rework. The bottleneck is usually a queue or a manual step rather than the decision itself, so measuring where time is actually spent is more useful than asking people where they think the delay is. Measure the clock, not the opinion. BA Takeaway Map the process, measure where time is actually spent, and

entries.title: Every test passed, and UAT still failed
entries.text: Every test passed, and UAT still failed Core All test cases pass. UAT still fails. The suite is green, and the business need is unmet, because the tests never represented the real business journeys. Here is how it happens: → Test cases all pass → Test design has gaps → Test data does not represent real business use → Expected outcomes are wrong → The unmet business need was never covered by a test at all → Acceptance fails The assumption was: "All tests pass, so we are ready." Why? Passing test cases do not prove the business need is met. Check the test design for gaps, the representativeness of the test data, the expected outcomes for correctness, and whether the unmet business need was ever covered by a test at all. Passing tests are not proof. Representation is. BA Takeaway Check design, data, expected outcomes and coverage of the real business need before calling a suite ready. Keep these controls separate: → Test design → Test data → Expected outcomes and coverage The real

entries.title: The same change, requested every sprint
entries.text: The same change, requested every sprint Core The same change is requested every sprint. It is implemented every sprint. It keeps coming back, because the root cause was never fixed. Here is how it happens: → Same change is requested → It is implemented again → The unresolved root need is never found → Weak discovery missed the real requirement → Policy uncertainty leaves the team guessing → No one owns the decision, so no one can say no → The request returns next sprint The assumption was: "Add it to the backlog again." Why? The root cause is usually unresolved: an unresolved root need that the change does not actually satisfy, weak discovery that missed the real requirement, policy uncertainty, or a lack of decision ownership. Fixing the root cause stops the repeated request; implementing the same change again will not. Repeat requests are a symptom, not a backlog. BA Takeaway Stop re-implementing and find the root cause: the need, the discovery, the policy or the ownership. Keep

entries.title: The rule the developers guessed, and the EUR 25,000 payment that proved them wrong
entries.text: The rule the developers guessed, and the EUR 25,000 payment that proved them wrong Core A rule for a EUR 25,000 payment is stated as a business sentence. The developer guesses the boundary. The payment proves the guess wrong, and the rule has to be rewritten after the build. Here is how it happens: → Rule is stated as a business sentence → Triggers that start the rule are never stated → Conditions that apply are never stated → Data involved is never stated → Expected behaviour is never stated → Failure outcomes are never stated → Developer guesses, and the guess is wrong The assumption was: "The business sentence is enough." Why? A rule stated as a business sentence leaves the developer guessing about the boundary, while a rule stated with triggers, conditions and failure outcomes can be built and tested without further questions. Precision at the boundary is what makes a rule buildable. BA Takeaway State triggers, conditions, data, expected behaviour and failure outcomes for every

entries.title: The test that could not pass or fail
entries.text: The test that could not pass or fail Core A test is written for a EUR 30,000 payment scenario. It has steps, but no expected result. It runs, and nobody can say whether it passed or failed. Here is how it happens: → Business scenario is translated into a test → Positive scenario is written → Negative scenario is written → Boundary scenario is written → Regression scenario is written → No expected result is stated for any of them → The test cannot pass or fail The assumption was: "Write the test steps." Why? Positive scenarios prove the happy path works, negative scenarios prove invalid input is handled, boundary scenarios prove the limits behave correctly, and regression scenarios prove existing behaviour still works. Each scenario needs an expected result, because a test without an expected result cannot pass or fail. A test without an expected result cannot pass or fail. BA Takeaway Give every scenario an expected result, across positive, negative, boundary and regression coverage.

entries.title: Feature complete, and the business problem still standing
entries.text: Feature complete, and the business problem still standing Core A feature for a EUR 130,000 payment flow is delivered complete, on time. The business problem is still there. The team celebrates delivery, while the users keep working around the problem. Here is how it happens: → Feature is built as specified → Hypothesis behind the feature is never revisited → Actual user behaviour is never checked → Process adoption is never checked → Operational constraints are never checked → Outcome measures are never checked → Delivery is celebrated, and the problem remains The assumption was: "Delivery is success." Why? The gap is usually that the feature was built as specified but the hypothesis was wrong, or that users did not adopt it, or that an operational constraint was missed. Measuring the outcome rather than the delivery reveals the gap. Measuring the outcome rather than the delivery reveals the gap. BA Takeaway Revisit the hypothesis, the user behaviour, the adoption, the constraints and

entries.title: Loan approval: two hours became two days
entries.text: Loan approval: two hours became two days Core Loan approval time grows from two hours to two days. The team wants to change something, anything. Nobody knows which of the five causes is actually responsible. Here is how it happens: → Approval time grows from two hours to two days → Queue time is never analysed → Manual reviews are never analysed → Document quality is never analysed → Decision rules are never analysed → Hand-offs are never analysed → A change is made blind The assumption was: "Change something, anything." Why? Queue time shows where applications wait, manual reviews show where human effort adds delay, document quality shows where rework is created, decision rules show where the logic is slow, and hand-offs show where work is lost between teams. The fix depends on which of these is actually causing the delay. Measure before changing anything. BA Takeaway Analyse queue time, manual reviews, document quality, decision rules and hand-offs, then fix the cause the

entries.title: The change request that came back, again and again
entries.text: The change request that came back, again and again Core Stakeholders repeat the same change request, release after release. It is implemented, again and again. The cycle repeats, because the cause is never fixed. Here is how it happens: → Same change request is repeated → It is implemented again → Root need was never satisfied → Decision took so long the requester assumed it was ignored → Discovery missed the real requirement → Feedback loop never closed with the requester → The request comes back The assumption was: "Implement it again." Why? The root need may never have been satisfied, the decision may have taken so long that the requester assumed it was ignored, the discovery may have missed the real requirement, or the feedback loop may never have closed the loop with the requester. Each cause has a different fix. Implementing the change again without fixing the cause will only repeat the cycle. BA Takeaway Investigate the root need, the decision latency, the incomplete discovery

entries.title: EUR 50,000 supplier payment stalled, and no one owned the fix
entries.text: EUR 50,000 supplier payment stalled, and no one owned the fix Core A EUR 50,000 supplier payment sat unreleased for three days. Every team said it was someone else's job. The BA owned the outcome, but no team reported to the BA. Here's how that happens: → pacs.008 held for a missing approval → Operations waited for Compliance → Compliance waited for the business → No one chased the decision, so nothing moved The requirement said: "The BA owns delivery." But ownership came with no authority over any team, no decision record and no date. Why? Ownership without authority fails when the ask is vague. Each team assumed another team was acting, and with no recorded decision there was nothing to follow up on and no one to escalate to. Authority is borrowed. Clarity is owned. What proves a blocked payment is actually moving again? BA Takeaway State what is needed and by when, in writing. Record every decision so accountability is visible. Follow up on actions instead of assuming they will

entries.title: The client said our new process broke their EUR 120,000 payroll run
entries.text: The client said our new process broke their EUR 120,000 payroll run Core A client's EUR 120,000 payroll run failed on the first day of the new process. Four hundred salaries were held. The client said the new process had damaged their operations. Here's how that happens: → New release went live on Monday → Client payroll file failed validation → EUR 120,000 in salaries held → Support blamed the client file before checking the change The assumption was: "The client must be doing something wrong." Nobody checked what the release had changed first. Why? A changed validation rule rejected a field the old process had accepted. The file was fine. The process had changed underneath it, and the team defended the release instead of reading the evidence. Empathy first, evidence second, blame never. What proves the new process, and not the client file, caused the failure? BA Takeaway Acknowledge the impact first. That does not admit fault, it shows the client is taken seriously. Provide a safe

entries.title: EUR 2 million in payments, and no one could prove where they were
entries.text: EUR 2 million in payments, and no one could prove where they were Core Volumes tripled in an hour during a payment surge. EUR 2 million of payments were in flight. Timeouts rose, and no one could prove which payments had settled and which had not. Here's how that happens: → Volumes tripled in one hour → Timeout rates climbed across the gateway → Gateway responses mixed success and failure → Reconciliation showed gaps nobody could explain The instruction was: "Just restart it and see." Restarting without evidence would have risked paying twice or losing payments entirely. Why? Without transaction IDs, gateway responses, API logs, timestamps and reconciliation status, the team was guessing. Each piece of evidence answers a different question, and only together do they show where the money is. Without evidence, incident response is guesswork. What proves a payment in the surge settled, failed, or is still stuck? BA Takeaway Collect transaction IDs to link evidence to individual payments.

entries.title: Five teams, one EUR 500,000 outage, five different stories
entries.text: Five teams, one EUR 500,000 outage, five different stories Core A EUR 500,000 payment run stopped mid-flight. Business, development, QA, gateway and support each opened their own ticket. Each team worked from a different picture of the same outage. Here's how that happens: → Payment run stopped mid-flight → Five teams opened five separate tickets → Two teams chased the same gateway error → No team owned the customer message The assumption was: "Each team will sort its own part." Nobody owned the whole incident, so work overlapped and the customer heard nothing. Why? Without one incident view, teams duplicate effort and the incident lasts longer than it should. Clear owners stop work falling between teams, and a regular update cadence keeps everyone aligned. Without one incident view, teams duplicate effort and the incident lasts longer than it should. What proves the incident is under control, not just busy? BA Takeaway Build one incident view first. Name a clear owner for each

entries.title: Five certificates, but no proof of one real payment project
entries.text: Five certificates, but no proof of one real payment project Core A BA showed five certificates for a EUR 250,000 payments migration. The panel asked for one artefact from the work. There was nothing to show. Here's how that happens: → Certificates listed on the CV → Panel asked for the problem statement → No process map, no user story, no API contract → No UAT evidence that anything was delivered The assumption was: "Theory proves capability." Theory shows what was studied. It does not show what was actually done. Why? A portfolio built only from courses has no chain from problem to delivered outcome. A reviewer cannot see the scope, the decisions or the result, so the certificates carry no weight. Show the chain, not the certificate. What proves this BA delivered the work, not just studied it? BA Takeaway Build the portfolio from real work: a problem statement, process maps, user stories, an API contract and UAT evidence. Each piece shows one link in the chain from problem to

entries.title: The interview answer listed tasks, but the EUR 1 million result was missing
entries.text: The interview answer listed tasks, but the EUR 1 million result was missing Core A BA walked through a EUR 1 million payments project for ten minutes. The panel heard tasks, tools and meetings. They never heard what the project delivered. Here's how that happens: → Project described as a list of tasks → Role and decisions never stated → Systems named, risks never mentioned → No measurable result at the end The assumption was: "Listing what I did shows my value." A list of tasks shows time occupied. It does not prove value delivered. Why? Measurable results matter most, because they prove the work delivered value rather than simply occupying time. Without the result, the panel cannot tell whether the project succeeded. Measurable results matter most, because they prove the work delivered value rather than simply occupying time. What proves this project delivered value? BA Takeaway Structure the walkthrough around the problem, the role played, the decisions made, the systems involved,

entries.title: Seven questions in, the EUR 750,000 project walkthrough still had no shape
entries.text: Seven questions in, the EUR 750,000 project walkthrough still had no shape Core A BA started walking through a EUR 750,000 live payments project. Seven questions in, the panel still did not know the scope, the stakeholders or the outcome. The walkthrough had become a list of tasks. Here's how that happens: → Context never set → Scope never stated → Stakeholders never named → Deliverables and outcomes never reached The assumption was: "Start at the beginning and the story will shape itself." Without a structure, a walkthrough drifts, and the listener fills the gaps with guesses. Why? Context sets the scene, scope shows the size of the work, stakeholders show who was involved, systems show the technical landscape, deliverables show what was produced, decisions show judgement, and outcomes show the result. Miss any link and the story has a hole. A walkthrough without structure becomes a list of tasks. What proves the listener understood the project, not just heard about it? BA Takeaway

entries.title: EUR 80,000 came back, but the return was sent to the wrong bank
entries.text: EUR 80,000 came back, but the return was sent to the wrong bank Core A beneficiary bank returned EUR 80,000. The originator bank waited for it. The return never arrived, because it was sent straight to the originator instead of back through the chain. Here's how that happens: → pacs.008 sent EUR 80,000 to the beneficiary → Beneficiary bank returns it with pacs.004 → Return sent directly to the originator, skipping the intermediary → Originator cannot match it, and the funds sit unreconciled The assumption was: "A return goes straight back to where the payment came from." In a three-bank chain, the return must travel the chain in reverse. Why? The intermediary that received the pacs.004 must send a new pacs.004 back to the originator bank, carrying the reference to the original payment. Skip the intermediary and the link between the return and the original payment breaks. A return travels the chain in reverse, or it travels nowhere. entries.title: EUR 80,000 arrived back, but no one could say which payment it was
entries.text: EUR 80,000 arrived back, but no one could say which payment it was Core EUR 80,000 arrived back at the originator bank. The credit sat in the account for two days. No one could say which payment it belonged to. Here's how that happens: → → pacs.004 arrives as a credit → → Original instruction identification missing from the trail → → Original end-to-end identification missing too → → Reconciliation cannot place the credit The assumption was: "A credit is a credit. Book it and move on." A credit with no story cannot be booked against any payment. Why? A pacs.004 carries the original instruction identification and the original end-to-end identification, and those two references tie it to the payment it returns. Without them the return is only a credit, and reconciliation cannot prove which payment it belongs to. Without those references a return is only a credit with no story. What proves this credit belongs to that payment? BA Takeaway Never book a return on amount alone. Match the

entries.title: EUR 120,000 recalled, and the recall had to cross three banks
entries.text: EUR 120,000 recalled, and the recall had to cross three banks Core A customer asked for EUR 120,000 back. The payment had already crossed an intermediary bank. One message could not bring it back, because the money sat at the end of a chain. Here's how that happens: → → Originator bank sends camt.056 to the intermediary → → Intermediary forwards camt.056 to the beneficiary bank → → Beneficiary bank checks whether the recall is feasible → → Beneficiary bank returns funds with pacs.004 → → Intermediary sends pacs.004 back to the originator The assumption was: "Send one recall and the money comes back." A recall is a chain of messages, not a single message. Why? Each bank in the chain must act in turn. The funds come back only when every bank in the chain acts, so a recall that stops at any link leaves the money where it is. A recall is a chain of messages, not a single message. What proves every bank in the chain acted on the recall? BA Takeaway Send the camt.056 through the same chain

entries.title: EUR 60,000 returned, and both ends claimed the return was theirs to start
entries.text: EUR 60,000 returned, and both ends claimed the return was theirs to start Core EUR 60,000 had to come back. The originator bank said it would start the return. The beneficiary bank said it would start the return. Both were right, and the team argued about it for a day. Here's how that happens: → → Originator side recalls the payment → → Beneficiary side rejects a payment it cannot apply → → Both use the same message, pacs.004 → → Only the initiating bank and the reason differ The assumption was: "A return can only start at one end." A return can be started from either end of the payment. Why? The originator side starts a pacs.004 when it recalls or reverses a payment, and the beneficiary side starts one when it rejects or returns a payment it cannot apply. The message is identical in both cases. The message is identical in both cases. Only the initiating bank and the reason differ. What proves who started this return, and why? BA Takeaway Read the initiating bank and the reason code

entries.title: EUR 45,000 recall sent, and the only answer was silence
entries.text: EUR 45,000 recall sent, and the only answer was silence Core A EUR 45,000 payment went to the wrong beneficiary. The originator bank sent a camt.056 recall. Days passed. No answer came, and no one could close the case. Here's how that happens: → → camt.056 recall sent → → No camt.029 received → → Funds still with the beneficiary bank → → Originator cannot close the recall The assumption was: "The recall was sent, so the case is moving." Sending a recall proves nothing. Only the answer closes the question. Why? A camt.029 answers a camt.056 by stating whether the recall has been accepted or refused. The originator bank cannot close the recall until that response arrives and confirms whether the funds are coming back. No camt.029 means no closure. Silence is not an answer. What proves the recall was accepted or refused? BA Takeaway Track the recall as open until the camt.029 arrives. entries.title: EUR 30,000 returned with a reason code no bank recognised
entries.text: EUR 30,000 returned with a reason code no bank recognised Core EUR 30,000 came back as a pacs.004. The reason code on it did not exist in the scheme rulebook. The next bank in the chain rejected the return, and the money sat in limbo. Here's how that happens: → → Payment returned with a pacs.004 → → Reason code invented by the returning bank → → Next bank does not recognise the code → → Return rejected, funds stuck The assumption was: "Any code that describes the problem will do." A reason code is a controlled vocabulary, not a free-text field. Why? The reason code comes from the bank that refused the payment, and the scheme rulebook lists the codes that bank may use. A bank that invents one risks the return being rejected by the next bank in the chain. A reason code is a controlled vocabulary, not a free-text field. What proves this reason code is one the next bank will accept? BA Takeaway Use only codes from the scheme rulebook. Check the code against the rulebook before sending,

entries.title: EUR 95,000 rejected, and the pacs.002 said nothing useful
entries.text: EUR 95,000 rejected, and the pacs.002 said nothing useful Core A EUR 95,000 pacs.008 was rejected. The pacs.002 that reported it named the payment and nothing else. The originator bank spent a day guessing what had gone wrong. Here's how that happens: → → pacs.008 sent for EUR 95,000 → → Payment rejected → → pacs.002 arrives with no status and no reason code → → Originator bank guesses at the cause The assumption was: "Reporting the rejection is enough." A report without a reason is a message, not an answer. Why? When a pacs.008 is rejected, the pacs.002 must identify the original payment and carry the status and the reason code, so the originator bank knows the payment did not settle and why. A pacs.002 without status and reason leaves the originator guessing. What proves why this payment was rejected? entries.title: EUR 200,000 announced, but the funds had not arrived yet
entries.text: EUR 200,000 announced, but the funds had not arrived yet Core An MT103 announced EUR 200,000 to the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary called, asking where the money was. The funds leg had not arrived yet, and the beneficiary had not been credited. Here's how that happens: → → MT103 reaches the beneficiary bank first → → MT202 COV still in transit → → Beneficiary bank holds the instruction → → Beneficiary asks for money that has not settled The assumption was: "The MT103 arrived, so the money is here." In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV travel separately. Why? The beneficiary bank must hold the instruction and wait for the cover, because it cannot credit the beneficiary until the funds have settled. This timing gap is a normal feature of the cover method, not an error. MT103 first, funds later, is normal. Crediting early is the error. What proves the funds have settled, not just been announced? BA Takeaway Hold the MT103 until the cover arrives. Credit only on settled

entries.title: EUR 200,000 cover arrived, and it looked like an ordinary transfer
entries.text: EUR 200,000 cover arrived, and it looked like an ordinary transfer Core EUR 200,000 arrived at the beneficiary bank as an MT202 COV. Nothing on it said which customer payment it was for. An MT103 for the same amount was waiting, unmatched, and the beneficiary was not credited. Here's how that happens: → MT202 COV arrives at the beneficiary bank → No reference links it to the waiting MT103 → Cover looks like an ordinary bank-to-bank transfer → Beneficiary bank cannot match it, so it holds the funds The assumption was: "The amount is the same, so the match is obvious." Amounts repeat. References are the bridge. Why? When an MT202 COV reaches the beneficiary bank, the bank must recognise that its purpose is to cover a specific MT103, and the link is the reference and the fields that tie the two messages together. Without that link the cover looks like an ordinary transfer. The reference is the bridge between the information leg and the funds leg. What proves this cover belongs to that

entries.title: EUR 150,000 cover sent to the wrong bank
entries.text: EUR 150,000 cover sent to the wrong bank Core A EUR 150,000 cover payment was sent. The MT202 COV went to a bank that held no settlement account for it. The funds landed where no one expected them, and settlement stopped. Here's how that happens: → MT202 COV addressed to the wrong bank → Funds land in an account that was not expecting them → Beneficiary bank waits for a cover that never comes → Settlement stops The assumption was: "The address on the cover is an administrative detail." The address is part of the settlement design. Why? In a chain, the MT202 COV is addressed to the bank that holds the account from which the funds will settle, and each bank addresses its own cover leg to the next bank that will fund it. Addressing the cover to the wrong bank breaks settlement. The address is part of the settlement design, not an administrative detail. What proves this cover was addressed to the bank that will fund it? BA Takeaway Address each cover leg to the bank holding the settlement

entries.title: EUR 150,000 cover rejected, and the refund went to the wrong bank
entries.text: EUR 150,000 cover rejected, and the refund went to the wrong bank Core A EUR 150,000 cover payment was rejected. The bank holding the funds sent them back. They went to the wrong bank, and one exception became two. Here's how that happens: → Cover payment is rejected → Bank holding the cover returns the funds → Return sent to the wrong bank in the chain → Second exception opened on top of the first The assumption was: "Any bank in the chain can return the funds." The funds must travel back along the same correspondent path they came on. Why? When a cover payment is rejected, the funds leg and the information leg have different senders, so the bank holding the rejected cover must return the funds to the bank that sent them. A return sent to the wrong bank creates a second exception on top of the first. A return sent to the wrong bank creates a second exception on top of the first. entries.title: EUR 90,000 cover, and two different ordering customers
entries.text: EUR 90,000 cover, and two different ordering customers Core A EUR 90,000 cover payment arrived. The MT103 named one ordering customer. The MT202 COV named a different one. The operations team spent a day arguing over who had sent the payment. Here's how that happens: → MT103 names the instructing customer → MT202 COV names the funding bank → Team treats them as one party → Screening and reporting land on the wrong party The assumption was: "One payment, one ordering customer." Each message has its own ordering party for its own leg. Why? The MT103 names the customer who instructed the payment, while the MT202 COV names the bank moving the funds. Treating them as one party confuses the screening, the reporting and the audit trail. Each message has its own ordering party for its own leg. What proves which party counts for which leg? BA Takeaway Read the ordering party per message, per leg. Screen the MT103 party as the instructing customer and the MT202 COV party as the funding bank,

entries.title: EUR 75,000 cover, and field 72 sent the funds to the wrong place
entries.text: EUR 75,000 cover, and field 72 sent the funds to the wrong place Core A EUR 75,000 cover payment was sent with a free-text instruction in field 72. The next bank read it the wrong way. The funds went to the wrong place, and settlement stopped. Here's how that happens: → MT202 COV sent with field 72 filled → Instruction written loosely, in free text → Next bank acts on the wrong reading → Funds sent astray, settlement delayed The assumption was: "Field 72 is free text, so any wording will do." Free text is exactly why discipline matters. Why? Field 72 carries sender-to-receiver information, and in a cover payment it tells the next bank what the cover is for and what to do with it. A wrong instruction can send the funds to the wrong place or delay settlement. Put only the instruction the next bank needs, in the form the next bank expects. entries.title: USD 100,000 sent, USD 99,850 received, and no one could explain the gap
entries.text: USD 100,000 sent, USD 99,850 received, and no one could explain the gap Core A customer sent USD 100,000 by serial payment. The beneficiary was credited USD 99,850. USD 150 had vanished, and no one at the bank could explain where it went. Here's how that happens: → Ordering customer sends USD 100,000 → First intermediary deducts its charge → Second intermediary deducts its charge → Beneficiary credited USD 99,850 The assumption was: "The beneficiary receives what the sender sent." In a serial payment, every intermediary deducts its own charge on the way. Why? The ordering customer bears the charges, and each intermediary bank deducts its own charge from the amount as the payment passes through. The beneficiary therefore receives the amount minus the charges deducted at each step. In a serial payment, every deduction in the chain lands on the beneficiary. What proves each deduction in the chain was agreed and expected? BA Takeaway Price a serial payment by accounting for every

entries.title: USD 100,000 sent, two deductions, one credit that did not add up
entries.text: USD 100,000 sent, two deductions, one credit that did not add up Core USD 100,000 was sent through two intermediary banks. Each took a charge. The beneficiary bank could not prove the final credit was right, because the fields that explain the deductions were missing. Here's how that happens: → Two intermediaries each deduct a charge → Field 71A states who bears the charges → Field 71F states each charge deducted → Beneficiary bank works out the final credit from those fields The assumption was: "The credit speaks for itself." Without fields 71A and 71F, the credit is a number with no story. Why? Field 71A states who bears the charges, and field 71F states the amount of each charge deducted, so the credit can be reconciled against the amount the ordering customer sent. Without those fields the beneficiary cannot reconcile the credit against the amount sent. Without fields 71A and 71F, the beneficiary cannot reconcile the credit against the amount sent. entries.title: USD 100,000, and the charges were counted twice
entries.text: USD 100,000, and the charges were counted twice Core A USD 100,000 payment mixed serial and cover legs. Charges were deducted on the serial leg, then charged again on the cover leg. The beneficiary was short, and the customer was charged twice for the same journey. Here's how that happens: → Serial leg deducts charges step by step → Cover leg handles its charges separately → Payment mixes the two methods → Beneficiary short, customer double-charged The assumption was: "Charges work the same way in every payment." Charge arithmetic follows the payment method. Why? In a serial payment charges are deducted step by step as the payment passes through each intermediary, while in a cover payment the charges on the information leg and the funds leg are handled separately. A payment that mixes the two methods without care can double-charge or under-charge. Know which method applies before working out what the beneficiary will receive. entries.title: USD 85,000 return that tried to jump the chain
entries.text: USD 85,000 return that tried to jump the chain Core A USD 85,000 MT103 was returned. The return was sent straight to the originator bank. It never arrived, because the chain it had travelled on was skipped. Here's how that happens: → MT103 is returned → Return sent directly to the originator → Intermediary banks skipped → Return cannot be matched, funds sit unreconciled The assumption was: "A return is a new payment, so send it direct." A return is not a new payment. Why? When an MT103 is returned, the funds come back through the same chain of banks that carried the payment forward, each bank sending the return to the bank that sent it the payment. The charges on the return follow fields 71A and 71F, so the amount that comes back is the amount sent minus the charges already deducted. A return is not a new payment. It is the original payment travelling backwards. What proves the return travelled back through the same chain? BA Takeaway Send the return through the same banks that

entries.title: USD 40,000 sent to an account that did not exist
entries.text: USD 40,000 sent to an account that did not exist Core USD 40,000 was sent to a beneficiary account. The account number was wrong. The beneficiary bank could not credit anyone, and the customer asked where the money was. Here's how that happens: → Beneficiary bank finds the account invalid → Wrong number, closed account or mismatched name → Beneficiary bank returns the payment → Return travels back through the intermediary to the originator The assumption was: "The beneficiary bank can sort it out and keep the funds." The beneficiary bank cannot keep funds it cannot apply. Why? When the beneficiary bank finds the customer account invalid, it returns the payment, and the return must travel back through the intermediary to the originator bank. It cannot return the funds directly to the originator while an intermediary sits in between. An invalid account is the most common reason for a return, and the handling never changes. What proves the return is on its way back through the chain? BA

entries.title: EUR 60,000 settled, and the recall had nowhere to go
entries.text: EUR 60,000 settled, and the recall had nowhere to go Core A customer asked for EUR 60,000 back after the payment had settled. The originator bank sent a camt.056 recall. The clearing house did not support the message, so the recall went nowhere. Here's how that happens: → Payment settles through the clearing house → Originator bank sends camt.056 → Clearing house does not support the recall message → Recall cannot reach the beneficiary bank The assumption was: "Every clearing system carries recalls." Some clearing houses do not support the camt.056 recall message. Why? The originator bank and the clearing system cannot send a recall to the beneficiary bank for a payment that has already settled when the clearing house does not support the message. The Estonian clearing house is a real example: it does not support the recall message, so a settled payment cannot be recalled through that route. entries.title: EUR 110,000 recalled after the beneficiary had already spent it
entries.text: EUR 110,000 recalled after the beneficiary had already spent it Core EUR 110,000 was paid to the wrong beneficiary. By the time the customer noticed, the beneficiary had already spent it. The recall went out anyway, and the customer expected the money back. Here's how that happens: → Payment executed and funds spent → camt.056 sent to ask for the return → Beneficiary bank asks its customer whether it agrees → Funds no longer there, recall cannot complete by message alone The assumption was: "A recall reverses a payment." Once the money has been spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal. Why? A camt.056 can still be sent to ask the beneficiary bank to return the money, but the beneficiary bank must ask its customer whether it agrees. If the funds are no longer there, the recall cannot be completed by message alone, and the customer must take action against the beneficiary. Once the money has been spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal. What proves the funds are still there to

entries.title: EUR 70,000 recall for a third party, sent to the wrong bank
entries.text: EUR 70,000 recall for a third party, sent to the wrong bank Core A EUR 70,000 recall was made in favour of a third-party beneficiary. The recall was sent straight to the third party. It sat unread, because the third party was never meant to receive it. Here's how that happens: → Recall made for a third-party beneficiary → Recall sent directly to the third party → Third party cannot act on it → Recall stalls, funds stay put The assumption was: "The recall goes to the party the money is for." The third party never receives the recall directly. Why? The recall is sent to the first agent in the chain, the bank that must return the credit, and that bank then passes the recall onward. entries.title: EUR 55,000 recall rejected, with a reason code that did not belong there
entries.text: EUR 55,000 recall rejected, with a reason code that did not belong there Core A EUR 55,000 recall was refused. The refusal came back as a pacs.004 carrying the reason code GVC. GVC is not a code for a return, so the handling was wrong, and the case had to be reopened. Here's how that happens: → camt.056 recall request sent → Recall refused → Refusal returned as pacs.004 with GVC → Code does not belong on a return, second exception opened The assumption was: "Any reason code explains a refusal." A reason code must match the message and the situation. Why? A camt.056 recall request can itself be rejected, and the reason code on the refusal must fit the message carrying it. A pacs.004 carrying GVC is a code used in the wrong place, and it creates a second exception on top of the first. A reason code must match the message and the situation.
