entries.title: EUR 25,000 stuck, and the team sent a camt.056 when they needed a camt.026
entries.text: EUR 25,000 stuck, and the team sent a camt.056 when they needed a camt.026 Core EUR 25,000 could not be applied by the receiving bank. The team sent a camt.056 to recall it. Nothing happened, because a recall asks for money back, and this payment needed a report that it could not be applied. Here's how that happens: → Payment cannot be applied → Team sends camt.056 recall → No funds to recall, nothing happens → Correct message, camt.026, never sent The assumption was: "Both messages are about a payment that did not complete, so either will do." They do different jobs. Why? A camt.056 requests a recall of a payment, asking the beneficiary bank to return funds that have already been credited. A camt.026 reports that a payment cannot be applied, telling the sender that the instruction could not be processed. One asks for money back. The other reports it could not be applied. What proves we sent the message that matches what actually happened? BA Takeaway Ask first what happened: were

entries.title: EUR 180,000 returned without a pacs.004, and the chain lost the link
entries.text: EUR 180,000 returned without a pacs.004, and the chain lost the link Core EUR 180,000 had to come back. The returning bank sent the funds by another route, not a pacs.004. The money arrived, but no bank in the chain could prove which payment it belonged to. Here's how that happens: → Payment must be returned → Return sent by another route, not pacs.004 → Funds arrive with no link to the original payment → Chain cannot match the return The assumption was: "Any route that moves the money is good enough." Using another route breaks the link. Why? The pacs.004 is the ISO 20022 message designed for returns in the SEPA interbank space, and it carries the link to the original payment that lets every bank in the chain match it. Using another route breaks that link. Using another route breaks the link, which is why the pacs.004 is the expected message for a return. What proves this return belongs to that original payment? BA Takeaway Return with a pacs.004, every time. Carry the original

entries.title: EUR 130,000 cover, screened on one leg and missed on the other
entries.text: EUR 130,000 cover, screened on one leg and missed on the other Core A EUR 130,000 cover payment was screened and cleared. The MT103 was checked. The MT202 COV was not. The funds leg carried a sanctioned party, and the payment went through anyway. Here's how that happens: → MT103 screened before credit → MT202 COV never screened → Sanctioned party on the funds leg missed → Payment credited, gap found later The assumption was: "Screening the instruction screens the payment." The information leg and the funds leg are screened separately. Why? An MT103 and its MT202 COV are both subject to sanction screening, and the screening must happen before the payment is credited to the beneficiary. A hit on either leg stops the payment. A bank that screens only the MT103 and not the cover, or the reverse, leaves a gap that a regulator will find. Screening one leg only leaves a gap a regulator will find. What proves both legs of this cover payment were screened? BA Takeaway Screen the MT103 and the

entries.title: EUR 130,000 cover, and the two legs disagreed by EUR 500
entries.text: EUR 130,000 cover, and the two legs disagreed by EUR 500 Core A EUR 130,000 cover payment arrived. The MT103 said EUR 130,000. The MT202 COV said EUR 129,500. The beneficiary bank would not credit a cent until someone explained the EUR 500 gap. Here's how that happens: → MT103 announces EUR 130,000 → MT202 COV arrives for EUR 129,500 → Amount and reference do not agree → Bank investigates before crediting The assumption was: "A EUR 500 difference is a minor data error." A mismatch is a break in the link between the legs. Why? In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV must agree on amount and on the references that link them, and a mismatch between the two creates an exception that stops settlement. The discrepancy can be a different amount, a missing reference or details that do not line up. A mismatch is not a minor data error. It is a break in the link between the information leg and the funds leg. What proves the two legs of this cover payment agree? BA Takeaway Compare amount

entries.title: USD 95,000 serial recall that tried to skip a bank
entries.text: USD 95,000 serial recall that tried to skip a bank Core A USD 95,000 serial MT103 had to be recalled. The originator bank sent the recall straight to the beneficiary bank. It failed, because the bank that was skipped still held the funds. Here's how that happens: → Originator bank sends the recall → Recall skips the intermediary banks → Skipped bank still holds the funds → Recall fails, money stays put The assumption was: "The recall only needs the two ends." A serial MT103 can be recalled, but the recall must travel the same chain. Why? The originator bank sends the recall to the next bank in the chain, and each bank passes it on until it reaches the beneficiary bank, which decides whether the funds can be returned. A recall that skips a bank cannot work, because the bank that was skipped still holds the funds. A recall that skips a bank cannot work, because the bank that was skipped still holds the funds. What proves the recall travelled the same chain as the payment? BA Takeaway

entries.title: USD 50,000 to a bank that is not on SWIFT
entries.text: USD 50,000 to a bank that is not on SWIFT Core USD 50,000 had to reach a bank that is not a SWIFT member. The MT103 could not be sent to it directly. The payment sat for a day while the team argued whether it could be sent at all. Here's how that happens: → Beneficiary bank is not a SWIFT member → MT103 cannot be sent to it directly → Member bank forwards the instruction as intermediary → Payment follows the usual serial or cover logic The assumption was: "No SWIFT membership means no payment." Non-membership does not stop the payment. It adds a step to the chain. Why? The payment must reach the beneficiary bank through a bank that is a member and can forward the instruction. The forwarding bank becomes an intermediary in the chain, and the payment follows the same serial or cover logic as any other payment with an intermediary. Non-membership does not stop the payment. It adds a step to the chain. What proves the payment can reach a bank outside SWIFT? BA Takeaway Route the payment

entries.title: EUR 65,000 MT103 arrived with field 57 empty
entries.text: EUR 65,000 MT103 arrived with field 57 empty Core An MT103 for EUR 65,000 arrived with field 57 empty. It named no beneficiary bank. The receiving bank held it, unsure whether the payment was broken or meant to be handled in house. Here's how that happens: → MT103 arrives with field 57 empty → No beneficiary bank named → Receiving bank works out the route from the other fields → Payment held while the team decides The assumption was: "An empty field is an error." The empty field is not necessarily an error. Why? An empty field 57 can mean the payment is to be handled by the receiving bank itself, or that the beneficiary bank is identified elsewhere in the chain. The analyst must read the whole message before deciding whether the empty field is a gap or a deliberate omission. Read the whole message before deciding whether the empty field is a gap or a deliberate omission. What proves this empty field is deliberate, not a gap? BA Takeaway Read the whole MT103 before judging field 57.

entries.title: Parent paid EUR 300,000 for three subsidiaries, and the screening landed on the wrong party
entries.text: Parent paid EUR 300,000 for three subsidiaries, and the screening landed on the wrong party Core A parent company paid EUR 300,000 for three subsidiaries with one MT101. The bank reported all three payments under the parent. Screening and accounting landed on the wrong party for every one of them. Here's how that happens: → Parent instructs with an MT101 → General instruction sequence carried → Subsidiary named per transaction → Bank reports under the parent, not the subsidiary The assumption was: "The sender is the party that matters." The subsidiary is the ordering customer for its own transaction. Why? The MT101 carries a general instruction sequence and a per-transaction sequence, and the subsidiary appears as the ordering customer in the per-transaction sequence. The parent's bank must then report each transaction under the correct subsidiary, so the accounting and the screening both land on the right party. entries.title: EUR 40,000 MT103 STP stopped because one field used the wrong option
entries.text: EUR 40,000 MT103 STP stopped because one field used the wrong option Core An MT103 STP for EUR 40,000 was sent to straight-through processing. It stopped for manual handling. One field had used an option other than A, and the system could not identify the bank. Here's how that happens: → MT103 STP sent for straight-through processing → Field 57 uses an option other than A → System cannot identify the bank without human help → Payment stops for manual handling The assumption was: "Any option that names the bank will do." An MT103 STP only allows option A for fields such as 52, 54 and 57. Why? Option A carries the party identifier and the BIC, so the receiving system can identify the bank without human help. Any other option leaves the bank to work out who the party is by hand, which is why those options are not allowed in an STP message. Any other option leaves the bank to work out who the party is by hand. What proves every party field in this STP message uses option A? BA Takeaway

entries.title: EUR 120,000 credited twice because a notification was sent as an MT103
entries.text: EUR 120,000 credited twice because a notification was sent as an MT103 Core EUR 120,000 was credited to a customer. The bank then sent an MT103 to report the credit. The receiving bank read it as an instruction to pay, and debited the account a second time. Here's how that happens: → Credit already made to the customer → Bank sends an MT103 to report it → Receiving bank reads it as an instruction to pay → Account debited a second time The assumption was: "An MT103 can report a credit." An MT103 instructs a payment. It is not a notification. Why? An MT103 instructs the receiving bank to debit the sender's account and pay the beneficiary, so it is an instruction to move money. When a bank only wants to say that an account has already been credited, it uses an MT910 confirmation of credit or an MT950 or MT940 statement instead. An instruction is not a notification. Sending one as the other moves money twice. What proves this message instructs a payment, rather than reporting one? BA

entries.title: USD 75,000 MT103, and the intermediary was named in the wrong field
entries.text: USD 75,000 MT103, and the intermediary was named in the wrong field Core A USD 75,000 MT103 travelled through an intermediary bank. The intermediary was named in field 55 instead of field 56. The funds went for reimbursement through a bank that was never meant to handle them. Here's how that happens: → MT103 names the intermediary in field 55 → Field 56 left empty → Funds routed as a reimbursement, not a forward → Payment goes astray The assumption was: "Fields 55 and 56 both name banks in the middle, so either will do." Field 56 names the intermediary. Field 55 names a third reimbursement institution. Why? Field 56 names the intermediary institution, the bank that receives the payment from the sender and forwards it to the account with institution in field 57. entries.title: EUR 90,000 debited, and the customer demanded proof that never came
entries.text: EUR 90,000 debited, and the customer demanded proof that never came Core EUR 90,000 was debited on an MT103 instruction. The customer asked for proof of the debit. No MT900 ever arrived, and the customer assumed the payment had failed. Here's how that happens: → Bank debits the account on the MT103 → No MT900 confirmation sent → Customer sees the debit but no proof → Customer assumes the payment failed The assumption was: "Every debit is confirmed with an MT900." Whether one is sent depends on the agreement between the two banks. Why? When a bank debits an account on the instruction of an MT103, it can confirm the debit with an MT900, a confirmation of debit. The MT900 is a separate message, not part of the MT103 itself, and a payment can therefore settle correctly without any MT900 being exchanged. entries.title: USD 250,000, no account relationship, and the wrong route chosen
entries.text: USD 250,000, no account relationship, and the wrong route chosen Core A Canadian bank had to pay USD 250,000 to a United States beneficiary. It held its dollars with Wells Fargo. The beneficiary held its account with Citibank New York. The bank sent a single serial MT103, and the payment had nowhere to settle. Here's how that happens: → Canadian bank holds USD with Wells Fargo → Beneficiary holds account with Citibank → No account relationship between the sending bank and Citibank → Serial MT103 sent, settlement fails The assumption was: "One MT103 reaches any beneficiary." Account relationships decide serial or cover. Why? Because the sending bank had no account relationship with Citibank, the correct route was a cover payment: an MT103 sent directly to Citibank and an MT202 COV sent to Wells Fargo. If the sending bank had held an account with the beneficiary's bank, a single serial MT103 would have been enough. Account relationships decide the route. No relationship means cover, not

entries.title: EUR 200,000 cover arrived EUR 150 short
entries.text: EUR 200,000 cover arrived EUR 150 short Core An MT103 announced EUR 200,000. The cover arrived for EUR 199,850. An intermediary had taken its EUR 150 charge from the cover, and the beneficiary bank refused to credit the short amount. Here's how that happens: → MT103 announces EUR 200,000 → Intermediary takes EUR 150 from the MT202 COV → Cover arrives EUR 150 short → Beneficiary bank holds the payment The assumption was: "An intermediary can take its charge from the cover." It is forbidden to take charges from an MT202 COV. Why? The cover amount must never be lower than the amount announced in the MT103. If an intermediary needs to be paid for its part in the chain, it asks the sending bank to pay through an MT191 or debits the account directly under the agreement between the banks. A cover that arrives short of the announced amount is an exception, not a normal deduction. What proves the cover matches the announced amount in full? BA Takeaway Never deduct from a cover. entries.title: EUR 100,000 MT103 refused before it was even read
entries.text: EUR 100,000 MT103 refused before it was even read Core EUR 100,000 was due to a beneficiary. The MT103 was sent. The receiving bank's system refused it outright, before anyone read it, because no RMA existed for the sender. Here's how that happens: → MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank → No RMA set up for the sender → Receiving system refuses the message → Payment never starts The assumption was: "The RMA can be sorted out afterwards." Without an RMA the receiving bank's system will not accept the message. Why? Before one bank can send an MT103 to another over SWIFT, the receiving bank must set up an RMA, a relationship management authorisation, for that sender. The RMA is therefore a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards. The RMA is a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards. entries.title: EUR 100,000 cover rejected even though the amounts agreed
entries.text: EUR 100,000 cover rejected even though the amounts agreed Core A EUR 100,000 cover payment arrived with the amounts matching exactly. The beneficiary bank rejected it anyway. Sequence B of the MT202 COV did not mirror the MT103. Here's how that happens: → MT103 and MT202 COV amounts agree → Sequence B of the cover differs from the MT103 → Beneficiary bank rejects the cover → Funds stop even though the amounts agree The assumption was: "If the amounts agree, the cover will pass." Some banks reject a cover whose sequence B does not match the announcement. Why? In sequence B of an MT202 COV, only the ordering and beneficiary customer information in fields 50a and 59a is mandatory, and the other fields are optional. When the bank does provide a field such as field 72 or field 59, it must match the same field in the MT103 exactly, or the field must be left empty. A mismatch in sequence B stops the funds even when the amounts agree. What proves sequence B of the cover mirrors the MT103? BA

entries.title: USD 175,000 with no SSI on file, and no one knew where to send it
entries.text: USD 175,000 with no SSI on file, and no one knew where to send it Core USD 175,000 had to be paid to a beneficiary bank. The sending bank had no standing settlement instruction on file for that bank. No one knew which correspondent to send the funds to, and the payment waited. Here's how that happens: → Payment due to the beneficiary bank → No SSI on file for that bank in USD → Correspondent unknown → Payment held while the route is found The assumption was: "The payment engine will know where to send it." Without an SSI, the engine has nothing to build the payment from. Why? Banks tell each other how to send them funds in each currency through standing settlement instructions, exchanged as MT670 and MT671 messages and stored in payment engine databases. An SSI names the correspondent of the receiver and any intermediaries on the route, so the sending bank can build the MT103 and the cover from the database instead of asking every time. entries.title: USD 175,000 took the long route when a shorter one was on file
entries.text: USD 175,000 took the long route when a shorter one was on file Core USD 175,000 was sent by the preferred route. It took three days. A shorter route was on file the whole time, and no one used it because the preferred instruction felt like an order. Here's how that happens: → Bank publishes several SSIs for USD → One route marked as preferred → Sender uses the preferred route by default → Beneficiary waits three days, shorter route unused The assumption was: "Preferred means we must use it." The preferred route is an option, not an order. Why? A bank can publish several standing settlement instructions for one currency, marking one as preferred, but the preferred route is an option, not an order. The sender may use a shorter route, even one that passes through a bank named in a non-preferred instruction, because the aim is for the funds to reach the beneficiary. Preferred is an option, not an order. If the beneficiary is paid faster on the shorter route, no one will complain. What

entries.title: EUR 80,000 sent to the wrong bank because field 57a was read the same way twice
entries.text: EUR 80,000 sent to the wrong bank because field 57a was read the same way twice Core EUR 80,000 was sent in a cover payment. The team read field 57a the way it works in a serial MT103. The funds went to the beneficiary bank's correspondent instead of the beneficiary bank. Here's how that happens: → Serial MT103 read first, field 57a noted → MT202 COV read the same way → Field 57a points at a different bank in each leg → Funds sent to the wrong bank The assumption was: "Field 57a always means the same bank." The same field number points at a different bank in each leg. Why? In a serial MT103, field 57a names the bank that holds the beneficiary's account, and field 56 names the intermediary that forwards the payment to it. In an MT202 COV the roles shift: field 58a names the beneficiary bank, while field 57a names the correspondent bank of the beneficiary bank. The same field number points at a different bank in each leg. What proves we read field 57a for the leg we are actually in? BA

entries.title: EUR 140,000 cover treated as a different kind of payment
entries.text: EUR 140,000 cover treated as a different kind of payment Core A EUR 140,000 cover payment arrived. The team treated it as a different kind of movement from a serial payment. They built separate handling for it, and the cover leg stalled while they worked out rules that already existed. Here's how that happens: → MT202 COV arrives → Team treats it as a new kind of payment → Separate handling built from scratch → Cover leg stalls The assumption was: "A cover is a different kind of movement." The cover is the same serial mechanism carrying the funds leg. Why? Looked at on its own, an MT202 COV is a serial payment: the sender instructs the receiver to debit the sender's account and credit the next bank in the chain. Each bank in the cover chain debits the previous bank's account and instructs the next bank, until the funds reach the beneficiary bank. The cover is the same serial mechanism carrying the funds leg of a customer payment. What proves we handled the cover leg with the rules we

entries.title: EUR 1,200 in charges taken from a EUR 200,000 cover
entries.text: EUR 1,200 in charges taken from a EUR 200,000 cover Core A EUR 200,000 cover payment arrived EUR 1,200 short. An intermediary had taken its charges straight from the cover. An MT191 then arrived, claiming the same charges again. Here's how that happens: → Cover arrives EUR 1,200 short → Intermediary took charges from the cover → MT191 arrives claiming the same charges → Customer charged twice for one leg The assumption was: "Charges come out of the funds in transit." Charges must not be deducted from a cover payment. Why? When one bank owes another bank charges or interest on a payment, the claim travels in an MT191, a request for payment of charges, and the advice travels in an MT190. These messages exist because charges must not be deducted from a cover payment, so an intermediary that is owed money asks for it separately instead of taking it from the funds. An MT191 in a chain is the charges leg, not the payment itself. What proves the charges were claimed separately, not taken

entries.title: USD 60,000 sent in dollars, credited short after a double conversion
entries.text: USD 60,000 sent in dollars, credited short after a double conversion Core USD 60,000 was sent to a United States dollar account. The beneficiary was credited short. An intermediary had converted the payment twice on the way, and no one had asked for a conversion. Here's how that happens: → Sender sends USD 60,000 → Intermediary converts the payment → Second intermediary converts it again → Beneficiary credited short in dollars The assumption was: "Intermediaries can convert as they pass the payment on." No intermediary may change the currency. Why? The sender decides the currency of a transaction, and no intermediary may change it on the way. If the beneficiary's account is in a different currency, the conversion happens as a separate foreign exchange step, and the beneficiary is credited in the currency of the account. A payment sent in dollars to a dollar account that arrives short after a double conversion has gone wrong. What proves no intermediary changed the currency on the way?

entries.title: USD 45,000 missing for two weeks, and everyone said to wait
entries.text: USD 45,000 missing for two weeks, and everyone said to wait Core USD 45,000 was sent to a supplier. Three days passed. Then a week. Then two. Everyone said to wait a little longer, while the supplier threatened to stop deliveries. Here's how that happens: → Transfer sent in a major currency → 48 to 72 hours pass, nothing arrives → One week passes, still nothing → Two weeks pass, still nothing The assumption was: "Cross-border payments just take a while." After two weeks, there is definitely a problem. Why? A transfer in a major currency such as the United States dollar or the euro usually arrives in 48 to 72 hours, while a transfer in a less common local currency takes longer because the currency is harder to buy. A large amount can also slow a payment down, because it may need extra checks before it is released. If the money has not arrived after two weeks, there is definitely a problem. What proves this payment is still moving, rather than lost? BA Takeaway Ask the sending bank to

entries.title: USD 100,000, and the beneficiary received less than the sender instructed
entries.text: USD 100,000, and the beneficiary received less than the sender instructed Core A sender instructed USD 100,000 with field 71A as BEN. The beneficiary was credited as if the instruction had been SHA. The beneficiary received less than the sender had instructed, and the bank copy showed a different code from the sender's instruction. Here's how that happens: → Sender instructs 71A BEN → Each bank deducts its charge → Beneficiary bears every charge → Bank copy shows SHA, beneficiary credited differently The assumption was: "The bank copy is just a copy." A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is a discrepancy worth querying. Why? When field 71A carries BEN, every charge in the chain is borne by the beneficiary, and each bank deducts its charge from the amount as the payment passes through. The sender does not prepay the downstream charges, because the beneficiary is the one who pays them. A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is a discrepancy

entries.title: USD 100,000 credit that did not match the equation
entries.text: USD 100,000 credit that did not match the equation Core USD 100,000 was instructed. The beneficiary bank credited an amount that did not fit the charges equation. The operations team could not say whether the credit was right, because no one had checked the arithmetic. Here's how that happens: → Field 33B states the amount instructed → Field 71G states receiver charges prepaid by the sender → Field 71F states each charge deducted → Field 32A must equal 33B plus 71G minus all 71F The assumption was: "The system works the credit out, so the arithmetic takes care of itself." The relationship always holds, and it must be checked. Why? Field 32A is the amount that settles between banks, field 33B is the amount the ordering customer instructed, field 71G is the receiver's charges prepaid by the sender, and field 71F is each sender's charge deducted along the way. The relationship always holds: 32A equals 33B plus 71G minus all the 71F charges. 32A equals 33B plus 71G minus all the 71F

entries.title: EUR 55,000 MT103 with a BIC stuffed into field 57B
entries.text: EUR 55,000 MT103 with a BIC stuffed into field 57B Core A EUR 55,000 MT103 arrived with field 57B carrying a BIC. The receiving system could not route it straight through. The payment stopped for manual handling, because a BIC must never be passed in option B. Here's how that happens: → Field 57B carries a BIC → Receiving system cannot straight-through process it → Payment stops for manual handling → Correct option, A, never used The assumption was: "The BIC is in the field, so the bank is identified." Option B carries a party identifier, generally an account number, with the location of the account. Why? Field 57 offers four options, and option A, with a BIC, is the one that allows straight-through processing. Option D needs no routing code at all and can simply carry the bank's name and address, while the /C/ or /D/ code before an account number is part of the standard but almost never used in practice. Option A is the default whenever a BIC is available. What proves the right

entries.title: USD 80,000 to a US bank, and the clearing account was a guess
entries.text: USD 80,000 to a US bank, and the clearing account was a guess Core USD 80,000 was sent to a United States bank. Field 57A carried only the BIC. The receiving bank had several clearing accounts, and the operations team had to guess which one the payment was for. Here's how that happens: → Field 57A carries the BIC only → Receiving bank holds several clearing accounts → No CHIPS UID to pin down the account → Payment held while the account is confirmed The assumption was: "The BIC alone is always enough." Using the BIC alone is valid, but the UID removes any doubt. Why? In option A of field 57, the line before the BIC is the party identifier, and for a United States payment that identifier can be the beneficiary bank's CHIPS UID. The CHIPS UID identifies the bank in the United States clearing system, while the BIC identifies it on SWIFT, so the two sit together in the same field. The BIC alone is valid, but the UID removes any doubt about which clearing account should be used. What

entries.title: EUR 110,000 debited from the wrong nostro account
entries.text: EUR 110,000 debited from the wrong nostro account Core A bank held three euro accounts with the same correspondent. EUR 110,000 was debited from the wrong one. Liquidity planning for the week broke, because field 53B had never named the account to debit. Here's how that happens: → Bank holds several accounts with one correspondent → Field 53 left vague → Wrong nostro account debited → Liquidity plan breaks The assumption was: "Field 53 always means the nostro account." Field 53 does not always contain the sender's nostro account. Why? A bank can hold more than one account with the same correspondent in the same currency, and field 53B exists to say exactly which account must be debited. Using option B tells the receiver that the sender has many accounts with it and wants a specific one used to settle the transaction. Field 53B exists to say exactly which account must be debited. What proves the right account was debited? BA Takeaway Use field 53B to name the exact account to debit

entries.title: EUR 35,000 remittance reference that broke the 16-character limit
entries.text: EUR 35,000 remittance reference that broke the 16-character limit Core A EUR 35,000 payment carried a remittance reference in field 70. The reference after /RFB/ ran past 16 characters. The beneficiary's system could not match it, and the payment sat unreconciled. Here's how that happens: → Field 70 carries several references → /RFB/ reference runs past 16 characters → Beneficiary system cannot match it → Payment sits unreconciled The assumption was: "A longer reference is a clearer reference." The reference that follows /RFB/ is limited to 16 characters. Why? Field 70 carries remittance information, and several references can be given if they are separated by a double slash, but one code such as /RFB/ or /INV/ cannot serve two references of the same kind. A longer description must continue on the following lines of the field instead of stretching the reference. A field 70 that repeats a code or overruns the limit is not a valid instruction. What proves field 70 follows the limits? BA

entries.title: EUR 48,000 credited to the named beneficiary when it belonged further on
entries.text: EUR 48,000 credited to the named beneficiary when it belonged further on Core EUR 48,000 was sent to a named beneficiary. The funds were meant for an account beyond that beneficiary. The beneficiary bank credited the named beneficiary directly, because no instruction told it to look further. Here's how that happens: → MT103 names the beneficiary in field 59 → Funds meant for a further account → No /FFC/ instruction in field 72 → Beneficiary credited directly, onward account never paid The assumption was: "The beneficiary bank will know where the funds really belong." Without the code, the bank has no instruction to look beyond the beneficiary named in field 59. Why? When the funds must be credited to an account other than the beneficiary's own account, the instruction travels as /FFC/, for further credit, in field 72, sender to receiver information. The beneficiary bank reads the code and passes the funds on to the account named after it, instead of crediting the beneficiary directly.

entries.title: EUR 160,000 late, and the MT103 copy proved nothing
entries.text: EUR 160,000 late, and the MT103 copy proved nothing Core EUR 160,000 was late by four days. The customer produced a copy of the MT103 as proof the money had moved. The copy proved nothing, and the bank could not trace the payment from it. Here's how that happens: → Payment late by four days → Customer shows a copy of the MT103 → Copy proves nothing about whether the money moved → Bank cannot trace the payment from the copy The assumption was: "An MT103 copy proves the money moved." A copy of an MT103 on its own proves nothing about whether the money moved. Why? The unique end-to-end transaction reference, the UETR, is carried in field 121 of block 3 of the message header, not in the body of the MT103. When a payment is late or a bank cannot trace it, the UETR is the reference to give the bank, because every bank in the chain can use it to follow the payment across the network. A copy of an MT103 on its own proves nothing about whether the money moved. What proves this payment moved,

entries.title: EUR 22,000 ordering name rejected for spilling onto a second line
entries.text: EUR 22,000 ordering name rejected for spilling onto a second line Core An ordering customer had a long company name. It ran over two lines in field 50K. The receiving bank rejected the MT103, saying a name must fit on one line. Here's how that happens: → Ordering customer name spans two lines in field 50K → Receiving bank rejects the message → Payment for EUR 22,000 stops → Sender told the name must fit on one line The assumption was: "A name must fit on the first line." The standard does not restrict the name to the first line. Why? Option K of field 50a allows the ordering customer's name and address in up to four lines of 35 characters each. The name does not have to fit on the first line: it can sit on one line with the address on the rest, or run over two or three lines with the address on what remains. The standard does not restrict the name to the first line, so a name split across lines is valid. What proves a name split across lines is valid in field 50K? BA Takeaway Use the

entries.title: EUR 140,000 cover arrived from a bank the announcement never named
entries.text: EUR 140,000 cover arrived from a bank the announcement never named Core An MT103 announced EUR 140,000 and named the correspondent that would send the cover. The cover arrived from a different bank entirely. The beneficiary bank could not match the two legs and would not credit the beneficiary. Here's how that happens: → MT103 announcement states field 53 → Beneficiary bank knows where funds will come from → Cover arrives from an unmentioned bank → Beneficiary bank will not credit The assumption was: "The cover will arrive from somewhere. The source does not matter." The announcement must name the cover's source. Why? In a cover payment the MT103 announcement should state in field 53 which correspondent will send the cover, so the beneficiary bank knows where the funds will come from. When the cover arrives from a bank the announcement never mentioned, the beneficiary bank cannot match the two legs and will not credit the beneficiary. The fix sits with the sender, whose bank must

entries.title: EUR 70,000 MT103 with an IBAN but no name
entries.text: EUR 70,000 MT103 with an IBAN but no name Core An MT103 for EUR 70,000 arrived showing only the beneficiary's IBAN and address in field 59. No name at all. The beneficiary bank held the payment, unable to confirm the account belonged to the person the payment was meant for. Here's how that happens: → MT103 shows only IBAN and address in field 59 → No beneficiary name → Bank cannot confirm the account owner → Bank holds the payment and asks for confirmation The assumption was: "An IBAN identifies the beneficiary." Field 59 is meant to identify the beneficiary. Why? Field 59 is meant to identify the beneficiary, so a missing name leaves the beneficiary bank unable to confirm that the account belongs to the person the payment was meant for. The bank may hold the payment and ask for confirmation instead of crediting it, and the sender's bank is the one that must supply the missing name. A missing name leaves the bank unable to confirm the account belongs to the right person. What proves

entries.title: EUR 85,000 MT101, and the two references pointed at two different owners
entries.text: EUR 85,000 MT101, and the two references pointed at two different owners Core An MT101 for EUR 85,000 carried two references. Field 20 and field 21R showed different values. The operations team treated them as the same reference, and the reconciliation broke. Here's how that happens: → Field 20 assigned by the sending bank → Field 21R assigned by the ordering customer → Team treats them as one reference → Reconciliation breaks The assumption was: "Two references on one message are the same reference." They belong to different parties. Why? Field 20 is the sender's reference, assigned by the bank that sends the MT101 to identify the payment. Field 21R is the ordering customer's reference, assigned by the customer who ordered the payment, and it stays the same across every message sent for one order. The two references can coincide when the sender is also the ordering customer, but they belong to different parties, and field 21R is optional while field 20 is mandatory. Field 20 belongs

entries.title: EUR 120,000 paid by a parent, and the beneficiary thanked the wrong company
entries.text: EUR 120,000 paid by a parent, and the beneficiary thanked the wrong company Core A parent company paid EUR 120,000 on behalf of a subsidiary. The beneficiary thanked the parent for a payment the subsidiary had really made. The subsidiary's own records showed nothing, because the beneficiary had been told the payment was from the subsidiary, and no one had read the field that said so. Here's how that happens: → Parent sends the MT101 → Subsidiary named in the Instructing Party field → Beneficiary sees the parent as the sender → Beneficiary thanks the wrong company The assumption was: "The sender is the party the payment is from." The beneficiary is told the payment is from the subsidiary through the Instructing Party field. Why? When a parent company sends an MT101 to pay on behalf of a subsidiary, the parent company stands as the sender, not the subsidiary. The beneficiary is told the payment is from the subsidiary through the Instructing Party field, which names the subsidiary even

entries.title: EUR 95,000 drawn on the parent's account with no authority on file
entries.text: EUR 95,000 drawn on the parent's account with no authority on file Core A subsidiary instructed a EUR 95,000 payment from its parent company's account. The payment went through. No authorisation was on file, and the parent only found out when the statement arrived. Here's how that happens: → Subsidiary wants to use the parent's account → No authorisation on file → Payment drawn from the parent's account → Parent learns of it from the statement The assumption was: "A subsidiary can use the parent's account. It is the same group." An authorisation is required before the subsidiary may draw on the parent's account. Why? In the MT101 the subsidiary appears as the Instructing Party in field 50L, while the parent company appears as the ordering customer in field 50H, because the parent owns the account that will be debited. The same need for authorisation applies whenever the sender of an instruction is not the owner of the account being debited. The same need for authorisation applies

entries.title: One MT101 for EUR 500,000 across six banks, or six MT101s
entries.text: One MT101 for EUR 500,000 across six banks, or six MT101s Core A large corporate held accounts at six banks. It had to pay EUR 500,000 across them. The team prepared six separate MT101s, one per bank, and spent a day on work one message could have done. Here's how that happens: → Corporate holds accounts at many banks → Six MT101s prepared, one per bank → Day spent on six messages → One MT101 to a concentrating bank would have done it The assumption was: "Each bank needs its own MT101 from us." One MT101 to a concentrating bank is enough. Why? A large corporate with accounts at many banks can send a single MT101 to one concentrating bank, and that bank forwards the instruction to each bank that holds an account to be debited. The alternative is for the corporate to prepare a separate MT101 for every bank, which is slower and harder to manage. The forwarding service is a genuine value-added service, and the concentrating bank charges for it. What proves one MT101 reached every bank

entries.title: EUR 2 million payroll split across five MT101s, and one arrived late
entries.text: EUR 2 million payroll split across five MT101s, and one arrived late Core A EUR 2 million payroll order was too big for one MT101. It was split across five messages, numbered 1 of 5 to 5 of 5. Message 4 arrived a day late, and the bank processed the rest without it. Here's how that happens: → Order exceeds the 10,000 character limit → Order split across five MT101s → Messages numbered in field 28D → Message 4 arrives late, others processed alone The assumption was: "Each message in the chain can be processed as it arrives." Banks hold a chained message until every message in the chain has arrived. Why? An MT101 message is limited to 10,000 characters, so an order with many transactions must be split across several MT101 messages, numbered in field 28D as 1 of 5, 2 of 5, and so on. Processing one element alone could pay the wrong amounts. Banks hold a chained message until every message in the chain has arrived. What proves every message in the chain arrived before any was processed?

entries.title: EUR 15,000 moved inside one bank, and the team still sent an MT103
entries.text: EUR 15,000 moved inside one bank, and the team still sent an MT103 Core EUR 15,000 moved between two accounts at the same bank. The team sent an MT101, then an MT103 as well. The MT103 went nowhere, because the payment never left the bank. Here's how that happens: → Same bank holds both accounts → Payment never leaves the bank → Single MT101 sent → MT103 sent too, for a payment that needs no interbank message The assumption was: "Every payment needs an MT103." An MT103 is only required when the beneficiary's bank is different from the debtor's bank. Why? If the same bank holds both the debtor's account and the beneficiary's account, the payment never leaves the bank, so no interbank message is needed. A single MT101 is enough: the bank debits the debtor's account and credits the beneficiary's account on its own books. An MT103 is only required when the beneficiary's bank is different from the debtor's bank. What proves this payment needed no interbank message? BA Takeaway Check

entries.title: EUR 4 million statement, and the closing balance appeared twice
entries.text: EUR 4 million statement, and the closing balance appeared twice Core A EUR 4 million statement was split across several MT940 messages. An intermediate message carried tag 62F, the final closing balance. The client system treated the statement as finished and never generated the messages that followed. Here's how that happens: → Statement split across several MT940s → Intermediate message carries tag 62F → Client system treats the statement as finished → Later messages never generated The assumption was: "Every message can carry a closing balance." There is only one closing balance for the whole statement. Why? A statement split across several MT940 messages must use the intermediate closing balance, tag 62M, in every message except the last. Only the final message carries the final closing balance, tag 62F. There is only one closing balance for the whole statement. What proves the closing balance appears only on the final message? BA Takeaway Use tag 62M on every intermediate message

entries.title: EUR 4 million statement, and the intermediate balance dates did not match
entries.text: EUR 4 million statement, and the intermediate balance dates did not match Core A EUR 4 million statement arrived as several MT940s. The intermediate balance dates did not match the last entry in each message. The receiver questioned the statement, even though the balances themselves were right. Here's how that happens: → Statement split across several MT940s → Tags 60M and 62M show the wrong dates → Balances correct, dates do not match the last entry → Receiver questions the statement The assumption was: "Only the balances matter, the dates do not." The dates that truly matter are the opening, closing, closing available and forward available balances, and the intermediate dates should match the last entry. Why? When a statement is split across several MT940 messages, the intermediate opening balance tag 60M and the intermediate closing balance tag 62M should ideally show the date of the last entry in that message.
