entries.title: A customer confirmed a EUR 8,000 transfer, then found the real cost was EUR 8,400
entries.text: A customer confirmed a EUR 8,000 transfer, then found the real cost was EUR 8,400 Advanced A customer sent EUR 8,000 across borders. The screen showed the amount and a confirm button. After confirming, the customer found the total cost was EUR 8,400, and the delivery date was three days later than expected. Here's how it happened: → Customer enters EUR 8,000 to send → Screen shows the amount, hides the fee breakdown → Exchange rate shown, but not the rate actually applied → No expected delivery status shown → Customer confirms, then learns the real cost and the real date The assumption was: "Transparency can be added as a footnote." Why? A customer sending money across borders needs to see the total cost, the applied exchange rate, the fee breakdown, and the expected delivery status before confirming. If any of those are hidden or unclear, the customer cannot judge whether the payment is good value or when it will arrive. A hidden cost is a broken promise. BA Takeaway Transparency is

entries.title: A EUR 45,000 payment carried rich remittance data, and the last bank in the chain threw it away
entries.text: A EUR 45,000 payment carried rich remittance data, and the last bank in the chain threw it away Advanced A EUR 45,000 payment was sent with structured purpose and remittance data. The data was meant to help compliance screening and let the beneficiary reconcile against the right invoice. The last bank in the chain dropped it, and the beneficiary could not match the payment. Here's how it happened: → Payment sent with structured purpose and remittance data → First bank captures it correctly → Second bank maps it inconsistently → Last bank in the chain drops it, its system cannot consume it → Beneficiary cannot reconcile against the right invoice The assumption was: "Rich data helps by itself." Why? Structured purpose and remittance data helps compliance screening and lets the beneficiary reconcile the payment against the right invoice. But the data is only useful if it is captured correctly, mapped consistently, and consumed by the downstream systems that need it. Poor data quality in

entries.title: A EUR 5,000 payment had to clear in 10 seconds, and the sanctions check needed 40
entries.text: A EUR 5,000 payment had to clear in 10 seconds, and the sanctions check needed 40 Advanced A customer sent a EUR 5,000 instant payment. It had to complete in 10 seconds. The sanctions check needed 40 seconds, and the team was asked to skip it to meet the speed promise. Here's how it happened: → EUR 5,000 instant payment sent → Rail allows 10 seconds to complete → Sanctions, anti-money laundering and fraud checks still required → Checks take longer than the rail allows → Pressure to bypass the checks to meet the speed promise The assumption was: "Speed and controls can trade off against each other." Why? An instant payment that completes in 10 seconds still needs sanctions, anti-money laundering and fraud checks. The controls must be fast and automated, with a clear escalation path and a full audit trail when a payment is held. The speed target and the control standard have to hold at the same time. A 10-second payment still needs its controls. BA Takeaway Design the controls to fit

entries.title: A fraudster moved EUR 9,000 out of an account in 20 seconds, before the customer noticed
entries.text: A fraudster moved EUR 9,000 out of an account in 20 seconds, before the customer noticed Advanced A fraudster gained access to a customer's account. In 20 seconds, EUR 9,000 had left it through instant payments. The customer noticed the next morning, long after the money was gone. Here's how it happened: → Fraudster gains access to the account → Instant payments settle in seconds → EUR 9,000 moves out before the customer notices → No intervention point stops the flow → Post-transaction monitoring finds it the next day, too late The assumption was: "One fraud control is enough." Why? Instant payments settle in seconds, which is what customers want and what fraudsters want too. An authorised push payment scam can also persuade the customer to send the money themselves. No single control can cover a journey that completes in seconds, so the controls must work together. Seconds to settle means seconds to steal. BA Takeaway Layer the controls: risk signals, velocity checks, confirmation of

entries.title: A EUR 250 payment went out wrong, and the team sent the wrong message to fix it
entries.text: A EUR 250 payment went out wrong, and the team sent the wrong message to fix it Advanced A legitimate EUR 250 payment was executed in error. The team sent a cancellation request. The payment had already settled, so the cancellation could not work, and the money stayed where it was. Here's how it happened: → EUR 250 payment executed with the wrong details → Team sends camt.055 cancellation request → Bank B has already settled the payment → Cancellation refused, settlement has cleared → Refund now needs camt.056 or pacs.004, not camt.055 The assumption was: "Cancellation fixes any wrong payment." Why? Settlement status decides the instrument. Cancellation suits a payment still unsettled, while a settled payment needs a return. A camt.055 works only before Bank B settles, and once settlement has cleared, the bank seeks the funds back through a camt.056 or a pacs.004. The refund route follows the standing agreement, and an unanswered camt.055 leaves pacs.004 as the fallback request.

entries.title: No pacs.002 after 20 seconds, EUR 5,000 gone, and the customer asked for it to be sent again
entries.text: No pacs.002 after 20 seconds, EUR 5,000 gone, and the customer asked for it to be sent again Advanced A customer sent a EUR 5,000 instant payment. Twenty seconds passed. No pacs.002 arrived. The account stood debited, the funds had left, and the customer asked for the payment to be sent again. Here's how it happened: → EUR 5,000 SCT Inst payment sent → 20 second timeout passes, no pacs.002 → Customer account debited, funds gone, credit unconfirmed → Customer asks to resend the payment → Resending would risk a duplicate EUR 5,000 payment The assumption was: "No confirmation means the payment failed, so send it again." Why? In SCT Inst, absence of a pacs.002 after the 20 second timeout leaves the payment in limbo. The debit is posted and the funds have left, but credit to the beneficiary stays unconfirmed. Resending would risk a duplicate, so the sender bank must instead issue a pacs.028 status request and let the recipient bank investigate. No confirmation is not a failure. It is a

entries.title: SAR 250,000 left the account, the beneficiary was paid, and the nostro showed nothing
entries.text: SAR 250,000 left the account, the beneficiary was paid, and the nostro showed nothing Advanced A SAR 250,000 payment left the customer account and was sent onward. The beneficiary was credited. But the statement showed no nostro debit, and Operations wanted to send the payment again. Here's how it happened: → SAR 250,000 debited from the customer account → Payment sent onward to the correspondent → Beneficiary credited → Corresponding nostro debit never posts → Statement shows no debit, team proposes re-effecting the payment The assumption was: "No nostro debit means the payment never went." Why? This is a Payment Missing a Nostro Entry. The payment left and the beneficiary may already stand credited, but the nostro debit never posted. Re-effecting would duplicate the payment and break the nostro at reconciliation. The governing discipline is evidence before action. A missing entry is not a missing payment. BA Takeaway Prove the payment state first with pacs.002, camt.052 or camt.053,

entries.title: One pacs.008 for EUR 5 million went to the wrong system, because the route code was never read
entries.text: One pacs.008 for EUR 5 million went to the wrong system, because the route code was never read Advanced A pacs.008 for EUR 5 million was sent. It arrived in the wrong settlement system. The message was perfect. The route code on it was never read. Here's how it happened: → pacs.008 for EUR 5 million prepared → BAH BizSvc code declares the route, not the message → Payment meant for T2, central bank money settlement via ESMIG to the ECB → BizSvc read as a CBPR+ route, sent cross-border through SWIFT FINplus → Payment lands in the wrong system, settlement, timing, cost and risk all wrong The assumption was: "The message decides the route." Why? The same pacs.008 resolves to a different route according to its destination, and the BAH BizSvc code, not the message, declares that route. A T2 payment travels through ESMIG to the ECB, identified by a BizSvc such as trgt.002.001.01, while a CBPR+ payment travels cross-border through SWIFT FINplus, identified by a BizSvc such as

entries.title: A USD 10 million payment was two days late, and the interest bill proved the value date mattered more than the booking
entries.text: A USD 10 million payment was two days late, and the interest bill proved the value date mattered more than the booking Advanced A USD 10 million payment was delayed by two days. It was booked on the day it was processed. The interest bill arrived anyway, because interest runs from the value date, not the booking date. Here's how it happened: → USD 10 million payment processed, booked on the processing day → Value date differs from the booking date by two days → Customer leg credited on Monday at a Monday value date → Nostro leg booked later at that same value date → Interest charged on the value date gap, no one had checked it The assumption was: "The booking date decides the interest." Why? Back valuation is a mismatch between value date and booking date, and it matters because interest runs from the value date, not the booking date. In a single-sided case the mismatch sits on one side, while in a double-sided case it sits on both sides. The working sequence is to confirm the value

entries.title: A EUR 100,000 payment was tracked to the wrong person, and tracking could not stop it
entries.text: A EUR 100,000 payment was tracked to the wrong person, and tracking could not stop it Advanced A EUR 100,000 payment was sent to the wrong beneficiary. The team watched it on tracking, and it showed ACSC, credited, within 30 minutes. They sent a stop message. It had no effect, because the money was already with the beneficiary. Here's how it happened: → EUR 100,000 sent to the wrong beneficiary → Tracking shows the payment moving, then ACSC within 30 minutes → Team sends a stop message → Stop has no effect, the payment is already credited → Recovery now needs a Stop and Recall request The assumption was: "Tracking a payment means we can stop it." Why? Tracking only shows where a payment is, while stopping it prevents credit to the beneficiary, and the two must never be confused. Once credited, the bank needs a Stop and Recall request, routed by urgency: FAST, acknowledged within 2 hours when the payment is settled and credited; MEDIUM, answered within 12 hours when the beneficiary

entries.title: One settlement code was mapped wrong, and a EUR 150,000 payment was debited twice
entries.text: One settlement code was mapped wrong, and a EUR 150,000 payment was debited twice Advanced A EUR 150,000 payment arrived with the settlement code INGA. The migration mapped it as INDA. The sending bank account was debited again, and the double posting was found at day-end as a reconciliation break. Here's how it happened: → pacs.008 arrives with INGA, the instructing agent has already settled this leg → Migration maps INGA as INDA → Engine follows INDA logic, the instructed agent settles this leg → Sending bank account debited again, a double posting → Reconciliation break found at day-end The assumption was: "MT to MX migration is a one-to-one field replacement." Why? It is not. The settlement method code on a pacs.008 changes the accounting: INDA means the instructed agent settles this leg, while INGA means the instructing agent has already settled it. Information once implied is now explicit and carries business meaning, so an incoming INGA payment wrongly mapped as INDA makes the

entries.title: One leg of a USD 250,000 payment failed, and the team nearly recalled the leg that was fine
entries.text: One leg of a USD 250,000 payment failed, and the team nearly recalled the leg that was fine Advanced A USD 250,000 cover-method payment went from India to Europe. The pacs.008 was rejected by the bank system before sending. The team reached for the recall button, even though the pacs.009 COV had already been processed and was sound. Here's how it happened: → pacs.008 rejected before sending → pacs.009 COV already processed → Team proposes an instant recall → Three questions decide the path: has the cover been released, has it settled, is the beneficiary bank USD cut-off still open → If the cover has not been released, halt it, resolve the fault and rebuild both legs → If it has settled and the cut-off is still open, fixing the issue and sending the pacs.008 may complete the payment without a recall The assumption was: "A failed leg means recall everything." Why? Recalling straight away can make things worse, because unwinding a sound cover and processing it again can push the credit

entries.title: A pacs.002 RJCT arrived for USD 180,000, and the bank nearly refunded money it did not have
entries.text: A pacs.002 RJCT arrived for USD 180,000, and the bank nearly refunded money it did not have Advanced A USD 180,000 cover-method payment was sent. A pacs.002 RJCT arrived on the pacs.008. The team moved to credit the remitter, even though the cover was still sitting at the correspondent. Here's how it happened: → pacs.008 sent to the beneficiary bank → pacs.009 COV sent, funds move through the correspondent → pacs.002 RJCT arrives on the pacs.008 → Instinct is to credit the remitter at once → Cover still at the correspondent, not yet returned → Crediting now would refund the customer while the cover is still out, a loss the bank absorbs The assumption was: "A rejection means the money is back." Why? Under the cover method the pacs.008 goes directly to the beneficiary bank while the pacs.009 COV moves the funds through the correspondent, so a pacs.002 RJCT on the pacs.008 does not by itself justify crediting the remitter. The first question is the status of the cover: not yet processed,

entries.title: A regulatory deadline and a EUR 1 million client project collided, and the team was told to pick one
entries.text: A regulatory deadline and a EUR 1 million client project collided, and the team was told to pick one Advanced A team had two pieces of work: CBPR+ structured-address work for a regulatory date, and a strategic client Cash Pooling project worth EUR 1 million. Leadership said the regulatory work came first and the client work waited. The team challenged the assumptions instead of the authority, and found both could be phased. Here's how it happened: → Regulatory date set for CBPR+ structured-address work → Strategic client Cash Pooling deprioritised against it → Team asks what is truly mandatory, what can be phased, and what the capacity impact is → Cash Pooling side might need only domestic pooling first → Regulatory side might sequence incoming support before outgoing → Plan agreed: incoming structured-address support first, domestic Cash Pooling on track, outgoing support plus international and cross-currency pooling in the next phase The assumption was: "A regulatory date means the

entries.title: A camt.055 arrived for a EUR 75,000 payment, and the team sent a camt.056 before asking where the payment sat
entries.text: A camt.055 arrived for a EUR 75,000 payment, and the team sent a camt.056 before asking where the payment sat Advanced A camt.055 cancellation request arrived for a EUR 75,000 payment. The team sent a camt.056 straight away. The payment was future-dated and had not been released, so the whole interbank chase was unnecessary. Here's how it happened: → camt.055 cancellation request arrives → Team sends camt.056 without checking the lifecycle → Payment was future-dated, warehoused, never released → It could have been cancelled before execution, internally → Interbank messages sent for a payment that never left the bank The assumption was: "A cancellation request means send a camt.056." Why? When a camt.055 arrives, do not assume a camt.056 should be sent straight away. The first question is where the original payment sits in its lifecycle. A future-dated or warehoused payment that has not been released may be cancelled before execution, a payment pending a compliance decision must be

entries.title: A candidate could name every recall message, and still could not explain a EUR 20,000 recall
entries.text: A candidate could name every recall message, and still could not explain a EUR 20,000 recall Advanced A candidate was asked to explain a EUR 20,000 recall. The candidate named camt.055, camt.056, pacs.004 and camt.029, one by one, perfectly. Then the interviewer asked what happened to the money, and the candidate had no answer. Here's how it happened: → Customer asks the debtor bank to recall a EUR 20,000 payment → Bank starts an investigation and sends a camt.056 to the creditor agent → Creditor bank checks whether the payment was credited and whether the beneficiary agrees → Financial outcome follows the creditor decision on the return of funds → Investigation response closes the journey → Candidate lists the messages but cannot connect them into this journey The assumption was: "Naming the messages proves payments knowledge." Why? It does not. Many candidates can describe the messages one by one but cannot connect them into the business journey. The interview answer should follow

entries.title: Four messages, one recall, and a EUR 35,000 question no one could answer
entries.text: Four messages, one recall, and a EUR 35,000 question no one could answer Advanced A EUR 35,000 payment needed recalling. The team had four messages in front of them: camt.055, camt.056, pacs.004 and camt.029. They argued for an hour about which one was not used in the flow, and the payment waited. Here's how it happened: → Customer cancellation request, camt.055 → Interbank cancellation request, camt.056 → Payment return, pacs.004 → Resolution of investigation, camt.029 → Team debates which message is not used in the flow → EUR 35,000 payment waits while the debate runs The assumption was: "The debate matters more than the journey." Why? It does not. The end-to-end recall journey runs through camt.055, camt.056, pacs.004 and camt.029, and connecting the four messages into one journey is the point of the exercise, not naming each message on its own. The question of which message is not used stays open, and guessing it does not move the money. Connect the journey first. Debate second.

entries.title: A EUR 60,000 payment vanished between states, and no one could say which state it was in
entries.text: A EUR 60,000 payment vanished between states, and no one could say which state it was in Advanced A customer sent a EUR 60,000 payment. It never arrived. Operations searched for it, but no one could say which state it was in, because no state had a named owner or a piece of evidence. Here's how it happened: → Initiation creates the instruction with an instruction ID and an end-to-end ID → Validation checks the instruction → Routing chooses the rail → Clearing moves it through the scheme → Settlement moves the funds between banks → Posting records it in the ledger → Confirmation tells the customer it is done → The payment stopped somewhere in the chain, and the evidence stopped with it The assumption was: "The payment will be found by asking around." Why? A payment moves through a chain of states from initiation to confirmation, and each state needs a named owner and a named piece of evidence. When a payment goes missing, the investigation follows this chain state by state, because the

entries.title: A EUR 2,500 card payment was declined at authorisation, and the team investigated settlement
entries.text: A EUR 2,500 card payment was declined at authorisation, and the team investigated settlement Advanced A customer tried to pay EUR 2,500 by card. The payment was declined at the terminal. The team spent a day investigating settlement, because no one had named which stage the failure belonged to. Here's how it happened: → Terminal sends card and transaction details to the acquirer → Scheme routes them to the issuer → Issuer checks card status, available credit and fraud rules → Issuer declines and places no hold on the funds → Team investigates clearing and settlement, the wrong stages → The failure was at authorisation, in seconds The assumption was: "A card failure is a card failure, any stage will do." Why? A credit card transaction has four distinct stages with different owners and different evidence. Authorisation happens in seconds, clearing exchanges the transaction records, settlement moves the funds between the banks, and billing and dispute touchpoints handle the customer

entries.title: The app said a EUR 850 payment failed, but the account was debited anyway
entries.text: The app said a EUR 850 payment failed, but the account was debited anyway Advanced A customer sent EUR 850 through a mobile app. The app showed the payment as failed. Yet the account statement showed the EUR 850 debit, and the customer asked for the money back. Here's how it happened: → Customer sends EUR 850 through the mobile app → App shows the payment as failed → Account statement shows the EUR 850 debit → Payment is in an uncertain state: the debit may mean it reached clearing and is still processing, or the ledger posted while the payment status update failed → Customer asks to retry the payment The assumption was: "Failed on screen means failed everywhere." Why? It does not. The debit may mean the payment reached the clearing system and is still processing, or it may mean the ledger posted while the payment status update failed. Treat the payment as one transaction with one identity across every system, and use the original instruction ID, end-to-end ID and ledger posting

entries.title: Gateway said success, EUR 40,000 never posted
entries.text: Gateway said success, EUR 40,000 never posted Advanced A payment gateway returns success for a EUR 40,000 supplier payment. The channel shows the payment as accepted. Hours later the supplier has not been paid, and the finance team finds no debit in the core banking ledger. Here's how that happens: → pain.001 instruction submitted through the channel → Gateway returns a success response → Channel shows the payment as accepted → Core banking ledger shows no debit → Payment engine still shows the payment as in progress The requirement said: "If the gateway says success, the payment is done." The gateway is authoritative for one thing only: acceptance of the instruction. Posting the debit to the ledger is a separate step, and it failed silently. The engine state agreed with neither side, because it was never reconciled against the ledger. Gateway success ≠ Ledger posted. BA Takeaway Separate the three facts and find the authoritative source for each. The gateway proves acceptance. The

entries.title: Screen timed out, EUR 25,000 supplier payment in limbo
entries.text: Screen timed out, EUR 25,000 supplier payment in limbo Advanced A corporate customer submits a EUR 25,000 supplier payment through the online channel. The screen spins, then times out. No confirmation appears and no reference is shown. The payment may have been accepted, executed, or never received. Here's how that happens: → Instruction submitted through the online channel → Screen spins and times out → No confirmation and no reference shown → Payment state is unknown The assumption was: "If the screen times out, the payment failed." A timeout only means the response was lost on the way back. The instruction may already have been accepted and executed downstream, so a retry on the same instruction can create a duplicate payment. A timeout is not a failure. It is an unknown. BA Takeaway Make the timeout path explicit in the product. The channel must show a pending or unknown state, never a success and never a failure, until the outcome is confirmed. The status enquiry uses the

entries.title: Supplier paid twice, EUR 12,000 doubled
entries.text: Supplier paid twice, EUR 12,000 doubled Advanced A supplier payment appears twice on the account statement for the same amount, to the same supplier, on the same day. The supplier confirms receiving two credits. EUR 12,000 has left the account twice. Here's how that happens: → Payment submitted for EUR 12,000 → Statement shows two debits, same amount, same day → Supplier confirms two credits received The assumption was: "Same amount, same day, so it must be one payment shown twice." Two identical credits are two payments until the evidence says otherwise. Reconstruct both payments end to end from the same evidence set: channel timestamp, idempotency key and payload hash, gateway reference, payment engine reference, ledger posting reference and clearing acknowledgement. Comparing the two sets shows whether the duplicate came from a client retry, a gateway redelivery or a missing idempotency check, and each cause has a different fix. Two identical credits are two payments until the

entries.title: New channel live, customers charged twice
entries.text: New channel live, customers charged twice Advanced A new corporate payment channel goes live. Days later the operations team notices duplicate debits: several corporate customers charged twice for the same instruction, and a few suppliers paid twice. The release passed testing. The duplicates are real. Here's how that happens: → New channel released → Duplicate debits noticed across customers → Some suppliers paid twice for one instruction The assumption was: "The release passed testing, so duplicates cannot happen." Testing passed, but the live path still created duplicates. Contain the failure first by confirming whether duplicates are still being created and, if so, stopping the affected path or routing it through a manual check. Then establish the affected population using stable identifiers rather than guesswork, matching on idempotency key, instruction reference, end-to-end identification, debtor, creditor, amount, currency and value date, and separate confirmed duplicates from

entries.title: 500 unmatched out of 20,000, and a INR 40 lakh figure that was not a loss
entries.text: 500 unmatched out of 20,000, and a INR 40 lakh figure that was not a loss Advanced A bank processed 20,000 transactions in a day. The morning reconciliation showed 500 transactions unmatched between the ledger and the clearing reports. A report called it a INR 40 lakh loss before anyone had investigated a single item. Here is what happened: → 20,000 transactions processed → Ledger compared with clearing reports → 500 transactions unmatched, an unmatched rate of 2.5 percent → Illustrative exposure calculated as 500 multiplied by an average of INR 8,000, giving INR 40 lakh → The illustrative figure reported as a confirmed loss The requirement said: "Report the unmatched exposure as the loss." So a framing figure became a headline loss, and the real investigation started on the back foot. Why? Unmatched is not lost. Most unmatched items turn out to be timing differences, late clearing files, or posting lags that resolve on their own. The INR 40 lakh figure frames the scale of the

entries.title: App says EUR 4,120, the bank says EUR 3,850
entries.text: App says EUR 4,120, the bank says EUR 3,850 Advanced A customer checks the mobile app and sees a balance of EUR 4,120. She calls the contact centre, and the agent's screen shows EUR 3,850. The difference is EUR 270, exactly the amount of a card payment she made that morning. Here's how that happens: → Card payment of EUR 270 made this morning → Mobile app shows EUR 4,120 → Contact centre screen shows EUR 3,850 The assumption was: "One balance must be wrong." Neither balance is wrong. The ledger balance is the posted balance in the core banking system and it is authoritative for posted funds, while the app balance may include pending or unposted items. The EUR 270 difference is the pending card payment, so the two balances are both accurate for what they represent, and the fix is to explain the difference rather than to change either balance. Two balances can both be right. They measure different things. BA Takeaway Start by defining what each balance means before touching either one.

entries.title: One payment, three different amounts
entries.text: One payment, three different amounts Advanced A cross-border payment complaint shows one amount in the online banking screen, a different amount transmitted by the API, and a third value held in the database. The beneficiary address looks complete on screen, but arrives truncated in the payment message. EUR 8,000 was sent. Nobody can agree what the payment actually says. Here's how that happens: → Customer enters the payment on screen → Screen displays one amount and a full address → API transmits a different amount → Database holds a third value → Payment message arrives with a truncated address The assumption was: "If the screen looks right, the payment is right." The value changed somewhere between the screen and the message. Fix the record first: pick one affected payment and its stable identifier, such as the end-to-end identification, and use that single identifier at every layer so the comparison is about the same record. Then capture the value at each point, what the customer

entries.title: Migration rehearsal: thousands of mismatches
entries.text: Migration rehearsal: thousands of mismatches Advanced A bank migrates from a legacy core system to a new platform. The first rehearsal shows thousands of mismatches: names that do not match, addresses that cannot be placed into the new structured format, dates in different formats, and payment records whose beneficiary details are incomplete. Thousands of customers, and the new platform cannot tell who they are. Here's how that happens: → Legacy data extracted → Field mapping applied → Data transformed and loaded → Control totals fail at every stage The assumption was: "Move the data, then check it." A migration without proof at each stage is a hope, not a plan. Define the migration as a controlled data movement with proof at every stage: start with a field-level mapping from the legacy system to the new platform, with every source field, its target field, its transformation rule, its validation rule and its owner, then prove the movement with control totals and exception handling at

entries.title: Failed instant payments spike just after 09:00
entries.text: Failed instant payments spike just after 09:00 Advanced Just after 09:00 the monitoring dashboard shows a sharp rise in failed instant payments. Customers report payments stuck in pending. The contact centre queue is growing, and nobody has declared an incident yet. Here's how that happens: → Failed instant payments spike on the dashboard → Customers report payments stuck in pending → Contact centre queue grows The assumption was: "Start fixing before declaring, so the incident looks smaller." The first responder must act in a fixed order and not improvise. First, confirm the incident is real using monitoring, error rates and customer reports, and declare it through the agreed channel with a severity based on customer impact, not on the suspected cause. Then establish the impact, the affected population, the containment, the ownership, the evidence and the update cadence, so that the response is organised from the first minutes rather than assembled under pressure. The first minutes

entries.title: 300 complaints in 20 minutes, one shape
entries.text: 300 complaints in 20 minutes, one shape Advanced On a weekday morning between 09:12 and 09:32, a contact centre receives more than 300 complaints with the same shape. Customers report a debit that does not match the payment status shown in the app, or a credit they expected that has not appeared. Three hundred voices, one pattern, and no incident bridge yet. Here's how that happens: → Complaints arrive with the same shape → Debits do not match the app status → Expected credits have not appeared The assumption was: "Find the root cause first, then protect the customers." Start with an incident bridge that separates three workstreams: customer and financial containment, technical root cause analysis, and communications. Containment owns the affected-transaction register, the decision on the next batch and any remediation, while the other workstreams proceed in parallel, so that customers are protected even before the root cause is known. Protect customers before you understand the

entries.title: UPI, cards, net banking and wallets all failing on the same day
entries.text: UPI, cards, net banking and wallets all failing on the same day Advanced On the same day, UPI payments fail with timeouts, card payments fail at the gateway, net banking sessions drop before confirmation, and wallet payments fail after the wallet is debited. Four rails, four failure shapes, one very bad day. Is it one cause, or several? Here's how that happens: → UPI payments time out → Card payments fail at the gateway → Net banking sessions drop before confirmation → Wallet payments fail after the wallet is debited The assumption was: "One bad day means one cause." Build one incident table segmented by rail and channel, gateway, bank, response code, time window and transaction state, and join each row to its ledger and clearing evidence by correlation ID. For each segment, establish whether the payment left the customer account, whether it reached clearing or the scheme, and what its authoritative state is now. Segmenting the incident this way shows whether there is one cause or

entries.title: Zero-fee weekend: volume hits 300 percent of peak
entries.text: Zero-fee weekend: volume hits 300 percent of peak Advanced A bank launches a zero-fee weekend campaign for retail payments. Within the first hour payment volume rises to 300 percent of a normal peak, three times the usual load. Latency climbs, channel sessions start timing out, and the clearing connector queue grows faster than it drains. Here's how that happens: → Campaign launches, zero fees → Volume rises to 300 percent of a normal peak → Latency climbs and sessions time out → Clearing queue grows faster than it drains The assumption was: "The system handled last year's peak, so it will handle the campaign." Averages hide the risk, and this surge is not an average day. Treat the surge as a capacity problem with three controls: intake, queue and recovery. At intake, apply back-pressure through the API gateway and channel, queue or gracefully defer non-critical traffic, show a clear pending state instead of a silent timeout, and throttle campaign traffic to a rate the downstream

entries.title: Rs 18,500 debited, the order never arrived
entries.text: Rs 18,500 debited, the order never arrived Advanced A customer pays Rs 18,500 for an order through a retailer's checkout. The bank account is debited, the payment gateway reports success, and the order remains pending. No confirmation, no dispatch, no delivery date. The money is gone and the goods never move. Here's how that happens: → Customer pays Rs 18,500 at checkout → Bank account debited → Gateway reports success → Order stays pending, no confirmation The assumption was: "Gateway success means the order exists." The payment outcome was lost at one of four boundaries, and the fulfilment path and the refund path depend on which one failed. Start by fixing the reference: take the payment reference from the customer's bank statement and the gateway transaction ID, and confirm they belong to the same payment. Then trace the four boundaries in order, the gateway, the bank, the merchant callback and the order creation, to find where the payment outcome was lost. A debit without an

entries.title: Paid and confirmed, but the shop never saw the order
entries.text: Paid and confirmed, but the shop never saw the order Advanced A retailer runs a checkout where the payment gateway returns a success response. The customer sees a confirmation screen, and then nothing happens. The order system never receives the callback, so no order is created, no goods are picked, and the customer is charged for a purchase the retailer cannot see. Here's how that happens: → Gateway returns success → Customer sees a confirmation screen → Order system never receives the callback → No order created, customer charged The requirement said: "Show the customer success as soon as the gateway answers." The outcome was lost between the gateway and the order system. Contain the impact by identifying every payment with no matching order, stop telling customers a payment succeeded until its outcome is known, and give support a holding message that is honest about the uncertainty. Then trace one affected payment end to end using its correlation ID, from the gateway request and

entries.title: The retailer, the bank API and the missing outcome
entries.text: The retailer, the bank API and the missing outcome Advanced A retailer wants its checkout connected directly to a bank's payment API, so orders can be paid without leaving the retailer's site. On a EUR 60,000 day of orders, the question is not how to call the API. It is how the retailer learns whether each payment actually completed. Here's how that happens: → Retailer submits payment instructions to the bank API → Bank returns a response → Retailer must learn the final outcome → Order is created only when the outcome is known The assumption was: "An API is just endpoints." Walk through the integration in layers and make each layer testable, starting with the contract, the endpoints, the request and response schemas, mandatory and optional fields, validation rules and error codes, then the authentication, the asynchronous status path and the recovery procedures. An acceptance response is never completion, and the retailer needs a status enquiry path for every payment whose outcome is

entries.title: Fast, secure, easy: the gateway brief with no requirements
entries.text: Fast, secure, easy: the gateway brief with no requirements Advanced A retailer sells online and in store and wants a third-party payment gateway for card and instant payments at checkout. The requirements are three words: fast, secure and easy to integrate. Three words, and no one can build from them. Here's how that happens: → Retailer wants card and instant payments at checkout → Brief says fast, secure and easy → No methods, currencies, channels or journeys defined The assumption was: "Fast, secure and easy is a requirement." Start from the customer and finance outcomes, not from the provider brochure: list the payment methods, currencies, channels and customer journeys in scope, and for each one define the expected flow, authorisation, capture, refund, partial refund, void, chargeback handling and settlement timing. Then define the API capabilities, the request and response contracts, the error handling, the security, the retries and the reconciliation, so the provider can be

entries.title: SIT passed clean. Production failed on day one.
entries.text: SIT passed clean. Production failed on day one. Advanced A merchant payment API integration passes system integration testing cleanly, every test case returning the expected response. It fails in production on day one. The same calls, the same payloads, and a failure rate climbing by the hour. Here's how that happens: → SIT passes every test case → Production fails from the first submissions → Failure rate is rising The assumption was: "If it passed SIT, production is the same." Contain the impact first by stopping new submissions if the failure rate is rising, telling the partner what is known and what is not, and confirming which payments have a financial effect and which do not. Then compare the environments side by side in a fixed order: endpoint and configuration, credentials and scopes, certificates and expiry dates, network routes and firewall rules, feature flags, downstream dependency versions and production data. The difference between test and production is usually in one

entries.title: HTTP 200, order unpaid, account debited
entries.text: HTTP 200, order unpaid, account debited Advanced A fintech partner integrates with a bank's payment API to submit customer credit transfers for its merchants. In testing, the API returns a successful HTTP response, but the merchant's downstream order record is not created. In one case the payment is debited while the merchant dashboard still shows the order as unpaid. Here's how that happens: → API returns HTTP 200 → Merchant order record is not created → Payment debited, dashboard shows unpaid The assumption was: "HTTP 200 means the payment completed." Start from the contract, not from the code: the API definition must state, for each endpoint, what a success response promises, receipt, validation, acceptance or completion, and what the caller must do next in each case. Then review authentication, schema, mandatory fields, business validation, response codes, idempotency and observability, because a success response that promises completion when it only means receipt will mislead

entries.title: The API contract that forgot to say what success means
entries.text: The API contract that forgot to say what success means Advanced A bank is publishing a Payment API for corporate customers and retail partners. The first draft of the contract is a list of fields with no rules. It does not say which fields are required, what happens when a field is missing, which error code means what, whether a success response means the payment completed, or how a caller should safely retry. A list of fields, and EUR 100,000 a day will flow through it. Here's how that happens: → Contract drafted as a list of fields → No required or optional rules → No error code meanings → No statement of what success means → No safe retry rule The assumption was: "A list of fields is a contract." Define every field with its name, type, cardinality, validation rule and error code, and state explicitly which fields are required, which are optional, and which are conditionally mandatory by rail, destination or product. Where a field is optional under the message schema but the bank's

entries.title: Two weeks to build a Payment API integration
entries.text: Two weeks to build a Payment API integration Advanced A retailer needs a Payment API integration delivered in a two-week sprint. The checkout must submit payment instructions to the bank, receive a clear acceptance or rejection, and create the order only when the payment outcome is known. Two weeks, and the contract is still unwritten. Here's how that happens: → Sprint starts, two weeks on the clock → Checkout must submit instructions to the bank → Order created only when the outcome is known The assumption was: "Start building, the contract can follow." Start the sprint with discovery compressed into the first two days: confirm the business outcome, the checkout journey, the payment types in scope, the expected volumes and the response contract. The contract definition matters most, so agree in writing what each response means, so that an acceptance response is never mistaken for completion, and define the status enquiry path the retailer uses when a payment outcome is unclear. The

entries.title: Customers start onboarding, then vanish at document upload
entries.text: Customers start onboarding, then vanish at document upload Advanced A bank wants more new retail customers to complete digital onboarding, but only a small share of started applications reach an active account. Customers abandon the journey at document upload and at identity verification. Many who do finish are later held for manual review because documents are unclear or data does not match. Here's how that happens: → Application started → Identity details entered → Document upload, customers abandon here → Identity verification, more abandon here → Manual review holds the rest → Account opened, first transaction rare The assumption was: "Customers abandon because they are not interested." Start with evidence, not opinions, and measure the funnel stage by stage: started, identity details entered, document uploaded, identity verified, screening complete, account opened and first transaction. Then map the friction, the document collection, the validation, the screening, the exception

entries.title: SCT Inst has no maximum, 10 seconds, payee check mandatory
entries.text: SCT Inst has no maximum, 10 seconds, payee check mandatory Advanced A bank must change its instant euro payments to match the current scheme rules. There is no longer a scheme-level maximum amount for SCT Inst, execution must complete within 10 seconds, and verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments. The change touches the mobile app, the payment engine, the sanctions and fraud services, the clearing adapter, the ledger and the customer notifications. Six systems, one scheme change. Here's how that happens: → Scheme rules change: no maximum, 10 seconds, payee verification → Mobile app, engine, sanctions, fraud, clearing, ledger and notifications all affected The assumption was: "It is a small scheme change." Build the impact analysis as a map, not as a list of opinions: start from the change and walk upstream to find which channels, products and customer journeys can submit an instant euro payment, which limits and validations apply today, and which of those must

entries.title: One day to go-live, compliance finds a missing requirement
entries.text: One day to go-live, compliance finds a missing requirement Advanced A bank is one day from deploying an upgrade to its instant euro payment service. UAT is signed off, regression evidence is filed, the deployment window is booked and the customer communications are ready. Late in the afternoon the compliance team raises a requirement nobody recorded: verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments. Here's how that happens: → UAT signed off, deployment booked → Compliance raises an unrecorded requirement → One day to go-live The assumption was: "UAT sign-off means the requirements are complete." First classify the item precisely as a defect against an agreed requirement, a safety or compliance obligation, or genuinely new scope, and confirm the obligation at its source, for example verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments from 9 October 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/886, and SCT Inst execution has a 10-second maximum with no scheme-level maximum since

entries.title: UAT morning one: most collections rejected
entries.text: UAT morning one: most collections rejected Advanced A bank is starting user acceptance testing for a new SEPA direct debit collection service. On the first morning the failure rate is critical: most test collections are rejected, mandate references cannot be found, and the test schedule shows collections submitted on the wrong day. The testers are ready. The environment is not. Here's how that happens: → UAT starts for SEPA direct debit collections → Most test collections rejected → Mandate references cannot be found → Collections submitted on the wrong day The assumption was: "Testers should push through and log the failures." Begin with a triage that separates the failure causes into four buckets, environment, test data, build and requirements, and check the environment first: whether the UAT build is the intended version, whether the endpoints, credentials and scheme adapters point at the right test systems, and whether the feature flags are set as the release notes state. Only

entries.title: A few customers, one wrong EMI
entries.text: A few customers, one wrong EMI Advanced A bank receives complaints from a small group of loan customers that their monthly EMI is wrong. Most customers are unaffected, which makes the problem harder, not easier. A handful of complaints, and a calculation that is wrong for some loans and right for the rest. Here's how that happens: → Small group complains the EMI is wrong → Most customers unaffected → Complaints share no obvious pattern The assumption was: "Only the complainers are affected." Start by defining the affected population precisely: list every complaining account and search for others with the same characteristics, so the fix covers silent cases as well as complaints. For each affected loan, capture the full calculation inputs: principal, sanctioned rate, rate change history with effective dates, tenure, schedule generation rules, rounding policy, part-payment history and customer data. The pattern only emerges when the cases are compared, because the affected loans share a

entries.title: Make payments faster: the brief with no user, no baseline, no target
entries.text: Make payments faster: the brief with no user, no baseline, no target Advanced A bank wants to launch an instant payment product for small business customers. The sponsor has asked the team to make payments faster. The request has no named user group, no baseline, no target speed and no statement of the problem customers actually face today. Faster than what, for whom, and by when? Nobody can say. Here's how that happens: → Sponsor asks for faster payments → No user group named → No baseline and no target speed → No statement of the customer problem The assumption was: "Faster is a requirement." Start by naming the target users precisely, for example small businesses that pay domestic suppliers on fixed weekly cycles, and exclude segments the product will not serve in the first release, then write a problem statement in the form of who suffers, what it costs them and how often, and gather evidence such as payment volumes, current settlement times, supplier discount losses and support

entries.title: The supplier file that passes through three screens and a phone call
entries.text: The supplier file that passes through three screens and a phone call Advanced A bank runs a legacy supplier payment process that has grown by accretion over a decade. A corporate customer sends a payment file, operations staff print exception lists, re-key corrected details into three different screens, phone the customer for missing information, and then release the file late in the day. One file, EUR 45,000 of supplier payments, and a whole afternoon of re-keying. Here's how that happens: → Payment file arrives from the customer → Exception lists printed → Corrected details re-keyed into three screens → Customer phoned for missing information → File released late in the day The assumption was: "Document the process, then improve it." Begin by observing the work as performed, not as documented: follow real files from intake to release, time each step, and record every workaround, hand-off and re-key, then quantify the pain with measures the business can compare, such as

entries.title: pacs.008 passed the clearing system. Where is the pacs.002?
entries.text: pacs.008 passed the clearing system. Where is the pacs.002? Advanced A EUR 75,000 payment is sent through the clearing system to the beneficiary bank. The pacs.008 has gone. The beneficiary bank is waiting, the customer is asking, and nobody can say where the status reply is. Here's how that happens: → pacs.008 sent to the clearing system → Clearing system processes the payment → pacs.008 reaches the beneficiary bank → pacs.002 status reply travels back through the clearing system The assumption was: "The clearing system is just a pipe." The clearing system sits between the originator bank and the beneficiary bank, so the pacs.008 passes through it and the pacs.002 returns through it. An analyst drawing the flow must include the clearing system as a party, not as a pipe, because it sends and receives messages of its own. The clearing system is a party, not a pipe. BA Takeaway Draw the clearing system as a party with messages of its own. The pacs.008 passes through it on the way out,

entries.title: Debited, rejected, and the EUR 20,000 must come back
entries.text: Debited, rejected, and the EUR 20,000 must come back Advanced The originator bank deducts EUR 20,000 from the customer for a payment. The payment never reaches the beneficiary, because the clearing system rejected it. The customer sees a deduction with no payment, and the money is sitting with the clearing system. Here's how that happens: → Originator bank deducts EUR 20,000 from the customer → Clearing system rejects the payment → Clearing system holds the rejected funds → Return travels back to the originator bank → Originator bank credits the customer The assumption was: "A rejected payment returns itself." The clearing system holds the funds it rejected, so the return starts there and travels back to the originator bank, which credits the customer. A rejection is not a return. Until the return message and the funds travel back, the customer has paid for nothing. A rejection without a return leaves the customer paying for nothing. BA Takeaway Trace the return, not just the

entries.title: The MT103 in a language nobody at the bank speaks
entries.text: The MT103 in a language nobody at the bank speaks Advanced A EUR 15,000 payment is sent to a beneficiary bank in a country whose language is not English. The names and addresses in the message are in the local language. The operations team stares at the MT103 and wonders whether it can even be processed. Here's how that happens: → MT103 arrives with names in the local language → Structured fields carry the account, currency and amount → Processing follows the coded fields The assumption was: "The message must be in English to be processed." When the beneficiary bank is in a country whose language is not English, the MT103 is still processed from its structured fields, which are coded and do not depend on the language of the country. The names and addresses in the message may be in the local language, but the fields that drive processing, such as the account number, the currency, and the amount, are numeric or coded. Processing therefore does not stop at a language barrier; it follows

entries.title: Two banks, no account between them, EUR 40,000 still arrives
entries.text: Two banks, no account between them, EUR 40,000 still arrives Advanced A customer wants to transfer EUR 40,000 to a bank that holds no account with the sending bank. There is no direct relationship, no nostro, no vostro. The payment still arrives. Here's how that happens: → Sending bank has no account with the beneficiary bank → Sending bank passes the instruction to its correspondent → Correspondent passes it onward → Payment reaches the beneficiary bank The assumption was: "No direct account means no payment." A customer can transfer funds to a bank that has no account with the sending bank, because the payment travels through correspondent and intermediary banks that do hold accounts with each other. The sending bank passes the instruction to its correspondent, which passes it onward until it reaches a bank that holds an account for the beneficiary bank. The chain exists precisely to connect banks that have no direct relationship. The chain exists precisely to connect banks that

entries.title: We hold each other's accounts. Do we still need an intermediary?
entries.text: We hold each other's accounts. Do we still need an intermediary? Advanced The ordering bank and the beneficiary bank already hold accounts with each other. A EUR 90,000 international payment needs to move between them. The operations team still routes it through an intermediary, paying the fee and adding a day, out of habit. Here's how that happens: → Ordering bank and beneficiary bank hold accounts with each other → Payment routed through an intermediary anyway → Extra fee charged, extra day added The assumption was: "An intermediary is always needed for a cross-border payment." A direct relationship can carry the payment without an intermediary, which is faster and cheaper, but an intermediary may still be used for a currency, a corridor, or a compliance reason. The choice is a design decision, not a rule, and it depends on the corridor and the banks involved. Direct is faster and cheaper, but the corridor decides. BA Takeaway Test the direct route first. entries.title: One misspelt name in field 50, EUR 30,000 sent back
entries.text: One misspelt name in field 50, EUR 30,000 sent back Advanced An MT103 for EUR 30,000 is sent to pay a supplier. The ordering customer name in field 50 is misspelt by one letter. The payment comes back. The supplier is unpaid, and the ordering customer cannot understand why one letter stopped EUR 30,000. Here's how that happens: → Name in field 50 is misspelt → Screening and reconciliation flag the name → MT103 returned to the originator bank The assumption was: "A small spelling error cannot stop a payment." The misspelling matters because screening and reconciliation match on the name, and a name that does not match the account can look like a different party. The return is therefore a data-quality failure, not a funds failure, and it is fixed by correcting the name and resending. A return over a name is a data failure, not a funds failure. BA Takeaway Check the name against the account before sending, not after the return. Screening matches on the name, and a name that does not

entries.title: Sent EUR 5,000, the employee received EUR 4,940
entries.text: Sent EUR 5,000, the employee received EUR 4,940 Advanced An ordering customer pays an employee EUR 5,000 with an MT103. An intermediary bank deducts its charges on the way. The employee receives EUR 4,940, and asks why EUR 60 is missing. The ordering customer has no answer, because nobody explained the charge rule before the payment was sent. Here's how that happens: → Ordering customer pays employee EUR 5,000 by MT103 → Intermediary deducts EUR 60 in charges → Beneficiary bank credits EUR 4,940 The assumption was: "The amount sent is the amount received." The beneficiary bank credits the amount that arrives after the deductions, and the ordering customer must explain the difference to the employee. The situation is a normal consequence of the serial method, and it is why the charge-bearer rule matters before the payment is sent. In a serial payment, every hand takes its charge. BA Takeaway Agree the charge-bearer rule before sending, and tell the beneficiary what will arrive. Under

entries.title: Faster Payments is not SEPA with a different name
entries.text: Faster Payments is not SEPA with a different name Advanced A team that knows SEPA is asked to build the flow for UK Faster Payments and BACS. They reach for the SEPA messages, because the concepts look the same: initiation, clearing, status reporting. Then the first GBP 25,000 payment fails, because the UK messages are not the SEPA messages. Here's how that happens: → SEPA concepts: initiation, clearing, status → UK Faster Payments messages differ from SEPA → BACS messages differ from SEPA → Payment fails on the wrong message set The assumption was: "SEPA messages work everywhere." The messages exchanged between banks in UK Faster Payments and in BACS are different from the messages used in SEPA. The SEPA message set is a good starting point, because the concepts of initiation, clearing, and status reporting are the same, but the actual messages and the clearing systems differ. An analyst who understands the SEPA flow can learn the UK flows by mapping each SEPA message to its UK

entries.title: The sterling leg went through CHAPS. The payment still had to leave the UK.
entries.text: The sterling leg went through CHAPS. The payment still had to leave the UK. Advanced A cross-border payment needs sterling settlement in the UK, so the team routes the domestic leg through CHAPS. The CHAPS leg settles cleanly in central bank money. Then the payment stops, because nobody arranged the leg out of the UK, and the GBP 120,000 sits in London. Here's how that happens: → Cross-border payment needs sterling settlement → CHAPS settles the domestic sterling leg → No correspondent or scheme arranged for the leg out of the UK The assumption was: "CHAPS can carry a payment abroad." CHAPS settles sterling payments between UK banks in central bank money, and a cross-border payment that needs sterling settlement in the UK can use it as the domestic leg. The cross-border leg itself still needs a correspondent or a scheme to carry the payment out of the UK, so CHAPS is one leg of the journey, not the whole journey. CHAPS settles sterling at home. The cross-border leg still needs a

entries.title: Faster Payments settles in seconds. Salaries still run on BACS.
entries.text: Faster Payments settles in seconds. Salaries still run on BACS. Advanced Faster Payments settles a payment in seconds. Yet every month, a business with 2,000 employees pays salaries through BACS, a system older than most of its staff. The faster rail is there, and the business still chooses the slower one. Here's how that happens: → Faster Payments settles single payments in seconds → Business pays 2,000 salaries through BACS → Bulk run arrives on schedule, at low cost The assumption was: "Faster makes BACS obsolete." Faster Payments is built for single, urgent payments, and it costs more per payment and carries limits that bulk runs do not want. BACS is built for bulk, scheduled, low-cost payments such as salaries and supplier runs. The two systems therefore serve different needs, and the older one survives because it fits the bulk use case better. The older rail survives because it fits the bulk use case. BA Takeaway Match the rail to the use case, not to the speed. Single and

entries.title: GBP 10,000 crossed borders with no SWIFT message at all
entries.text: GBP 10,000 crossed borders with no SWIFT message at all Advanced A customer sends GBP 10,000 to a beneficiary abroad. No SWIFT message is sent for either leg. The beneficiary is paid, on time, and the sending bank never touched the correspondent chain. Here's how that happens: → Customer funds a local account in the sending country → Provider pays the beneficiary from its local account abroad → Each leg settles domestically → Flows netted across customers The assumption was: "Every cross-border payment needs SWIFT." The provider holds local accounts in the countries it serves and settles each leg domestically. A customer paying from one country to another funds a local account in the sending country, and the provider pays the beneficiary from its local account in the receiving country, so no cross-border SWIFT message is needed for the legs. The model works because the provider nets the flows across its customers, and it is a different design from the correspondent banking chain. Two

entries.title: The MT103 says euros. The MT202 COV says dollars.
entries.text: The MT103 says euros. The MT202 COV says dollars. Advanced A cover payment is sent, and the two legs carry different currencies. The MT103 says euros. The MT202 COV says dollars. The operations team assumes one of them is wrong, and holds the EUR 150,000 payment. Here's how that happens: → MT103 instruction in euros → MT202 COV in dollars → Fields 52, 53 and 54 describe the chain → Payment held while the mismatch is investigated The assumption was: "Both legs must carry the same currency." In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 can carry different currencies, and the question is how the currency of each leg is decided and what fields 52, 53 and 54 carry. Field 52 identifies the ordering institution, field 53 identifies the sender's correspondent, and field 54 identifies the receiver's correspondent, so together they describe the chain of banks that will fund the payment. The currency of the cover leg follows the correspondent account it settles in, which is why the two legs can

entries.title: Cancelled, recalled, disputed: three words, three different acts
entries.text: Cancelled, recalled, disputed: three words, three different acts Advanced A EUR 40,000 SEPA payment has gone wrong. The team argues about whether to cancel it, recall it, or dispute it, as if the three words meant the same thing. They do not, and picking the wrong one sends the wrong message. Here's how that happens: → Payment has gone wrong → Is it settled or not? → Cancellation stops a payment before settlement → Recall requested with camt.056, answered with camt.029 → Return made with pacs.004 The assumption was: "Undoing a payment is one action." In SEPA, a dispute, a cancellation, and a recall are three different actions. A recall is requested with a camt.056 and answered with a camt.029, a return is made with a pacs.004, and a cancellation stops a payment before it settles. The three are often confused because they all undo a payment, but they apply at different stages and they use different messages. Cancellation, recall and return apply at different stages and use different

entries.title: The beneficiary bank has a BIC that cannot receive messages
entries.text: The beneficiary bank has a BIC that cannot receive messages Advanced A EUR 65,000 payment is addressed to a bank whose BIC has the digit 1 in position 8. That marks it as non-connected: a SWIFT participant that cannot receive messages directly. The MT103 bounces, and the payment has nowhere to go. Here's how that happens: → Beneficiary bank holds a non-connected BIC → MT103 and MT202 COV sent to a live BIC → Live BIC forwards the funds onward → Onward leg uses a normal serial MT103 The assumption was: "Every BIC can receive a message." Some banks hold a BIC with the digit 1 in position 8, which marks it as non-connected: it is a SWIFT participant but cannot receive messages directly. The MT103 announcement and the MT202 COV are then sent to a live BIC, which forwards the funds to the non-connected bank over an internal network, usually with a normal serial MT103. The same pattern appears in bank groups where SWIFT communication is centralised at the head office and the head office

entries.title: The instruction was complete. The payment waited for the currency.
entries.text: The instruction was complete. The payment waited for the currency. Advanced A customer instructs a EUR 80,000 payment in a foreign currency, with every field complete and every check passed. The payment does not move. Hours pass, and the instruction sits untouched, waiting for something the customer never sees. Here's how that happens: → Bank receives payment instructions → Orders collected until cut-off time → Bank checks its nostro balances → Buy, sell or do nothing, the decision is made → Payment waits for the currency position The assumption was: "A complete instruction is executed at once." A bank does not buy the currency of every payment the moment it is instructed, because it does not know in advance how much foreign currency it will need. It collects orders until a cut-off time and then decides whether to buy, sell or do nothing, based on the balance of orders and the funds already sitting in its nostro accounts. A payment can therefore wait for the bank's currency position

entries.title: Five returns in six weeks over one wrong field
entries.text: Five returns in six weeks over one wrong field Advanced A payment sent to Australia was returned five times over six weeks. Each time the note said the same thing: the beneficiary bank's SWIFT code had to appear in field 57A. The code was right there in the message, in field 72 and in field 52A, where the receiving bank could see it. It still came back, five times. Here's how that happens: → Payment sent to Australia → SWIFT code placed in field 72 and 52A → Payment returned, code required in field 57A → Beneficiary bank taken over, code changed → New code used in field 57A, payment applied The assumption was: "If the receiving bank can see the code, the field does not matter." The code had been placed in field 72 and in field 52A, where the receiving bank could see it, but that did not satisfy the validation: field 57A is the field the receiving bank reads to find the account with institution. The beneficiary bank had also been taken over and its SWIFT code had changed, so the sender

entries.title: Two legs, one payment, one thread: the UETR
entries.text: Two legs, one payment, one thread: the UETR Advanced A EUR 110,000 payment passes through a correspondent bank on its way abroad. The correspondent sees two payments: the incoming payment from the sender, and the outgoing payment to the next bank. Two legs, two messages, and the reconciliation team cannot prove they are the same payment. Here's how that happens: → Correspondent receives the incoming payment → Correspondent sends the outgoing payment onward → UETR travels unchanged in both legs → UETR carried in field 121 of block 3 → Bank reconciles incoming and outgoing legs The assumption was: "Each leg is a separate payment." The two legs are linked by the unique end-to-end transaction reference, the UETR, which travels unchanged from one message to the next and is carried in field 121 of block 3. No bank in the chain may modify field 121, because changing it would break the link that lets every bank reconcile the payment it received with the payment it sent. The UETR is the

entries.title: A future-dated MT103 for EUR 200,000, offered as security
entries.text: A future-dated MT103 for EUR 200,000, offered as security Advanced An MT103 value-dated far in the future is presented to a bank, and the holder asks the bank to discount it. EUR 200,000, dated months ahead, offered as if it were money already promised. The bank declines, and the holder cannot understand why a payment instruction is not a promise. Here's how that happens: → MT103 value-dated far in the future → Presented to the bank for discounting → MT103 is an instruction to pay → Payer account holds sufficient funds, or it does not The assumption was: "A future MT103 is proof the money will arrive." An MT103 is an instruction to pay, not a proof of financial commitment: when the due date arrives, execution depends on the payer account holding sufficient funds. If the payer does not pay, the beneficiary has no recourse, and neither does a bank that discounted it, unless it signed a separate contract with the payer. An MT103 is an instruction to pay, not proof of financial

entries.title: The MT101 debited the customer. Where did the money sit?
entries.text: The MT101 debited the customer. Where did the money sit? Advanced A corporate customer sends an MT101 to pay its suppliers. The debtor's account is debited at once. But the suppliers are not paid yet, and the EUR 95,000 sits somewhere inside the bank, on an account nobody on the customer side can see. Here's how that happens: → MT101 received from the customer → Debtor account debited to an intermediary account → MT103 generated to move the money onward → Funds debited from the intermediary account → Funds forwarded to the destination The assumption was: "The MT101 moves the money." Accounting is done on the MT101 itself, in part: the debtor's account is debited and the funds are placed on an intermediary account inside the bank. When the MT103 is generated to move the money onward, the funds are debited from that intermediary account and forwarded to the destination. The MT101 therefore does the customer-side accounting, and the MT103 does the interbank settlement. The MT101 does the

entries.title: French bank, German bank, dollars settled in New York
entries.text: French bank, German bank, dollars settled in New York Advanced A French bank sends USD 500,000 to a German bank. Two European banks, an American currency, and a payment that never leaves the United States to settle. The treasurer expects a cross-border journey. Settlement takes one domestic step. Here's how that happens: → French bank instructs its US correspondent → Nostro debited in the USA → German bank's US correspondent credited → Settlement completes in a single domestic step The assumption was: "A payment between two European banks settles in Europe." When a French bank sends USD to a German bank, it tells its US correspondent to debit the nostro and credit the German bank's account with that bank's own US correspondent. Settlement completes in a single domestic step, since both accounts sit in the USA. The sender finds the German bank's US correspondent in its Standing Settlement Instructions and states it in the MT103. When both accounts sit in the USA, settlement is one

entries.title: The letter of credit is issued. How does the money move?
entries.text: The letter of credit is issued. How does the money move? Advanced A letter of credit for USD 250,000 is issued with an MT700. The documents are accepted. Now the beneficiary asks a simple question: how does the money move? The MT700 does not say. Here's how that happens: → Credit issued with MT700 → Documents accepted → Parties agree the settlement instrument → Funds move by serial MT103, or by MT103 plus MT202 COV The assumption was: "The MT700 settles the credit." A letter of credit is issued with an MT700, but the standard does not fix how it must be settled, so the parties agree the payment instrument between themselves. In general the settlement runs through a serial MT103, or through an MT103 together with an MT202 COV. Either route moves the funds under the credit once the documents have been accepted. The MT700 issues the credit. The MT103 moves the money. BA Takeaway Agree the settlement instrument between the parties before the documents are accepted. Either a serial MT103

entries.title: France before SEPA: PNS, TBF, then CORE
entries.text: France before SEPA: PNS, TBF, then CORE Advanced Before SEPA, France already ran EBA systems for interbank payments alongside high value systems called PNS and TBF. Then SEPA arrived, and CORE, the retail clearing system, came after it to process XML format files. Old systems, new systems, and a market that changed underneath them, with a EUR 2 million retail file caught in the middle of the changeover. Here's how that happens: → PNS and TBF run high value payments → EBA systems handle interbank payments → SEPA arrives, market infrastructures change → CORE arrives after SEPA for retail The assumption was: "SEPA replaced everything overnight." The market infrastructures changed greatly with the SEPA project, with old and new systems sitting side by side for a time. CORE, the retail clearing system, arrived after SEPA to process XML format files and improve retail payment services. Old and new systems sat side by side while the market changed.
