entries.title: RuPay: the scheme that is also the clearing house
entries.text: RuPay: the scheme that is also the clearing house Advanced A RuPay card payment of Rs 12,000 is made between two RuPay member banks. The issuer expects the transaction to clear through a separate clearing house. It does not. The scheme clears it itself. Here's how that happens: → Issuer and acquirer are both RuPay members → Transaction clears through RuPay itself → NPCI operates RuPay in India The assumption was: "A scheme always needs a separate clearing house." On RuPay, clearing and settlement run between domestic and other network partners, with RuPay acting as both the card scheme and the clearing house. In India the clearing house role sits with NPCI, which operates RuPay. When issuer and acquirer are both RuPay members, they clear their transactions through RuPay itself rather than through a separate clearing house. Two RuPay members clear through RuPay itself. BA Takeaway Check membership before assuming a separate clearing house. When issuer and acquirer are both RuPay

entries.title: The MT103 has no town name. pacs.008 demands one.
entries.text: The MT103 has no town name. pacs.008 demands one. Advanced An MT103 arrives for a EUR 45,000 payment, and it must be translated into pacs.008. The MT103 carries no structured address. pacs.008 requires a town name and a country code, and the town cannot be invented. Guessing writes false data onto the payment. A blank fails validation. The payment is stuck between two message standards. Here's how that happens: → MT103 taken in exactly as sent → Tested against every field pacs.008 requires → Town name missing, no source in the message → Enrichment needed from an authoritative source → Unresolvable gaps go to exception handling The assumption was: "Translate the message and fill the gaps." MT to MX coexistence creates a data gap: an MT103 may carry no structured address, yet pacs.008 requires town name and country code. The missing town cannot be invented, guessing writes false data onto the payment and a blank fails validation. Handle the gap with explicit translation rules,

entries.title: The correspondent cut the limit without warning
entries.text: The correspondent cut the limit without warning Advanced A correspondent cuts an intraday credit limit without warning. The routing engine keeps feeding the same corridor, EUR 300,000 of payments queue up, and rejects arrive that nobody can explain. The corridor was fine yesterday. The limit changed, and the engine never noticed. Here's how that happens: → Correspondent cuts the intraday limit → Engine keeps feeding the same corridor → Payments queue and rejects arrive unexplained The assumption was: "Routing rules are written for the quiet day." Good routing rules are written for the bad day, not the quiet one: a correspondent can cut an intraday credit limit without warning, and an engine that keeps feeding the same corridor will queue payments and generate rejects it cannot explain. Build the rules with eligibility checks, fallback routes, a defined decision order, and an audit trail naming the affected payments and the reason. A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control

entries.title: Ten million a month, and the peak is the only number that matters
entries.text: Ten million a month, and the peak is the only number that matters Advanced Five new clients bring ten million transactions a month, roughly 330,000 a day on average. The average looks comfortable. Then payroll and supplier files arrive in concentrated morning windows, and the busiest hour is already at about 70 percent of measured capacity. The average fits. The peak does not. Here's how that happens: → Ten million a month added → 330,000 a day on average → Morning file windows concentrate the load → Busiest hour already at 70 percent of capacity The assumption was: "Plan for the average." With the busiest hour already at about 70 percent of measured capacity, the only question that matters is whether the peak fits. Convert the growth into throughput, concurrency, queue depth, storage, monitoring and resilience requirements before the clients go live. Averages hide peaks. Peaks break systems. BA Takeaway Size for the peak, not the average. Convert the growth into throughput,

entries.title: One extra hour, and every deadline moves
entries.text: One extra hour, and every deadline moves Advanced The business asks for the customer cut-off to move one hour later. One hour sounds small. But a cut-off is not a single time, it is the end of a deadline chain: channel cut-offs, scheme windows, liquidity checks and operational staffing. Move the hour, and every deadline in the chain moves with it. Here's how that happens: → Cut-off extended by one hour → Scheme windows tested → Liquidity tested for the extra hour → Staffing tested for the later window → Exception path for payments that still miss it The assumption was: "A cut-off is a single time." A cut-off is not a single time but the end of a deadline chain, channel cut-offs, scheme windows, liquidity checks and operational staffing. Adding an hour moves the whole chain, and the customer promise has to survive at the new time. entries.title: EUR 250,000 from Europe to India, and nobody owned the journey
entries.text: EUR 250,000 from Europe to India, and nobody owned the journey Advanced A European buyer pays an Indian exporter EUR 250,000. The payment crosses four legs: a domestic euro rail, a cross-border bridge, an FX conversion and a domestic Indian rail. Each participant reports only its own leg. The payment is late, and the chain of calls begins: exporter to buyer, buyer to bank, bank to bridge operator, and nobody can say where the money is. Here's how that happens: → Buyer pays on the domestic euro rail → Payment crosses the cross-border bridge → Euros convert to rupees → Exporter paid on the Indian rail → Nobody can say where the money is The assumption was: "Each party owns its own leg, so the journey is covered." With no owner of the end-to-end state, a late payment turns into a chain of calls, exporter to buyer, buyer to bank, bank to bridge operator, and nobody can say where the money is. Give the corridor a named owner for the whole journey, with every leg mapped to its rail, FX

entries.title: Credited already? The recall is only a request
entries.text: Credited already? The recall is only a request Advanced A EUR 18,000 payment has been credited to the wrong beneficiary. The sender bank wants the money back. It has no power to command it back. It can only ask. Here's how that happens: → Sender bank issues camt.056 → Beneficiary bank tests whether the funds are still available → camt.029 answers, accepted or rejected → pacs.004 moves the money only on acceptance The assumption was: "A recall commands the money back." Once the beneficiary bank has credited the customer, the sender bank has no power to command the money back; it can only request it. The sender sends a camt.056 cancellation request, the beneficiary bank tests whether the funds are still available and answers with a camt.029, and a pacs.004 moves the money only on acceptance. A rejection leaves the sender with a commercial claim outside the payment rails, so the camt.056 must go out fast, while the funds are still there. A recall is a request, not a command. BA Takeaway

entries.title: Two legs settled, two returns needed
entries.text: Two legs settled, two returns needed Advanced A EUR 60,000 cover payment settles twice over: the pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover that moved funds between correspondents. The customer payment is returned. The team closes the case, and the nostro ledger still disagrees by EUR 60,000. Here's how that happens: → pacs.008 instruction settles → pacs.009 cover settles between correspondents → Customer payment returned → Cover leg still open The assumption was: "Returning the customer payment unwinds the whole payment." Returning the customer payment unwinds only the first leg; the cover needs its own pacs.004, matched to the original cover by UETR and settlement references. Both legs post to the Nostro ledger, so reconciliation must pair all four messages, instruction, cover, return of instruction, and return of cover. One return unwinds one leg. A cover payment needs its own return. BA Takeaway Return both legs, and match each return to its original by UETR and settlement

entries.title: EUR 5,000 debited, failed, and the books disagree
entries.text: EUR 5,000 debited, failed, and the books disagree Advanced A 5,000 euro SEPA credit transfer debited the account. It failed between the engine and clearing. The customer is EUR 5,000 down, the books say the payment went, and reality says it never arrived. Here's how that happens: → Account debited EUR 5,000 → Payment failed between engine and clearing → Books and reality disagree The assumption was: "Fix the customer first, reconcile later." Before touching anything, establish the true state across core banking, payment engine, ISO 20022 messages, clearing, settlement and accounting, and rule out duplicates. Then reverse the debit or re-release the payment, post correcting entries with a clear audit trail, and bring every system to the same outcome. Never touch the money until the true state is known. BA Takeaway Establish the true state first, across core banking, engine, messages, clearing, settlement and accounting, and rule out duplicates. Then reverse the debit or re-release the

entries.title: Duplicate payouts: 90 percent recovered, 10 percent still missing
entries.text: Duplicate payouts: 90 percent recovered, 10 percent still missing Advanced A payout batch fires twice, and suppliers are paid double. The team starts diagnosing the cause while the batch is still running. More duplicates are being created while they investigate, and 10 percent of the duplicated value is still missing. Here's how that happens: → Payout batch fires twice → Duplicates still being created → Recovery at 90 percent, 10 percent still missing The assumption was: "Diagnose first, contain later." Duplicates demand containment before diagnosis: freeze the retry and payout batch so no more duplicates are created while the team investigates. Then identify the full population by reference or idempotency key, reverse the duplicates systematically, and track recovery until every case is closed. The cause here was a retry firing twice after a timeout through an idempotency gap, and the permanent fix is idempotency keys on every payout plus real-time reconciliation flagging double

entries.title: Acknowledged, then lost: the broker died before replication
entries.text: Acknowledged, then lost: the broker died before replication Advanced A payment is charged once. The retry charges it a second time. Nothing alerted, because each component behaved exactly as designed, and the failure lived in the interaction between them. Here's how that happens: → Leader acknowledges with acks=1 → Broker dies before replication → Message lost, payment already charged → Retry charges a second time → No alert fires The assumption was: "An acknowledgement means the message is safe." With acks=1 only the leader acknowledges, so a broker dying before replication loses the message, yet the payment had already been charged and the retry charged a second time. Nothing alerted because each component behaved as designed; the failure lived in the interaction. Fix the guarantees, acks=all with idempotent producers and dedup keys on every payment, add the transactional outbox pattern so the business record and the event cannot diverge, and keep reconciliation as the backstop.

entries.title: GBP 125,000 left. No trace, no rejection, no return.
entries.text: GBP 125,000 left. No trace, no rejection, no return. Advanced A 125,000 pound international payment left the sender. It never arrived. No rejection, no return, no confirmation. The beneficiary is waiting, the sender is asking, and the payment has vanished from every screen that matters. Here's how that happens: → Payment leaves the sender → No arrival, no rejection, no return → Beneficiary waiting, sender asking The assumption was: "No news means it failed. Send it again." Before acting, prove what happened: pull the UETR, check the tracker for the last confirmed hop, and ask whether the money sits with an intermediary, in a compliance review, or stuck in a queue. Never re-send until the original is accounted for, because a duplicate is worse than a delay, and keep both sender and expectant beneficiary updated. Never re-send until the original is accounted for. A duplicate is worse than a delay. BA Takeaway Prove first. Pull the UETR, find the last confirmed hop, and ask the three

entries.title: Processed, timed out, then paid twice
entries.text: Processed, timed out, then paid twice Advanced A core banking API processes a EUR 35,000 transaction. Then it times out before responding. The caller, believing it failed, re-submits a completed transaction, and the customer is debited twice. Here's how that happens: → API processes the transaction → Timeout before the response arrives → Caller retry re-submits the completed transaction → Customer debited twice The assumption was: "A timeout means it did not happen." The missing controls were idempotency keys, a smart timeout strategy, and a reconciliation layer. The fix is idempotency keys on every mutating call, a pending-state transaction model that checks state before acting, and a standing rule that on any timeout the true state is queried first, asking what actually happened to the money. On any timeout, ask what actually happened to the money. BA Takeaway Put idempotency keys on every mutating call, keep a pending-state model that checks state before acting, and make it a

entries.title: UPI debit landed. The credit never did.
entries.text: UPI debit landed. The credit never did. Advanced A UPI payment is made for Rs 45,000. The sender account is debited. The receiver is never credited, and the credit acknowledgement timed out somewhere between the two banks. Here's how that happens: → Local debit commits → Credit acknowledgement never arrives → Retry meets duplicate suppression → Message parks in an internal queue The assumption was: "A debit means the credit followed." A UPI debit committed locally while the credit acknowledgement timed out, a partial commit across two systems: the sender account debited, the receiver never credited. A retry hit duplicate-suppression logic and the message parked in a queue, leaving one system committed and the other uncertain. The mitigations are globally unique transaction references, idempotent processing at each bank, compensating transactions such as auto-reversal, and settlement-level balancing at the end of the cycle. One system committed, the other uncertain. That is a partial

entries.title: The rejected direct debit that landed in a third-party account
entries.text: The rejected direct debit that landed in a third-party account Advanced A direct debit collection of EUR 9,500 is rejected by the debtor bank. Normally it returns to the creditor bank, authorising it to debit the originator's account. This time the collection is booked to a designated third-party account instead, and the operations team is not sure the booking was ever allowed. Here's how that happens: → Collection rejected by the debtor bank → Normal path returns it to the creditor bank → Third-party account proposed instead → Preconditions checked, or skipped? The assumption was: "A reject always goes back the way it came." A debtor bank normally returns a rejected collection to the creditor bank, authorising it to debit the originator's account, but a collection can instead be booked to a designated third-party account. The third-party account is funded to meet regulatory obligations and to follow rejected payments through the general ledger, and it can be used only if the

entries.title: The consent arrived late. The 500 payments were still moving.
entries.text: The consent arrived late. The 500 payments were still moving. Advanced A set of 500 payments is being cancelled. A negative camt.029 arrives while the payment engine is still processing the set. Then a beneficiary consent arrives, after the expected timeframe, for payments that may already be on their way back. Here's how that happens: → camt.056 cancels the payment set → Negative camt.029 arrives mid-processing → Late beneficiary consent arrives → pacs.004 return follows, per payment or grouped The assumption was: "Late consent is just late." A negative camt.029 can arrive while a payment engine is still processing a set of 500 payments, and a beneficiary consent can then arrive after the expected timeframe, while the pacs.004 return that follows can be made per payment or grouped by customer, reason, value or compliance cause. The remaining payments have no universal answer: return them, complete them, or reject the late consent by accepting or overriding the rule, so each bank must

entries.title: The customer cut-off is 3:25 PM. The deadline is 4:00 PM.
entries.text: The customer cut-off is 3:25 PM. The deadline is 4:00 PM. Advanced A customer submits a EUR 70,000 payment at 3:30 PM and expects it out today. The downstream deadline is 4:00 PM. The payment misses the day, and the customer is told the cut-off was 3:25 PM, a time that appears nowhere in the product. Here's how that happens: → Downstream deadline 4:00 PM → Screening takes 20 minutes → Buffer takes 15 minutes → Customer cut-off lands at 3:25 PM The assumption was: "A cut-off is a time on the clock." A cut-off time is a calculated risk decision, not a time on the clock, and it starts from the downstream deadline, subtracting screening time, buffer, processing capacity, file size, treasury funding and expected rejections. In the worked example a 4:00 PM downstream deadline minus a 15-minute buffer minus 20 minutes of screening gives a 3:25 PM customer cut-off, with guaranteed service until 3:00 PM, best effort until 3:25 PM and next-day service after that. A cut-off is a calculated risk

entries.title: ISO 20022 ready? Eight gaps say otherwise
entries.text: ISO 20022 ready? Eight gaps say otherwise Advanced A bank is migrating to ISO 20022, and the project plan says the business is ready. The messages are mapped, the build is on track, and the go-live date is set. Then the first customer payment journey breaks, because nobody aligned the processes, the hand-offs, the training, the data quality or the control teams. Here's how that happens: → Messages mapped, build on track → Processes not aligned to customer journeys → Hand-offs unplanned, teams untrained → Systems cannot hold high data quality → Compliance, fraud and AML not aligned The assumption was: "Migration is a message format change." ISO 20022 migration is a transformation of the payments business model, not a message format change, and readiness fails where processes are not aligned to customer payment journeys, hand-offs are unplanned, business teams are untrained, systems cannot hold high data quality, and compliance, fraud and AML teams are not aligned. entries.title: The payment is visible end to end. Why not the complaint?
entries.text: The payment is visible end to end. Why not the complaint? Advanced A EUR 55,000 cross-border payment is debited, and the customer can track it end to end across linked payment systems. Then the payment goes wrong, and the customer raises a complaint. The complaint cannot travel the same way, and the hardest cross-border problem is back: nobody knows where the payment is. Here's how that happens: → Payment debited and tracked end to end → Payment goes wrong → Complaint raised, but it cannot travel on the linked rails → Nobody knows where the payment is The assumption was: "Interlinking is only a connectivity project." Interlinking connects payment systems across countries so a payment can be tracked end to end once it is debited, and the open question is whether the customer-side acceptance of payment instructions can travel the same way, and then complaints and investigations too. If instructions, status and complaints all travel on the interlinked rails, the hardest cross-border

entries.title: pacs.004 arrived. The debtor is still waiting.
entries.text: pacs.004 arrived. The debtor is still waiting. Advanced A pacs.004 arrives, and the operations team credits the debtor at once. The EUR 85,000 payment was a cover payment, a pacs.009, and the pacs.008 instruction was never rejected. The debtor has been credited for a payment that was never returned, and the original instruction is still live. Here's how that happens: → pacs.004 arrives → Team credits the debtor at once → Return relates to a rejected pacs.009 cover → pacs.008 instruction never rejected The assumption was: "A return means credit the debtor." A pacs.004 only says a payment was returned, so crediting the debtor on receipt is an event-to-action shortcut that skips the questions that matter: what the return is for, who initiated it, whether the original was a pacs.008 or a pacs.009, why it was returned, and what happened to the original payment. When the pacs.004 relates to a rejected pacs.009 cover payment, the related pacs.008 cannot be assumed rejected, since the cover

entries.title: AC06 became MS03, and nobody could say why
entries.text: AC06 became MS03, and nobody could say why Advanced A return code mapping changes: AC06 for a blocked account becomes MS03, reason not specified. It looks like a one-line change. Then the receiving bank asks why, the compliance team asks who approved it, and the payment engine cannot explain which blocked accounts produce AC06 at all. Here's how that happens: → Core banking knows the account is blocked → Business interpretation decides the code → Country rule applied → Engine sends the agreed code → Nobody can say why AC06 became MS03 The assumption was: "Mapping a return code is a one-line change." Mapping AC06 for a blocked account to MS03, reason not specified, looks like a one-line change until the BA asks how core banking communicates the condition, what the payment engine actually understands, and which conditions should produce AC06 at all. Core banking may know the account is blocked for a KYC restriction, a debit block, dormancy, or another restriction, while the engine only

entries.title: Blockchain for payments: four questions nobody has closed
entries.text: Blockchain for payments: four questions nobody has closed Advanced A EUR 40,000 payment is proposed on a shared ledger, and the room is full of confidence. Then four questions land, and nobody in the room can answer any of them. Who sees the confidential fields? Who maintains the ledger? What format does it use? And can one network really span domestic and cross-border payments? Here's how that happens: → Shared ledger proposed for payments → Confidential fields visible to every node → Formats vary by network → One network proposed for domestic and cross-border The assumption was: "Blockchain answers everything at once." Transparency means every node sees transaction detail, and control over confidential fields is still being built. A business relationship links each node with every other node, which simplifies maintenance of the shared ledger. Formats will vary with the algorithm each network uses, so one universal message and ledger format is ambitious yet not impossible. A single

entries.title: Who sends the pacs.002? It depends on the rail.
entries.text: Who sends the pacs.002? It depends on the rail. Advanced A EUR 30,000 payment is sent, and the status reply never arrives. The team waits for the beneficiary bank to answer. On this rail, the beneficiary bank was never the one who answers. Here's how that happens: → Payment sent → Status reply expected → Wrong party waited on → Reply already sent by the clearing mechanism The assumption was: "The beneficiary bank always sends the status." The sender of a status response depends on the rail the payment travelled. On a real time gross settlement system the clearing and settlement mechanism sends pacs.002, pacs.004 and camt.029 to the originator. On a cross-border payment the beneficiary bank, or instructed bank, sends them. On RTGS the clearing mechanism answers. Abroad, the beneficiary bank does. entries.title: The indirect participant the central bank never sees
entries.text: The indirect participant the central bank never sees Advanced An indirect participant sends EUR 20,000 through its direct participant. The payment moves, the direct participant's account is debited, and the central bank watches it all happen. The central bank sees the direct participant, and nobody else. Here's how that happens: → Indirect participant instructs the payment → Direct participant sends the debit → Central bank sees only the direct participant The assumption was: "The central bank watches every participant." From the central bank standpoint the risk is liquidity: whether the indirect participant can meet its financial obligations. Ensuring that funding is normally the direct participant business, since the direct participant must confirm the indirect participant holds enough before sending debit payments. The central bank sees only the direct participant, even when the payment belongs to the indirect participant, and oversees the direct participant as a whole rather than

entries.title: Cycle 00 arrived. The indirect participant got nothing.
entries.text: Cycle 00 arrived. The indirect participant got nothing. Advanced A direct participant signs up for scheme cycle 00. The cycle 00 transactions arrive, and the direct participant receives them all. The indirect participant, who never signed up, receives nothing, and its customers wait for payments that were never forwarded. Here's how that happens: → Direct participant signs up for cycle 00 → Cycle 00 transactions arrive → Indirect participant did not enrol → Nothing forwarded to the indirect participant The assumption was: "Signing up covers everyone downstream." Cycle sign-up belongs to the direct participant alone, so a direct participant enrolled for cycle 00 receives those transactions yet sends nothing to an indirect participant that did not enrol. Forwarding runs on a timetable the two agree separately, for instance once at the end of the day, and stays independent of the cycles. In classic SEPA only the direct participant exchanges files with the clearing and settlement

entries.title: Two fields in pacs.008 tell you who really paid
entries.text: Two fields in pacs.008 tell you who really paid Advanced A EUR 28,000 pacs.008 arrives, and the operations team cannot tell whether the payer was a direct participant or an indirect one. The answer is in the message, in two fields they never thought to read together. Here's how that happens: → pacs.008 arrives → Instructing agent named → Debtor agent named → Participation model revealed The assumption was: "The debtor agent is always the payer." Two agents in pacs.008 reveal the participation model behind a payment. Where the payer is a direct participant, both instructing agent and debtor agent name that direct participant. Where the payer is indirect, the instructing agent still names the direct participant while the debtor agent names the indirect participant. Two fields tell the story. Read them together. BA Takeaway Read instructing agent and debtor agent together. Direct payer: both name the direct participant. Indirect payer: the instructing agent still names the direct

entries.title: TAG 21 never leaves the MT101
entries.text: TAG 21 never leaves the MT101 Advanced A corporate customer sends an MT101 for EUR 18,000, with TAG 21 filled in for its own reporting. The MT103 that follows carries no TAG 21. The customer calls to ask where their reference went, and the operations team cannot explain why it stopped. Here's how that happens: → MT101 received with TAG 21 → MT103 generated without TAG 21 → Customer asks where the reference went The assumption was: "Every field travels forward." TAG 21 of an MT101 never maps into the MT103 that follows. It serves reporting to the ordering customer about the MT101, letting that customer reconcile the reporting automatically with the original transaction. TAG 21 stops there and never travels to the next party in the chain. TAG 21 stops there and never travels to the next party in the chain. BA Takeaway Tell the customer up front: TAG 21 is for reporting to the ordering customer, so they can reconcile the reporting with the original transaction. It never maps into the

entries.title: The cheapest rail that still arrives on time
entries.text: The cheapest rail that still arrives on time Advanced A debtor bank must send a EUR 75,000 payment, and the treasurer wants the cheapest route. The cheapest route takes three days. The beneficiary needs the money tomorrow, and the cheapest rail that arrives on time is not the cheapest rail. Here's how that happens: → Payment to send, EUR 75,000 → Cheapest route takes three days → Beneficiary needs it tomorrow → Routing rules pick the cheapest rail that arrives on time The assumption was: "Cheapest is always best." A debtor bank looks for the cheapest way to reach the beneficiary on time. When the receiver sits in the same country the payment goes through the local clearing and settlement mechanism or the local real time gross settlement system, and when the receiver sits abroad it goes through SWIFT. Routing rules set up in the payment engine apply that choice automatically, including for bulk MT101 and pain.001 files. Cheapest on time, not cheapest at any cost. BA Takeaway Write the

entries.title: E-mandates need a router. It does not have to be a CSM.
entries.text: E-mandates need a router. It does not have to be a CSM. Advanced A creditor bank needs to route e-mandate messages to debtor banks across the SEPA area. The team assumes only a clearing and settlement mechanism can do it. The mandate for EUR 2,000 a month waits while they look for a CSM to hire. Here's how that happens: → Creditor bank needs e-mandate routing → No CSM in the middle → Mandates wait for a router The assumption was: "Only a clearing system can route e-mandates." A creditor bank needs a player in between to route e-mandate messages to debtor banks, but that player does not have to be a clearing and settlement mechanism. The operating model defines two services for this: routing and validation, each delivered by a service provider, and either service can come from a debtor bank, a creditor bank or a CSM. Market players provide this kind of routing service, and a search for SEPA e-mandate providers finds more names. The operating model defines two services, routing and

entries.title: Cancelling a SEPA payment: the right message each time
entries.text: Cancelling a SEPA payment: the right message each time Advanced A customer asks to cancel a EUR 12,000 SEPA payment, and the team reaches for camt.056. The payment is a direct debit, not a credit transfer. The camt.056 goes nowhere, and the debit is collected anyway. Here's how that happens: → Customer asks to cancel a SEPA payment → Is it a credit transfer, a direct debit, or a pain.008? → Wrong message sent, payment proceeds The assumption was: "One cancellation message fits every SEPA payment." In the SEPA Credit Transfer scheme camt.056 is the message used to request cancellation of an SCT transaction. For SDD Core reversals the creditor bank sends pacs.007 against funds mistakenly debited. Corporations may also send camt.055 through their bank to cancel a pain.008: an unexecuted transaction is cancelled, while an executed one is reversed by the bank with pacs.007 instead. The message depends on the scheme and on whether the payment has executed. BA Takeaway Ask two questions

entries.title: MT103 cleared, the cover held, GBP 40,000 stuck
entries.text: MT103 cleared, the cover held, GBP 40,000 stuck Advanced GBP 40,000 left London for a supplier overseas. The customer was told the payment was sent. The supplier was never paid. Here is how that happens: → MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank → MT103 passes sanctions screening → MT202 COV held at an intermediary bank → Beneficiary bank waits for the cover → No credit is made The assumption said: "Screen the MT103. The cover follows the same path." So only the information leg was screened, and the funds leg was left to travel on trust. Why? An MT103 and its MT202 COV are screened separately, and a hit on either leg stops the payment. The intermediary held the cover for sanctions screening while the MT103 had already arrived, so the beneficiary bank had the instruction and no money to pay with. A clear MT103 is not a paid beneficiary. Screening the information leg does not clear the funds leg. BA Takeaway The MT103 is information. The cover is the money. Keep these controls separate: →

entries.title: First payment to a new bank, MT103 never left
entries.text: First payment to a new bank, MT103 never left Core EUR 25,000 was sent to a new beneficiary bank for the first time. The customer was told it was sent. Three days later, nothing had arrived. Here is how that happens: → MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank → Receiving bank system refuses the message → No RMA exists for this sender → Sender receives no credit advice → Customer waits for money that never left The assumption said: "Send the MT103. The relationship paperwork can follow." So the payment went out before anyone checked whether the receiving bank was authorised to accept it. Why? Before one bank can send an MT103 to another over SWIFT, the receiving bank must set up an RMA, a relationship management authorisation, for that sender. Without an RMA the receiving bank system will not accept the message at all. No RMA, no message. No message, no payment. An RMA is a precondition, not a formality to sort out afterwards. BA Takeaway An RMA is a precondition for the payment. Keep these

entries.title: IBAN correct, no name, EUR 12,000 in suspense
entries.text: IBAN correct, no name, EUR 12,000 in suspense Core EUR 12,000 was sent to pay a supplier invoice. The IBAN was correct. The money sat in suspense for a week. Here is how that happens: → MT103 sent with field 59 showing IBAN and address → No beneficiary name anywhere in field 59 → Beneficiary bank cannot confirm who the account belongs to → Payment held in suspense → Sender bank asked to supply the missing name The assumption said: "The IBAN is enough. The name is a nicety." So the payment carried an account number and no identity, and the receiving bank had to choose between guessing and holding. Why? Field 59 is meant to identify the beneficiary. An MT103 can arrive showing only the IBAN and address, with no name at all, and then the beneficiary bank cannot confirm that the account belongs to the person the payment was meant for. It holds the payment and asks for confirmation instead of crediting it. An account number is not an identity. A correct IBAN with no name is a payment the

entries.title: Reference cut at 16 characters, invoice never matched
entries.text: Reference cut at 16 characters, invoice never matched Core EUR 48,000 was paid against a supplier invoice. The supplier was credited in full. The supplier still chased the payment as unpaid. Here is how that happens: → MT103 sent with field 70 carrying a 24-character reference → The /RFB/ reference is cut at 16 characters → Beneficiary credited the full EUR 48,000 → Supplier reconciliation cannot match the truncated reference → Funds sit unapplied while the invoice shows overdue The assumption said: "Put the full reference in field 70. The system will carry it." So a reference longer than the field allows was sent anyway, and the part that identified the invoice never arrived. Why? Field 70 carries remittance information, and the reference that follows /RFB/ is limited to 16 characters. A longer description must continue on the following lines of the field instead of stretching the reference, and a field 70 that repeats a code or overruns the limit is not a valid instruction. Credited

entries.title: The intermediary quit the corridor, nobody told routing
entries.text: The intermediary quit the corridor, nobody told routing Core EUR 60,000 was sent to a supplier through the usual corridor. The payment was rejected downstream. The intermediary named in the instruction had stopped serving that corridor months earlier. Here is how that happens: → Payment instructed with Intermediary Agent 2 named → Routing trusts the stored intermediary data → Intermediary cannot serve the currency or the corridor → Payment rejected downstream → Repair starts, with no owner to fix the data The assumption said: "Reference data looks after itself." So nobody owned the intermediary data, nobody validated it, and the same dead bank kept being named until a rejection exposed it. Why? Reference data without an owner decays. Intermediary Agent 2 quietly points payments at a bank that no longer serves the corridor, and the failure is unreadable at first, because message mapping, routing reference data and routing logic all look equally guilty. Reference data without an owner

entries.title: Limit cut without warning, the queue filled fast
entries.text: Limit cut without warning, the queue filled fast Advanced A correspondent cut its intraday credit limit without warning. The payment engine kept feeding the same corridor. By the afternoon, payments were queuing, then rejecting, and nobody could explain why. Here is how that happens: → Correspondent cuts the intraday limit → Engine keeps sending at the old volume → Queue builds on the corridor → Payments reject with no clear reason → Operations cannot reconstruct which payments were affected The assumption said: "Routing rules are written for the quiet day." So the rules had no eligibility check, no fallback route and no audit trail, and the bad day arrived exactly as it always does, without warning. Why? A correspondent can cut an intraday credit limit without warning, and an engine that keeps feeding the same corridor will queue payments and generate rejects it cannot explain. Routing decisions must carry eligibility checks, fallback routes, a defined decision order and an audit

entries.title: Purpose code missing, EUR 90,000 held at the border
entries.text: Purpose code missing, EUR 90,000 held at the border Core EUR 90,000 was sent to settle a trade. The purpose code field was left blank. The beneficiary bank held the payment for compliance, and the trade could not settle. Here is how that happens: → Customer sends the payment without a purpose code → Payment travels the chain without it → Beneficiary bank compliance needs the code → Payment held pending the missing detail → Trade settlement waits on a blank field The assumption said: "The customer can leave it blank. Someone downstream will fill it in." So a code that was optional at the front and mandatory downstream had no owner, no enrichment source and no early validation. Why? A purpose code that is optional at the customer and mandatory downstream is a defect waiting for a payment. Enrichment needs a named owning source, and validation must happen early enough to catch a missing code before the payment reaches the system that needs it. Optional at the front is not optional

entries.title: Charges claimed by MT191, nostro debited months later
entries.text: Charges claimed by MT191, nostro debited months later Advanced A cover payment settled cleanly months ago. Then an MT191 arrived, claiming the intermediary charges. The nostro was debited, reconciliation broke, and nobody remembered the payment. Here is how that happens: → MT103 and MT202 COV settle in full → Intermediary is owed charges for its part in the chain → Intermediary claims them separately by MT191 → Nostro debited months after the payment → Reconciliation breaks on a payment everyone had closed The assumption said: "Charges are taken from the payment. There is nothing left to claim." So the team closed the books on the payment and never expected the charges leg to arrive on its own timetable. Why? Charges must never be deducted from a cover payment, so an intermediary that is owed money asks for it separately instead of taking it from the funds. The claim travels in an MT191, a request for payment of charges, and the advice travels in an MT190. A reader who sees an MT191

entries.title: CHAPS leg queued, the house completion missed its day
entries.text: CHAPS leg queued, the house completion missed its day Advanced A cross-border payment needed sterling settlement in the UK. The sterling leg went by CHAPS, for a house purchase completion that day. The completion missed its day. Here is how that happens: → MT103 arrives for the cross-border payment → Sterling leg sent to CHAPS → Payment queued for insufficient liquidity → Customer cut-off passes with the payment still queued → Settlement moves to the next working day The assumption said: "CHAPS settles the same day. Send it and the completion is safe." So the team promised the day without checking the balance behind it, and without remembering that the cross-border leg still needed its own route out of the UK. Why? CHAPS settles sterling payments between UK banks in central bank money, and a cross-border payment that needs sterling settlement in the UK can use it as the domestic leg. But CHAPS settles the same day only during business hours and only with liquidity behind the payment.

entries.title: Salary file a day late, payday moved a day
entries.text: Salary file a day late, payday moved a day Foundations The monthly salary file went to BACS a day late. Payday moved a day. No one could hurry it back. Here is how that happens: → Salary file submitted one day late → Day one for submission becomes day two → Day two for processing becomes day three → Day three for settlement becomes day four → Salaries land a day after payday The assumption said: "BACS is electronic. It can be hurried." So the file missed its submission day and the team discovered that the three-day cycle is a rule, not a suggestion. Why? BACS takes three working days: day one for submission, day two for processing, and day three for settlement. BACS is built for bulk, scheduled, low-cost payments such as salaries and supplier runs, and that is why it outlasts Faster Payments for bulk pay. Faster Payments is built for single, urgent payments, and it costs more per payment and carries limits that bulk runs do not want. BACS does not hurry. The calendar is the control. A

entries.title: Faster Payments at 2am, queued till morning
entries.text: Faster Payments at 2am, queued till morning Core A supplier payment went out at 2am by Faster Payments. It was meant to arrive in seconds. It arrived in the morning. Here is how that happens: → Payment sent at 2am by Faster Payments → Faster Payments runs around the clock → Sending bank hits its liquidity limit → Payment queues until liquidity returns → Supplier paid in the morning, not in seconds The assumption said: "Faster Payments runs around the clock, so it always arrives in seconds." So the team chose the rail for speed and never checked the liquidity behind it. Why? Faster Payments runs around the clock, but with liquidity limits. The scheme is always open, and the bank still needs the funds to settle. An urgent payment at 2am is fast only if the sending bank holds the liquidity to back it. Around the clock is the scheme. Liquidity is the bank. The rail was open all night. The money was not. BA Takeaway An urgent payment needs liquidity checked, not just the rail chosen. Keep

entries.title: Mandate silent for 36 months, the collection bounced
entries.text: Mandate silent for 36 months, the collection bounced Core A subscription collection was presented after three quiet years. It was returned. No message warned anyone it would happen. Here is how that happens: → Mandate signed, collections run for a while → Customer pauses the service, no orders for 36 months → Mandate lapses silently → New collection presented on the lapsed mandate → Collection returned, service cut off The assumption said: "The mandate is on file. It stays valid." So nobody tracked the last use of the mandate, and the first anyone knew it had expired was the return. Why? A SEPA mandate expires after 36 months with no orders related to it. Expiry triggers no message to any party. The mandate simply lapses quietly after three years without use. A mandate lapses quietly. Nobody is told. The file still held the mandate. The scheme no longer recognised it. BA Takeaway A mandate is a lifecycle. Track its last use or lose the collection. Keep these controls separate: →

entries.title: Amount changed, notice not updated, debtor disputed
entries.text: Amount changed, notice not updated, debtor disputed Core A creditor changed the collection amount for the month. The pre-notification still showed the old amount. The debtor disputed the collection, and it was returned. Here is how that happens: → Collection amount changes for the month → Pre-notification sent with the old amount → Collection presented at the new amount → Debtor sees a different amount from the notice → Debtor disputes, collection returned The assumption said: "Pre-notification is a formality. The file carries the real amount." So the notice and the file drifted apart, and the debtor was asked to pay an amount nobody had told them about. Why? Pre-notification is the notice the creditor sends the debtor before the collection, stating the amount and the date, while collection submission is a separate step. Pre-notification is not collection submission, and if the notice is not updated, the debtor can dispute the collection. The notice and the file must stay in step. The

entries.title: Warehoused Monday, listed Thursday, stopped Friday
entries.text: Warehoused Monday, listed Thursday, stopped Friday Advanced A EUR 5 million payment was accepted on Monday for Friday execution. The customer was promised Friday. On Thursday, the beneficiary was added to a sanctions list. Here is how that happens: → Payment accepted Monday for Friday execution → Payment warehoused until Friday → Sanctions list changes on Thursday → Friday revalidation checks sanctions status → Execution blocked, customer promise broken The assumption said: "Valid on Monday means valid on Friday." So the team treated warehousing as storage, and forgot that four days is enough for the world to change. Why? Warehousing turns a future-dated payment into a commitment to execute, not merely a stored instruction. Balance, account details, sanctions status and cut-off times can all move between submission and execution, so validity on Monday proves nothing about Friday. The payment must be re-validated on balance, account status, sanctions and cut-offs at execution, then

entries.title: EUR 200,000 instant, routed slow to TARGET2
entries.text: EUR 200,000 instant, routed slow to TARGET2 Advanced A customer with a EUR 300,000 limit sent EUR 200,000 instantly. It did not arrive instantly. It travelled to TARGET2 instead, slower and costlier. Here is how that happens: → Customer sends EUR 200,000 by SCT Inst → Routing rule sees an amount above EUR 100,000 → Payment routed to TARGET2 → Arrives later, at TARGET2 cost → Customer asks why the instant payment was not instant The assumption said: "The routing rule follows the scheme limit." So the rule kept enforcing a limit the scheme had already removed, and two live rules produced different outcomes for the same payment. Why? When the EU Instant Payments Regulation removed the EUR 100,000 scheme-level maximum for SCT Inst, the old routing rule that sent payments above EUR 100,000 to TARGET2 lost the scheme limit it was built on. A bank can now set its own customer limits, so a customer with a EUR 300,000 limit can send EUR 200,000 instantly while the unchanged routing rule still

entries.title: OCT Inst in 60 seconds, the conversion took longer
entries.text: OCT Inst in 60 seconds, the conversion took longer Advanced A cross-border payment was promised in 60 seconds. The euro leg cleared on time. The beneficiary was paid late, and short of the expected amount. Here is how that happens: → OCT Inst payment starts in Europe → Euro leg clears and settles in seconds → Non-euro leg conversion runs outside the euro area → Conversion is not complete before the beneficiary is due → Beneficiary paid late, for less than expected The assumption said: "Sixty seconds covers the whole payment." So the team sold the headline time and forgot that the second leg lives under different rules, different standards and different bank policies. Why? OCT Inst processes cross-border payments in 60 seconds, handling both the payment and the settlement, with both legs settled through the euro system. But the non-euro leg runs wholly outside the euro area, governed by non-euro rules, standards and bank policies, with conversion completed before the beneficiary is

entries.title: FX traded after cut-off, value date slipped a day
entries.text: FX traded after cut-off, value date slipped a day Core A supplier payment was promised with value today. It arrived with value tomorrow. The supplier charged a late fee. Here is how that happens: → Payment instruction complete and accepted → Bank collects orders until the FX cut-off → FX trade happens after the cut-off → Tenor counts from the next day, not today → Value date slips a day, late fee follows The assumption said: "The instruction is in. The value date is today." So the team promised the value date from the instruction time, and never checked the trade time. Why? An FX tenor such as Today, Tomorrow or Spot counts from the day the deal is traded, provided the trade happens before the FX cut-off time. Traded today before the cut-off, a Today tenor settles today, a Tomorrow tenor settles tomorrow, and Spot settles in two days or more. A trade after the cut-off settles a day later, because once the cut-off passes the bank is already working on the next day. The cut-off decides

entries.title: Statement 14 never arrived, the missing credit hid
entries.text: Statement 14 never arrived, the missing credit hid Core The MT940 statements arrived every day. The sequence ran 12, 13, 15. Inside the missing statement 14 sat a credit nobody noticed was gone for days. Here is how that happens: → MT940 statements arrive daily → Field 28C checked on each statement → Sequence shows 12, 13, then 15 → Statement 14 is missing, and no one asks for it → A credit inside statement 14 stays unreconciled for days The assumption said: "Reconcile the transactions. The statement numbers look after themselves." So the team reconciled what arrived and never noticed what did not arrive. Why? Field 28C carries the statement number and the sequence number, pinning down exactly which statement this is and where it sits in the run. A missing statement, or one arriving out of order, shows as a gap in the 28C sequence before any transaction is examined. That makes 28C the first completeness check on every MT940 received. A missing statement is found in the numbering, not

entries.title: Evidence a day late, EUR 4,800 lost to chargeback
entries.text: Evidence a day late, EUR 4,800 lost to chargeback Core A cardholder disputed a EUR 4,800 transaction. The merchant had delivery proof. The proof arrived a day after the scheme deadline, and the merchant bore the loss. Here is how that happens: → Cardholder disputes the transaction → Issuer raises the chargeback with the scheme → Merchant gathers delivery evidence → Evidence arrives after the scheme deadline → Loss stands against the merchant The assumption said: "Good evidence wins. The deadline is flexible." So the merchant built the perfect case and missed the only date that decided it. Why? A chargeback starts when a cardholder disputes a transaction and the issuer raises it with the scheme, and the acquirer and merchant respond with representment evidence while the scheme applies its timelines and reason codes. The financial impact moves between issuer, acquirer and merchant as the case progresses, so knowing the reason code matters: it decides what evidence is needed and who

entries.title: File retried after timeout, three on-us paid twice
entries.text: File retried after timeout, three on-us paid twice Core A corporate submitted a pain.001 file with ten payments. The file timed out with no confirmation. The file was re-sent whole, and three payments were paid twice. Here is how that happens: → pain.001 submitted with ten payments → Seven become pacs.008 to the next bank → Three are on-us, posted internally at once → Timeout, no confirmation received → Whole file re-sent, three on-us payments posted again The assumption said: "No confirmation means nothing happened. Re-send the file." So the retry treated an unknown as a failure, and the payments that never become pacs.008 were paid a second time. Why? A pain.001 file promises a batch of payments, yet not every payment in the file becomes a pacs.008. When a corporate submits ten payments and only seven pacs.008 messages reach the next bank, the other three are on-us payments, where sender and beneficiary hold accounts with the same bank and the payment is handled internally. Counting

entries.title: EUR 50,000 sent serial, but the chain had no account to settle through
entries.text: EUR 50,000 sent serial, but the chain had no account to settle through Foundations A supplier invoice for EUR 50,000 was due on Friday. The payment team sent it serial, straight down the chain, and marked the job done. On Monday the supplier had still not been paid. The money was sitting with an intermediary bank, going nowhere. Here is what happened: → MT103 sent serial to the first intermediary → Intermediary deducts its charge and passes it on → Next bank has no account relationship with the beneficiary bank → MT103 returned, funds parked, supplier unpaid The requirement said: "Send every MT103 serial unless told otherwise." So nobody checked whether the route could actually settle. Why? A serial payment only works where each bank in the chain holds an account with the next bank. The sending bank held no account with the beneficiary bank, so the correct route was a cover payment: an MT103 sent direct to the beneficiary bank, and an MT202 COV settling the funds through the

entries.title: USD 40,000 cover booked as the bank's own money, supplier never paid
entries.text: USD 40,000 cover booked as the bank's own money, supplier never paid Core A customer paid USD 40,000 to an overseas supplier. The supplier's bank confirmed it had received funds. The supplier was never credited. The money had landed in the beneficiary bank's own account, booked as the bank's own funds. Here is what happened: → MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank with the customer instruction → MT202 COV sent to the funding bank to settle the funds → Beneficiary bank reads the cover as a plain bank-to-bank transfer → Cover booked as proprietary funds, MT103 left unmatched → Supplier unpaid, nobody can see why The requirement said: "An MT202 is an MT202. Book it as bank funds." So the cover was processed without ever looking for its MT103. Why? An MT202 COV exists to settle one specific MT103. It carries the reference that binds the two messages together. A plain MT202 is a bank's own transfer, moving proprietary funds with no customer payment behind it. Both move money between banks,

entries.title: USD 25,000 "sent" on Monday, beneficiary paid on Thursday
entries.text: USD 25,000 "sent" on Monday, beneficiary paid on Thursday Foundations A customer sent USD 25,000 to pay an invoice and was told the payment had gone. Three days later the beneficiary called to say nothing had arrived. The payment had gone. The money had not. Here is what happened: → MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank → MT202 COV still travelling through the cover chain → Beneficiary bank holds the instruction and waits → Customer told "payment sent" on the MT103 date → Beneficiary unpaid until the cover settles The requirement said: "Confirm the payment as sent when the MT103 leaves." So the customer was told the job was done while the funds were still in transit. Why? In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV travel separately, so the MT103 can reach the beneficiary bank before the funds leg arrives. The beneficiary bank must hold the instruction and wait for the cover, because it cannot credit the beneficiary until the funds have settled. This timing gap is a normal feature of

entries.title: EUR 30,000 announced, EUR 29,965 arrived, nobody got paid
entries.text: EUR 30,000 announced, EUR 29,965 arrived, nobody got paid Core An MT103 announced EUR 30,000. The MT202 COV that arrived to settle it carried EUR 29,965. The beneficiary bank credited nobody and raised an exception. EUR 35 was missing, and the whole payment stopped. Here is what happened: → MT103 sent announcing EUR 30,000 → MT202 COV arrives for EUR 29,965 → Reference matches, amount does not → Sequence B of the cover does not mirror the MT103 → Beneficiary bank holds both legs and investigates The requirement said: "Match on the reference. Small amount differences can be adjusted later." So a EUR 35 gap was treated as a rounding problem instead of a broken link. Why? In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV must agree on amount and on the references that link them. A mismatch is not a minor data error. It is a break in the link between the information leg and the funds leg, and the bank must investigate before it credits the beneficiary. Sequence B of the cover must mirror the

entries.title: USD 10,000 cover arrived USD 35 short, and the payment stopped for two weeks
entries.text: USD 10,000 cover arrived USD 35 short, and the payment stopped for two weeks Core A cover payment of USD 10,000 was announced. The cover that arrived was USD 9,965. The beneficiary bank refused to credit the full amount, and the USD 35 gap turned into a two-week dispute. An intermediary had taken its charge straight out of the cover. Here is what happened: → MT103 announces USD 10,000 → MT202 COV sent for USD 10,000 → Intermediary deducts USD 35 from the cover → Cover arrives at USD 9,965 → Beneficiary bank holds the payment as an exception The requirement said: "Intermediaries may deduct their charges from the funds they handle." So the intermediary treated the cover like a serial payment and helped itself. Why? It is forbidden to take charges from an MT202 COV. The cover amount must never be lower than the amount announced in the MT103. If an intermediary needs to be paid for its part in the chain, it asks the sending bank to pay through an MT191, or debits the account directly

entries.title: EUR 5,000 salary sent, EUR 4,940 received, and nobody made an error
entries.text: EUR 5,000 salary sent, EUR 4,940 received, and nobody made an error Foundations A company paid an overseas employee EUR 5,000 in salary by MT103. The employee received EUR 4,940 and asked where the missing EUR 60 had gone. Nobody had made an error. The payment had simply passed through two intermediary banks. Here is what happened: → MT103 sent for EUR 5,000 → First intermediary deducts EUR 35 → Second intermediary deducts EUR 25 → Beneficiary bank credits EUR 4,940 → Employee asks why the salary is short The requirement said: "The amount sent is the amount the beneficiary receives." So nobody warned the employee, and nobody priced the route. Why? In a serial payment the ordering customer bears the charges, and each intermediary bank deducts its own charge from the amount as the payment passes through. The beneficiary therefore receives the amount minus the charges deducted at each step. The shortfall is the charge, not an error, and it is why the charge-bearer matters before the

entries.title: 71A said BEN, the copy said SHA, and the sender paid charges it never agreed to
entries.text: 71A said BEN, the copy said SHA, and the sender paid charges it never agreed to Advanced A sender instructed a payment of GBP 20,000 with field 71A set to BEN, so the beneficiary would bear every charge. The beneficiary was credited almost in full, and the sender was billed for charges it never agreed to pay. Somewhere in the chain, a bank copy showed SHA where the sender had instructed BEN. Here is what happened: → MT103 generated with 71A BEN → A downstream bank copy shows 71A SHA → Charges split between sender and beneficiary instead of falling on the beneficiary → Sender billed for charges it never agreed to bear → Reconciliation breaks, nobody can agree who owes what The requirement said: "Copy the charge code from the previous bank's message." So the code was retyped at every step instead of carried forward. Why? Field 71A is set by the bank that generates the MT103 and cannot be changed by later banks. Later banks can only add a field 71F when they take a charge. A bank copy

entries.title: USD 75,000 passed screening, but only on the leg that was checked
entries.text: USD 75,000 passed screening, but only on the leg that was checked Advanced A payment of USD 75,000 to an overseas supplier passed sanctions screening and was released. The supplier was never paid. The funds were sitting in a hold at an intermediary bank. Only one leg of the payment had been screened. Here is what happened: → MT103 screened, no hit, released → MT202 COV sent through the correspondent chain → Cover leg hits a sanctions list at an intermediary → Cover held for screening, MT103 left waiting → Originator believes the payment cleared screening The requirement said: "Screen the MT103 before release. The cover follows the same instruction." So the funds leg travelled unscreened until an intermediary stopped it. Why? An MT103 and its MT202 COV are both subject to sanction screening, and the screening must happen before the payment is credited to the beneficiary. The information leg and the funds leg are screened separately, and a hit on either leg stops the payment. A bank

entries.title: EUR 8,000 recalled the same day, but the beneficiary had already spent it
entries.text: EUR 8,000 recalled the same day, but the beneficiary had already spent it Core A customer sent EUR 8,000 to the wrong beneficiary by mistake. The recall went out the same day. The beneficiary had already spent the money. The bank sent the recall, received a polite answer, and the funds never came back. Here is what happened: → pacs.008 sent, EUR 8,000 credited to the wrong beneficiary → Beneficiary spends the funds the next day → camt.056 recall sent to the beneficiary bank → Beneficiary bank asks its customer whether it agrees → Customer refuses, no pacs.004 returns The requirement said: "If a payment went to the wrong person, recall it and the money comes back." So the customer was promised a reversal that no message can deliver. Why? A camt.056 can still be sent to ask the beneficiary bank to return the money, but the beneficiary bank must ask its customer whether it agrees. If the funds are no longer there, the recall cannot be completed by message alone, and the customer must

entries.title: USD 15,000 returned for a bad account, and the refund took the long way home
entries.text: USD 15,000 returned for a bad account, and the refund took the long way home Core A payment of USD 15,000 was returned because the beneficiary account did not exist. The customer waited a week, then asked where the refund was. The return was still travelling. It had to pass through every bank that carried the payment forward. Here is what happened: → pacs.008 sent for USD 15,000 → Beneficiary bank cannot apply it, account does not exist → pacs.004 sent back to the intermediary → Intermediary forwards a new pacs.004 to the originator bank → Originator bank credits the customer, minus charges already deducted The requirement said: "When a payment is returned, credit the customer the full amount straight away." So the customer was promised USD 15,000 while the return was still two banks away. Why? When a beneficiary bank returns a payment with a pacs.004, the intermediary that received it sends a new pacs.004 back to the originator bank, so the return travels the chain in reverse. The

entries.title: Returned five times in six weeks, the code was in the message but not in field 57A
entries.text: Returned five times in six weeks, the code was in the message but not in field 57A Core A payment to Australia was returned five times over six weeks. Each time the note said the same thing: the beneficiary bank's SWIFT code had to appear in field 57A. The code was in the message. It was in the wrong field. Here is what happened: → MT103 sent with the beneficiary bank code in field 72 → Returned, code must be in field 57A → Resent with the code in field 52A → Returned again, code must be in field 57A → Resent three more times, returned every time The requirement said: "Put the beneficiary bank code somewhere the receiving bank can see it." So the team moved the code around the message instead of putting it where the receiving bank reads it. Why? Field 57A is the field the receiving bank reads to find the account with institution. A code placed in field 72 or in field 52A can be seen by the receiving bank, but that does not satisfy the validation. The beneficiary bank had also been

entries.title: EUR 18,000 to a new bank, rejected before it was even read
entries.text: EUR 18,000 to a new bank, rejected before it was even read Foundations A company made its first ever payment to a new beneficiary bank: EUR 18,000 for an urgent order. The MT103 was rejected before it was even read. Nobody had asked the beneficiary bank to accept messages from the sending bank. Here is what happened: → New beneficiary bank identified, payment prepared → MT103 sent over SWIFT → Receiving bank system refuses the message → Payment never arrives, order delayed → Team resends the same MT103, rejected again The requirement said: "If we have the BIC, we can send the payment." So the payment was built, approved and sent with no check that the receiving bank would accept it. Why? Before one bank can send an MT103 to another over SWIFT, the receiving bank must set up an RMA, a relationship management authorisation, for that sender. Without an RMA the receiving bank's system will not accept the message. The RMA is therefore a precondition for the payment, not a formality that

entries.title: USD 60,000 paid in full, but the bank could not prove it was the same payment
entries.text: USD 60,000 paid in full, but the bank could not prove it was the same payment Advanced A payment of USD 60,000 passed through a correspondent bank on its way to the beneficiary. The beneficiary was paid. The originator bank could not prove it. Its reconciliation broke, because the thread linking the two legs had been cut. Here is what happened: → pacs.008 sent with a UETR in field 121 → Correspondent bank receives the incoming leg → Correspondent sends the outgoing leg onward → Field 121 changed on the outgoing leg → Originator cannot match the payment it sent with the payment that arrived The requirement said: "Each bank may set its own reference on the leg it sends." So the correspondent replaced the reference instead of carrying it forward. Why? When a payment passes through a correspondent bank, that bank sees two payments: the incoming payment from the sender and the outgoing payment to the next bank. The two legs are linked by the unique end-to-end transaction reference, the

entries.title: Nine days for a payment promised in three, the bank had not bought the currency yet
entries.text: Nine days for a payment promised in three, the bank had not bought the currency yet Core A customer sent a payment in a less common currency and was told it would arrive in two to three days. Nine days later it still had not arrived, and the customer assumed the money was lost. The money was not lost. The bank had not bought the currency yet. Here is what happened: → Payment instructed in a less common local currency → Bank collects orders until its cut-off time → Bank checks its nostro balances before buying → Currency bought late, payment released days after instruction → Customer told the standard timeline, not the real one The requirement said: "Tell every customer the payment takes 48 to 72 hours." So a payment that needed a currency the bank did not hold was promised the timeline of a major currency. Why? A bank does not buy the currency of every payment the moment it is instructed, because it does not know in advance how much foreign currency it will need. It collects orders

entries.title: USD 30,000 to a dollar account arrived USD 300 short after two conversions
entries.text: USD 30,000 to a dollar account arrived USD 300 short after two conversions Advanced A customer sent USD 30,000 to a supplier's US dollar account. The supplier received USD 29,700 and sent the invoice back unpaid. USD 300 had vanished in two currency conversions that should never have happened. Here is what happened: → MT103 sent in USD to a USD account → Intermediary converts USD to EUR → Next bank converts EUR back to USD → Beneficiary credited USD 29,700 → Supplier treats the invoice as unpaid The requirement said: "Each bank may settle in whatever currency suits its own books." So intermediaries converted the payment twice and charged for both conversions. Why? The sender decides the currency of a transaction, and no intermediary may change it on the way. If the beneficiary's account is in a different currency, the conversion happens as a separate foreign exchange step, and the beneficiary is credited in the currency of the account. In this lab you act as the business analyst who turns that business problem into a clear, testable set of requirements. You will define the objectives and the scope, identify the stakeholders, record the assumptions and dependencies, and write the business rules that govern cutoffs, charges and value dates. entries.title: Redesign the Payment Exception Repair Process
entries.text: Redesign the Payment Exception Repair Process Process modelling When a payment cannot be processed straight through, it lands in an exception queue where operations staff must repair it, return it or reject it. In many banks that queue is slow, opaque and full of rework, because nobody has mapped the process end to end. In this lab you model the as-is exception repair process, measure where time is lost, and design a to-be process that clears most exceptions on first touch. You will draw a BPMN diagram with clear swimlanes, add sequence diagrams for the system interactions, and model the exception flows for the most common failure types. You will also define the controls, the handoffs and the service levels for each step. By the end of the lab you will have a process design that operations can run, technology can build, and management can measure. In this lab you analyse and specify a payment initiation API from the business need down to the contract. You will define the endpoints, the HTTP methods, the request and response schemas, the authentication model, the error codes, and the rules for idempotency, correlation IDs, timeouts and retries. entries.title: What is a payment?
entries.text: A payment is the transfer of value from one party to another in order to settle an obligation. When you buy a coffee, pay rent, send a salary, or settle a supplier invoice, you are making a payment. The obligation can come from a purchase, a loan, a tax, a salary agreement, or any commitment where one party owes value to another. The payment discharges that obligation, fully or partly, and creates a record that the debt has been reduced or cleared. In a modern banking context, a payment almost always involves accounts held with regulated institutions and a set of instructions that tell those institutions what to move, from whom, to whom, and for what reason. The instructions travel as a payment message, while the actual value moves through accounts and settlement systems. A payment can be

entries.title: What is a payment rail?
entries.text: A payment rail is the infrastructure that carries a payment from one party to another. Think of it like a railway track. The train is the payment instruction, and the rail is the set of systems, rules, and connections that let the train reach its destination safely. A rail includes the network that moves the message, the clearing system that exchanges instructions between banks, the settlement system that moves value between banks, and the scheme rules that define cut off times, value dates, and liability when something goes wrong. Common examples help make this concrete. In India, UPI, IMPS, NEFT, and RTGS are different rails with different speeds, limits, and settlement models. entries.title: What is the difference between a payment instruction and settlement? Why does the distinction matter in system design?
entries.text: The payment instruction is the **pacs.008** or the **pain.001** that tells the bank to move money. Settlement is the actual movement of funds between banks that discharges the obligation. They are different events and they can happen at different times. When a customer submits a payment, the hub creates a pacs.008 and sends it through the clearing system. The clearing system processes it and returns a **pacs.002** with a status. When the status is ACSC, settlement has happened. Until then, the payment is only an instruction. The gap matters because a payment can be instructed but not settled, for example if the clearing house rejects it, or if the settlement account has insufficient funds. The bank must track both states separately. The **instruction status** tells the customer what

entries.title: What is the difference between a branch, a subsidiary and an entity in payment routing?
entries.text: These three words describe different legal structures, and they change how a payment moves. A branch is part of the same legal entity as the head office. A London bank with a branch in Singapore is one legal entity, so money moving between London and Singapore is an internal transfer, not a payment between two banks. A subsidiary is a separate legal entity owned by the parent bank. A UK bank with a subsidiary in India is two legal entities, so a payment between them is a real payment that must go through proper channels and be recorded as an intercompany transaction. An entity is the general word for a legal unit of the bank, and a large bank can have hundreds of entities across different countries. entries.title: What is a payment factory model and why do large banks use it?
entries.text: A payment factory is a model where a large bank centralises all payment processing into one shared service instead of letting each business unit run its own payments. In a bank like JP Morgan, the corporate banking team, the retail team and the private banking team all send their payment instructions to the same factory. The factory handles validation, routing, clearing and exceptions the same way for everyone. The benefit is scale and consistency. One team maintains the payment logic, one set of controls applies to all payments, and a change to a regulation is made once, not in five different systems. The factory also gives the bank a single view of all payment volumes, which helps treasury manage liquidity and helps risk manage exposure. The challenge is that different business units

entries.title: How does a bank join a clearing system as a direct participant versus using an indirect clearer? What changes operationally?
entries.text: A **direct participant** connects to the clearing system itself, holds a **settlement account** at the central bank, and settles its own payments. The bank must meet the clearing system's technical, financial, and operational requirements, hold enough collateral, and staff an operations team that can manage the connection, the queue, and the settlement account through the day. The bank has full control over its payments, its cut-off management, and its liquidity. An **indirect participant** uses a direct participant, called a clearer, to settle on its behalf. The bank sends its payments to the clearer, and the clearer settles them through its own central bank account. entries.title: What is straight-through processing and what breaks it?
entries.text: Straight-through processing, or STP, means a payment goes from instruction to settlement without any human touching it. The instruction arrives, the system validates it, routes it, sends it to clearing and confirms settlement, all automatically. STP is the goal for large banks because it is fast, cheap and consistent. A bank like Standard Chartered aims for a high STP rate, often above 95 percent for standard payments. What breaks STP is anything that needs a human decision. A missing field, for example a beneficiary name that does not match the account, stops the payment. A sanctions hit stops it. A payment above a limit needs manual approval. A payment with an unusual pattern triggers a fraud review. A repair queue is where these payments sit until someone fixes them. The BA's job is to

entries.title: What is straight through processing, and how do you design a payment system to maximise it? What is a realistic STP rate?
entries.text: Straight through processing means a payment goes from initiation to settlement without any manual touch. To design for it, you need four things. First, **complete data at initiation**. The channel must capture every mandatory field before the payment is accepted, so nothing is missing downstream. Second, **automated validation**. The hub checks the account, the balance, the sanctions lists and the message format without human help. Third, **clean routing rules**. The hub decides the clearing system, the settlement method and the charge option from static data, not from someone reading the payment. Fourth, **automated exception handling** for the common failures. If a payment is rejected for a missing field, the hub sends a clear message back to the channel instead of dropping it in a

entries.title: Walk me through a clean domestic credit transfer end to end, from the customer submitting the instruction to the beneficiary being credited. What does each stage look like when nothing goes wrong?
entries.text: A clean domestic credit transfer has five stages, and in a good flow none of them needs a human hand. First the customer submits the instruction, usually from a mobile app or corporate channel, as a **pain.001** message. The bank validates it immediately, checking the account, the balance, the beneficiary details, and the sanctions lists, and answers with a **pain.002** acceptance. Second, the payment engine builds the interbank message, a **pacs.008** for a credit transfer, and routes it to the domestic clearing system. Third, the clearing system settles it, moving funds between the banks through their settlement accounts. Fourth, the beneficiary bank receives the **pacs.008**, credits the customer account, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, which means settlement complete.

entries.title: Explain straight through processing. How does a payment go from instruction to settlement with no manual touch, and what tells you the STP rate is healthy?
entries.text: Straight through processing means a payment flows from initiation to settlement with no manual intervention. The customer submits the instruction through a channel, and the payment hub validates it automatically. The validation checks the account number format, the balance, the beneficiary details, and the sanctions lists, all in milliseconds.
